structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC Form 10-K for JPMorgan Chase & Co. for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022; Commission file number 1-5805; incorporated in Delaware (EIN 13-2624428); principal office at 383 Madison Avenue, New York, NY 10179; phone (212) 270-6000.
- Securities registered on exchanges include common stock (JPM, NYSE), multiple preferred depositary share series, Alerian MLP Index ETNs (AMJ, NYSE Arca), and a guarantee of callable fixed-rate notes (JPM/32, NYSE); no Section 12(g) securities.
- Compliance and filer status disclosures: timely filing of required reports and interactive data; large accelerated filer; auditor attestation on internal control over financial reporting; not a shell company.
- Market data: aggregate market value of common stock held by non-affiliates as of June 30, 2022 was approximately $327.6 billion; 2,943,355,459 common shares outstanding as of January 31, 2023.
- Documents incorporated by reference: portions of the 2023 Proxy Statement (Items 10–14 of Part III).
- Form 10-K index highlights:
  - Part I: Item 1 Business (overview, business segments, competition, human capital, supervision and regulation) and detailed statistical disclosures (assets/liabilities distribution, interest rates/differentials, ROE/ROA, investment securities, loans, allowance for credit losses, deposits); Item 1A Risk Factors; Items 1B–4 (unresolved staff comments, properties, legal proceedings, mine safety).
  - Part II: market for equity, MD&A, market risk disclosures, financial statements, controls and procedures, and other required items (Items 5–9C).
  - Part III: directors and governance, executive compensation, ownership, related-party transactions, auditor fees.
  - Part IV: exhibits and financial statement schedules.
- Business overview: JPMorgan Chase is a leading U.S.-based global financial services firm with $3.7 trillion in assets and $292.3 billion in stockholders’ equity at December 31, 2022; a leader in investment banking, consumer and small business banking, commercial banking, financial transaction processing, and asset management, serving U.S. consumers and global corporate, institutional, and government clients under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands.
- Principal subsidiaries and footprint: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (U.S. branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C.); J.P. Morgan Securities LLC (U.S. broker-dealer); key non-U.S. operating subsidiaries include J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.) and J.P. Morgan SE (Germany), both subsidiaries of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
- Website and governance disclosures: SEC filings available free on the Firm’s website; Investor Relations site hosts new and material information; adoption and availability of a firmwide Code of Conduct and a Code of Ethics for senior financial and finance-related professionals, with commitments to post amendments or waivers.
- Business segments: four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment; additional details referenced in MD&A and Note 32.
- Competition: operates in highly competitive markets against banks and a wide range of nonbank financial and technology firms; competes on product quality and breadth, execution, innovation, reputation, and price; competition varies by client type, industry, product, and geography; faces ongoing competitive pressure from digital and non-financial entrants that can disintermediate traditional banking services.

nodes.title: Human capital
nodes.heading: 1.4 Human capital
nodes.start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase believes that its long-term growth and success depend on its ability to attract, develop and retain a high-
performing and diverse workforce, with inclusion and accessibility as key components of the way the Firm does business.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Human capital, emphasizing the importance of attracting, developing, and retaining a high-performing, diverse, inclusive, and accessible workforce; data excludes contractors.
- Workforce size and growth: 293,723 employees as of December 31, 2022, up 22,698 year-over-year, driven primarily by hiring in technology, operations, and front office; employees span 63 countries with over 60% in the U.S.
- Geographic distribution: North America 178,599; Asia-Pacific 82,696; Europe/Middle East/Africa 27,514; Latin America/Caribbean 4,914.
- Business/Corporate distribution: Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) 135,347; Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB) 73,452; Commercial Banking (CB) 14,687; Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) 26,041; Corporate 44,196.
- Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI): Self-identification data presented for race/ethnicity (U.S., EEO categories), gender (global), LGBTQ+, veteran, and disability (U.S.); also reported for the Operating Committee and Board of Directors where applicable.
- Key DEI metrics (as of December 31, 2022):
  - Race/ethnicity (U.S. employees who self-identified): White 44%; Hispanic 21%; Asian 18%; Black 14%; Other 3%. Senior level: White 75%; Hispanic 6%; Asian 12%; Black 5%; Other 2%. Operating Committee: White 83%; Hispanic 11%; Asian 6%. Board: White 91%; Black 9%.
  - Gender (global employees who self-identified): Men 51%, Women 49%. Senior level: Men 73%, Women 27%. Operating Committee: Men 61%, Women 39%. Board: Men 64%, Women 36%.
  - LGBTQ+ (U.S.): 4% of employees; 3% senior level; 6% Operating Committee.
  - Military veterans (U.S.): 3% of employees; 2% senior level; 9% of Board.
  - People with disabilities (U.S.): 4% of employees; 3% senior level; disability status not requested for Board.
- Definitions and methodology: Senior level defined as Managing Director and above; percentages reflect only those who self-identified (race/ethnicity: 96% of U.S. employees, 95% of U.S. senior; gender: 98% global employees, 99% global senior). LGBTQ+, veteran, and disability percentages are for U.S. employees and applicable leadership groups. Operating Committee includes one member outside the U.S. Board data excludes a director elected in March 2023.

nodes.title: Firm culture
nodes.heading: 1.4.3 Firm culture
nodes.start_phrase:
The foundations of JPMorgan Chase’s culture are its core 
values and How We Do Business Principles, which are 
fundamental to the Firm’s success and are represented by 
four central corporate tenets: exceptional client service; 
operational excellence; a commitment to integrity, fairness 
and responsibility; and cultivation of a great team and 
winning culture.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasizes JPMorgan Chase’s firm culture grounded in core values and “How We Do Business” principles, centered on exceptional client service, operational excellence, integrity/fairness/responsibility, and a great team/winning culture.
- Reinforces an inclusive, respectful workplace through the Code of Conduct, awareness, education, communication, and training, supported by Business Resource Groups and global Diversity, Equity & Inclusion (DEI) centers of excellence focused on increasing equity and strengthening inclusion.
- Aims to attract and retain talent across all roles and career stages, offering internships through executive opportunities; in 2022, roughly two-thirds of roles were filled externally, with the rest internal, and hybrid work models used where appropriate.
- Prioritizes diverse hiring, with initiatives for gender diversity, underrepresented ethnic groups, LGBTQ+ individuals, people with disabilities, veterans, and others; DEI centers drive representation and advancement via coaching and mentorship; offers a returnship fellowship and, where appropriate, skills-based hiring over degree requirements.
- Supports employee development with required onboarding on the Code of Conduct, policies, and cybersecurity, plus extensive training in leadership, change management, analytical thinking, culture and conduct, DEI, and risk and controls; “Leadership Edge” builds a unified leadership culture.
- Maintains market-competitive compensation guided by pay-for-performance, alignment with shareholder interests, and reinforcement of culture and conduct, with processes to promote equitable and competitive pay.
- Provides comprehensive benefits and wellness programs, including healthcare, retirement, insurance, wellness centers, mental health resources, employee assistance, generous leave, backup child care, tuition reimbursement, and financial coaching; in 2022, enhanced U.S. medical coverage and paid time off for parental, caregiving, and bereavement needs.

- Attracting and retaining employees: Recruitment spans all roles and levels, with about two-thirds of 2022 hires external and the remainder internal; hybrid work models used where appropriate. Strong focus on diversity hiring (gender, underrepresented ethnic groups, LGBTQ+, people with disabilities, veterans), DEI-led coaching and mentorship to advance representation, a return-to-work fellowship program, and skills-based hiring practices.
- Developing employees: Required onboarding covers the Code of Conduct, policies, and cybersecurity. Ongoing training includes leadership, change management, analytical thinking, culture and conduct, DEI, and risk/controls. Leadership Edge fosters a unified leadership culture firmwide.
- Compensation and benefits: Market-competitive, pay-for-performance approach aligned with shareholder interests and risk/control considerations; equitable pay reviews. Comprehensive benefits include healthcare, retirement, life/disability insurance, wellness centers, mental health resources, EAP, generous leave policies, backup childcare, tuition reimbursement, and financial coaching. In 2022, U.S. health and wellness benefits were enhanced, including expanded medical coverage and paid leave for parental, caregiving, and bereavement.

nodes.title: Supervision and regulation
nodes.heading: 1.5 Supervision and regulation
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm is subject to extensive and comprehensive 
regulation under U.S. federal and state laws, as well as the 
applicable laws of the jurisdictions outside the U.S. in which 
the Firm does business.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: The document outlines the extensive U.S. and international regulatory framework governing JPMorgan Chase, emphasizing consolidated and entity-level oversight.
- Consolidated supervision: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a bank holding company and financial holding company subject to comprehensive, consolidated supervision by the Federal Reserve, with certain subsidiaries overseen by additional functional regulators.
- Bank-level regulation: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is supervised by the OCC and, for certain matters, the FDIC.
- Securities and derivatives regulation: U.S. broker-dealers are regulated by the SEC and FINRA; futures and swaps activities are overseen by the CFTC.
- Non-U.S. entities: J.P. Morgan Securities plc is regulated by the U.K. PRA and FCA; JPMSE (Germany) is regulated by the ECB and local authorities; other non-U.S. subsidiaries are subject to applicable local banking, securities, prudential, and conduct regulators.
- Permissible activities: The Bank Holding Company Act limits BHC activities; FHCs may engage in broader financial activities. The Federal Reserve can restrict activities, impose corrective measures, or require divestitures if eligibility standards are not met. Unsatisfactory CRA ratings restrict expansion into new FHC activities and acquisitions.
- Capital and liquidity: The Federal Reserve establishes Basel III–aligned capital, liquidity, and leverage requirements for the Firm; the OCC sets similar requirements for the bank. Non-U.S. units must meet local capital and liquidity standards. Global regulators are refining Basel III, and U.S. regulators are considering U.S. implementation of those reforms.
- Stress testing (CCAR): As a large BHC, the Firm is subject to Federal Reserve supervisory stress tests and must run annual company-run tests with an accompanying capital plan. The Fed’s severely adverse scenario determines the Firm’s Stress Capital Buffer. 2023 timeline: CCAR submission due April 5; indicative SCB by June 30; final SCB by August 31; effective October 1. The OCC requires similar annual stress tests for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. The Firm publishes annual stress test results.
- Enhanced prudential standards: As a SIFI, the Firm is subject to heightened prudential standards recommended by FSOC and implemented by the Federal Reserve, including enhanced risk management, corporate governance, liquidity, and related reporting requirements.

nodes.title: Financial holding company
nodes.heading: 1.5.1 Financial holding company
nodes.start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a bank 
holding company (“BHC”) and a financial holding company 
(“FHC”) under U.S. federal law, and is subject to 
comprehensive consolidated supervision, regulation and 
examination by the Board of Governors of the Federal 
Reserve System (the “Federal Reserve”).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of extensive U.S. and non-U.S. supervision and regulation of the Firm.
- Status as a bank holding company and financial holding company under U.S. law, with consolidated supervision by the Federal Reserve; additional oversight of subsidiaries by the OCC, FDIC, SEC, FINRA, CFTC, the U.K. PRA/FCA (for J.P. Morgan Securities plc), the ECB and local European regulators (for JPMSE), and other foreign authorities.
- Permissible activities: BHCs limited to banking and closely related activities; FHCs allowed broader financial activities. The Federal Reserve can restrict activities, impose corrective measures, or require divestitures if eligibility or CRA standards are not met.
- Capital, liquidity, and leverage requirements aligned with Basel III set by the Federal Reserve for the Firm and the OCC for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; non-U.S. entities subject to local regimes. Ongoing global refinements to Basel III and U.S. consideration of implementing reforms.
- Stress testing under the Federal Reserve’s CCAR: annual company-run tests, capital plan submissions, and determination of the Stress Capital Buffer based on supervisory “severely adverse” scenarios; 2023 timeline for CCAR filing and SCB notifications/effective date. OCC requires similar annual tests at the bank level; the Firm publishes results.
- Enhanced prudential standards for SIFIs: FSOC recommendations implemented by Federal Reserve rules covering risk management, corporate governance, and strengthened liquidity and risk standards.

nodes.title: Consolidated supervision
nodes.heading: 1.5.1.1 Consolidated supervision
nodes.start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a bank 
holding company (“BHC”) and a financial holding company 
(“FHC”) under U.S. federal law, and is subject to 
comprehensive consolidated supervision, regulation and 
examination by the Board of Governors of the Federal 
Reserve System (the “Federal Reserve”).
nodes.summary:
- Broad regulatory oversight: JPMorgan Chase operates under extensive U.S. federal and state regulations and the laws of non-U.S. jurisdictions where it does business.
- Consolidated supervision: As a bank holding company (BHC) and financial holding company (FHC), the Firm is subject to comprehensive consolidated supervision by the Federal Reserve; various subsidiaries are also directly regulated based on their specific activities and licenses.
- Key regulators by entity/activity: OCC and, for certain matters, FDIC for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; SEC and FINRA for U.S. broker-dealers; CFTC for futures and swaps activities; PRA and FCA for J.P.   - Certain non-U.S. subsidiaries and branches subject to local recovery and resolution regimes.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA) framework:
  - Potential FDIC-led resolution of the holding company upon systemic risk determinations by U.S. authorities.
  - FDIC’s “single point of entry” strategy aims to keep operating subsidiaries open while imposing losses on holding company shareholders and creditors.
  - Absent OLA, resolution proceeds under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code.
- “Source of strength” obligations requiring the holding company to support its insured depository subsidiaries.
- Acquisition regulations and limitations:
  - Federal Reserve approval for acquiring over 5% of an unaffiliated bank’s voting shares.
  - Prohibition on acquisitions that would cause a firm’s total liabilities to exceed 10% of aggregate liabilities of all financial companies.
  - Prior written notice to the Federal Reserve for certain acquisitions of companies (over $10 billion in assets) engaged in financial activities.
  - The Federal Reserve may restrict otherwise permissible FHC activities/acquisitions if eligibility standards are not met.
- Ongoing obligations under a September 29, 2020 Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the DOJ related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries markets and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank governance and supervisory framework:
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s activities limited by the National Bank Act and OCC interpretations.
  - OCC enforcement authority for unsafe or unsound practices, including potential activity limits or corrective requirements.
- FDIC deposit insurance assessments supporting insured deposits.
- FDIC powers in bank insolvency, including appointment as conservator/receiver and broad authority to transfer assets and liabilities.
- Prompt Corrective Action under FDICIA:
  - Mandatory remediation for undercapitalized banks.
  - Federal Reserve authority to act against the parent BHC and require guarantees of capital restoration plans.
- OCC Heightened Standards requiring large banks to maintain a robust, distinct risk governance framework with clear separation of the bank’s risk profile from that of the parent and enhanced board responsibilities.

nodes.title: OCC Heightened Standards
nodes.heading: 1.5.2.4 OCC Heightened Standards

nodes.title: Restrictions on transactions with affiliates
nodes.heading: 1.5.2.5 Restrictions on transactions with affiliates
nodes.start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A. and its subsidiaries are subject to restrictions 
imposed by federal law on extensions of credit to, 
investments in stock or securities of, and derivatives, 
securities lending and certain other transactions with, 
JPMorgan Chase & Co. and certain other affiliates.
nodes.summary:

nodes.title: Dividend restrictions

nodes.summary:

Morgan Securities plc. Rules cover sales/trading practices, offerings, research, customer funds, client financing, capital, recordkeeping, and conduct.

nodes.title: Depositor preference

nodes.summary:
- Overview of regulatory obligations affecting JPMorgan Chase across the U.S., EU, and U.K., including:
  - Requirements on segregation of counterparty collateral, business conduct, documentation, record-keeping, reporting, and anti-fraud/anti-manipulation under EMIR and MiFID II.
  - Registration status: J.P. Morgan Securities LLC as a CFTC-registered futures commission merchant and NFA member.
  - Global data, privacy, consumer protection, and cybersecurity rules that are rapidly evolving and vigorously enforced.

- Financial crime, sanctions, and anti-corruption compliance:
  - Bank Secrecy Act obligations (AML/CFT programs, record-keeping, reporting, KYC).
  - U.S. OFAC, EU, and U.K. sanctions regimes, and conflicts among jurisdictions.
  - Anti-corruption laws including the U.S. FCPA and U.K. Bribery Act.

- Compensation regulation and oversight:
  - U.S. Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC guidance on incentive compensation risk.
  - FSB standards; EU/UK frameworks under CRD V and EBA/UK guidelines.
  - Ongoing evolution of rules that may influence compensation design.

- Key international regulatory initiatives and reforms:
  - MiFID II: trading venue mandates, transparency, reporting, investor protection, commodities position limits; EU proposals for amendments (including a consolidated tape) under review.
  - U.K. Wholesale Markets Review and FSMB changes to secondary markets post-Brexit, with further consultations on transparency.
  - EMIR amendments proposed to enhance EU clearing competitiveness and CCP supervision.
  - CSDR mandatory buy-in regime deferred proposal to November 2025.
  - U.K. “Edinburgh Reforms” spanning retail banking, payments, markets, digital assets, and sustainable finance, with further 2023 consultations expected.
  - Basel III finalization in EU and U.K.: compliance from January 2025 with transitional periods; revisions to credit, operational, and market risk frameworks; reduced reliance on internal models; enhanced supervisory tools; ESG risk management and disclosure requirements; EBA sustainable finance standards (2023–2025); PRA climate risk policies.
  - EU IPU requirement for certain non-EU banks by December 30, 2023, with potential for a second IPU in defined circumstances.
  - Supervisory expectations from ECB and PRA on climate risk, IT/third-party reliance, operational resilience, and shock readiness, covering strategy, governance, risk management, scenario analysis, and disclosures.
  - Sustainability reporting and due diligence:
    - CSRD expanding ESG reporting scope with phased implementation starting 2024.
    - CSDDD proposal mandating human rights and environmental due diligence and potential climate transition plans, applicable to certain EU and non-EU entities.

- Risk Factors summary outlining principal risks to the Firm:
  - Regulatory risks: impacts of changing laws, differing jurisdictional regimes, enforcement penalties and collateral consequences, and resolution-related losses.
  - Political risks: effects of economic uncertainty or instability from political events.
  - Market risks: macroeconomic conditions, policies, rates/spreads, and market fluctuations affecting businesses, positions, earnings, liquidity, and capital.
  - Credit risks: counterparty/customer deterioration, collateral value declines, and concentration risks.
  - Liquidity risks: market-wide disruption, unforeseen needs, asset sale constraints, key participant defaults, outflows, confidence shocks, parent reliance on subsidiaries, ratings downgrades, and reference rate transition risks.
  - Capital risks: maintaining required levels/composition and impacts of changes to capital rules on distributions and business support.
  - Operational risks: system and workforce dependencies; third-party/service provider risks; new product/platform changes; data protection and cybersecurity threats; risk management models/judgments; disclosure and reporting controls; vendor oversight standards.
  - Strategic risks: execution of business strategy, intensifying competition, and climate change impacts on operations and clients.
  - Conduct risks: employee actions or misconduct and adherence to policies.
  - Reputation risks: potential harm from misconduct, security breaches, and related deficiencies.

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.heading: 1.a Risk Factors
nodes.start_phrase:
The following discussion sets forth the material risk factors 
that could affect JPMorgan Chase’s financial condition and 
operations.
nodes.summary: This partial document is Item 1A: Risk Factors from JPMorgan Chase’s filing. It outlines that numerous risks—alone or in combination—could materially and adversely affect the firm’s business, earnings, financial condition, capital, liquidity, competitive position, and reputation. It provides a summary of principal risk categories: regulatory risks (including shifting laws, cross-jurisdictional differences, enforcement penalties, less predictable regimes, and resolution-related loss absorption by security holders); political risks (economic uncertainty or instability from political developments); market risks (economic and policy changes, interest rate and credit spread movements, and market volatility affecting consumer, wholesale, investment, and market-making activities, as well as liquidity and capital); credit risks (counterparty and client deterioration, collateral value declines in stress, and concentration exposures); liquidity risks (market-wide disruptions, unforeseen funding needs, asset sale constraints, major participant defaults, unexpected outflows, confidence shocks, reliance of the parent on subsidiary cash flows, rating downgrades, and reference rate transition issues including litigation); capital risks (failure to maintain required levels/composition of capital or adverse regulatory changes constraining shareholder distributions and business support); operational risks (dependence on systems and staffing, third-party and market participant reliability, risks from new or changed products and platforms, data protection, cyber attacks and extraordinary events, model and estimation risks in stress testing and reporting, disclosure controls, and vendor oversight requirements); strategic risks (ineffective strategies, intensifying competition, and climate change impacts on operations and clients); conduct risks (employee actions or misconduct contrary to firm standards); and reputation risks (harm to stakeholder relationships stemming from misconduct, security breaches, or inadequate risk management). The section emphasizes that these are material risks but not an exhaustive list.

nodes.title: Summary
nodes.heading: 1.a.1 Summary
nodes.start_phrase:
The principal risk factors that could adversely affect 
JPMorgan Chase’s business, results of operations, financial 
condition, capital position, liquidity, competitive position or 
reputation include:
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: This Item 1A excerpt outlines the material risks that could, individually or collectively, adversely affect JPMorgan Chase’s business, results, financial condition, capital, liquidity, competitive position, and reputation. It cautions the list is not exhaustive.

- Summary of principal risk categories:
  - Regulatory: Effects of extensive global regulation and supervision; changes in laws, interpretations, or enforcement; competitive impacts from differing regimes; penalties, collateral consequences, and higher compliance/operational costs from investigations; unpredictability in certain countries’ frameworks; and losses borne by security holders in a resolution.
  - Political: Business impacts from economic uncertainty or instability due to political developments.
  - Market: Effects of economic/market conditions, government policies, interest rates, credit spreads, and market fluctuations on consumer/wholesale businesses, trading and market-making, earnings, liquidity, and capital.
  - Credit: Adverse changes in client/customer/counterparty/custodian/CCP financial condition; collateral value declines under stress; concentrations of credit and market risk.
  - Liquidity: Market-wide illiquidity or disruption; unforeseen liquidity/capital needs; asset sale challenges; default by significant participants; unexpected cash/collateral outflows; confidence shocks; parent’s reliance on subsidiary cash flows; rating downgrades’ impact on liquidity and funding cost; transition to alternative reference rates, including litigation risks.
  - Capital: Risk of failing to maintain required capital levels/composition or adverse changes to capital rules, potentially limiting capital distributions or business support.
  - Operational: Dependence on systems, staffing, and third parties; risks from product/service/platform changes; data privacy and safeguarding; cyber attacks and extraordinary events; limitations of risk management, models, estimations, stress testing, and disclosure/financial reporting controls; heightened standards for vendor/service provider oversight.
  - Strategic: Execution risks in business strategy; intensifying competition; climate change impacts on operations, clients, and customers.
  - Conduct: Employee actions or misconduct, and failures to adhere to policies and expectations.
  - Reputation: Effects from misconduct, security breaches, risk/compliance/operational failures, litigation/regulatory matters, ESG expectation shortfalls, conflicts of interest, and fiduciary lapses.
  - Country: Impacts from hostilities and local economic, political, regulatory, and social factors on businesses and revenues.
  - People: Importance of attracting/retaining qualified, diverse talent; risks from unfavorable immigration or travel policy changes.
  - Legal: Litigation and regulatory/government investigation risks.

- Expanded discussion on Regulatory risk:
  - Pervasive regulation globally shapes how JPMorgan Chase conducts and structures its businesses; new or changed requirements may force operational changes and raise costs, reducing profitability. New businesses or acquisitions may trigger additional rules.
  - Possible required responses to evolving laws/regulation: limit products/services; reduce market-making liquidity provision; forgo business opportunities; pay higher taxes (including potential minimum global tax regimes), assessments, and charges; incur losses from customer-targeted fraud; dispose of assets at disadvantageous times/prices; restrict activities; raise prices (potentially dampening demand).
  - Consequences of non-compliance: heightened scrutiny; enforcement actions; fines, penalties, sanctions; increased litigation exposure; reputational harm.
  - Regulatory inconsistencies and competitive effects: larger firms face stricter oversight; fintechs and non-traditional competitors may be less regulated or overseen by agencies with different priorities; some jurisdictions favor domestic institutions. These disparities can shift market share to less regulated competitors, particularly for unregulated products. Differences in how similar initiatives are implemented across jurisdictions further complicate operations and results.

nodes.title: Regulatory
nodes.heading: 1.a.2 Regulatory
nodes.start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase’s businesses are highly regulated, and 
the laws, rules and regulations that apply to JPMorgan 
Chase have a significant impact on its business and 
operations.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of key risk categories: reputational (from management, compliance, ESG, conflicts of interest, fiduciary issues), country/geopolitical risks, people/talent risks (including immigration/travel policy), and legal risks (litigation and regulatory investigations).
- Extensive regulatory environment: global compliance obligations materially shape business structure and operations; new or changing rules can force changes to offerings, market-making liquidity, pricing, taxes/assessments, and asset disposals, increasing costs and reducing profitability.
- Consequences of non-compliance: heightened scrutiny, enforcement actions, fines/penalties, increased litigation exposure, and reputational harm.
- Regulatory fragmentation and inconsistency: stricter oversight for larger firms, lighter regimes for fintech/non-traditional competitors, and home-country advantages can erode competitiveness; cross-border rule conflicts (e.g., ring-fencing, local capital/liquidity, IHCs, CCP clearing, derivatives position limits/reporting, governance/conduct/compensation rules) can drive restructurings, divestitures, higher capital/liquidity and compliance costs, product curtailment, pricing changes, and sanctions risk.
- Regulatory investigations/enforcement: history of significant penalties; potential requirements to admit wrongdoing or plead guilty increase litigation/reputation risk, client loss, product/business restrictions, and operational bans; failure to satisfy remediation can trigger additional penalties, restrictions, governance changes, or prosecution.
- Operating in less predictable legal regimes: inconsistent or ambiguous laws, weak contract/IP enforcement, state-controlled markets, corruption, arbitrary actions, and licensing risks increase compliance complexity, costs, and non-compliance risk.
- Resolution and loss-absorbency requirements: ongoing resolution planning may require structural/operational changes and add costs; deficiencies can lead to tighter prudential limits or forced restructurings/divestitures. In a resolution, holders of parent company equity and unsecured debt (including eligible long-term debt) absorb losses under a preferred single-point-of-entry strategy, though actual outcomes may vary and could be more adverse.
- Political and policy risks: monetary/fiscal shifts, responses to health emergencies, climate/ESG policies, protectionism/tariffs, sanctions, isolationism, and geopolitical tensions/hostilities can increase market volatility and uncertainty, undermine investor confidence and the U.S. dollar’s safe-haven status, provoke retaliatory measures, jeopardize support for U.S. GSEs, and raise concerns about U.S. government funding and debt servicing.

nodes.title: Political
nodes.heading: 1.a.3 Political
nodes.start_phrase:
Economic uncertainty or instability caused by political 
developments can negatively impact JPMorgan Chase’s 
businesses.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s resolution planning and key risk factors. It explains the role of eligible long-term debt (LTD) as loss-absorbing capacity in a potential resolution of the Parent Company, whether under Chapter 11 bankruptcy or FDIC Title II, emphasizing the preferred single point of entry strategy where only the Parent Company enters resolution while subsidiaries are recapitalized to continue operations or be wound down. It details creditor hierarchy, noting that Parent Company equity holders and unsecured creditors (including eligible LTD holders) would bear losses before subsidiary creditors and the Parent Company’s priority and secured creditors, and that recoveries for Parent Company debt holders depend on residual value from subsidiaries. It cautions that the FDIC has not formally adopted the single point of entry approach and that authorities are not obligated to follow JPMorgan Chase’s preferred strategy, which could increase losses for holders of Parent Company securities. The text then catalogs political risks, including shifts in monetary and fiscal policy, responses to health emergencies, climate/ESG-related actions, isolationist policies, geopolitical tensions, sanctions, tariffs, and other government actions, describing potential outcomes such as diminished investor confidence, government shutdowns, heightened market volatility, credit spread widening, reduced trade, currency redenomination, withdrawals from alliances, expropriation, and broader market dislocations. It highlights potential adverse effects on JPMorgan Chase’s financial performance—market-making and investment losses, liquidity and capital pressures, higher credit losses and charge-offs, operational challenges, and reputational harm. It also warns of conflicting governmental mandates across jurisdictions that may restrict business, trigger enforcement actions (including antitrust), or create reputational risks tied to decisions about serving sensitive industries or participating in social/environmental initiatives. Finally, it summarizes market risks—changes in sentiment, inflation/deflation/recession, labor market conditions, funding and liquidity, interest rates and credit spreads, asset price volatility, and extraordinary events (e.g., cyber attacks, climate events, pandemics)—as key drivers that can materially affect the firm’s businesses and results.

nodes.title: Market
nodes.heading: 1.a.4 Market
nodes.start_phrase:
Economic and market events and conditions can 
materially affect JPMorgan Chase’s businesses and 
investment and market-making positions.
nodes.summary:
- Geopolitical, economic, and policy uncertainty can trigger disruptions (e.g., government shutdowns, reliance on central banks, ratings deterioration, expropriation, currency redenomination, dissolution of alliances) that reduce JPMorgan Chase’s liquidity and capital, increase credit losses and charge-offs, impair service delivery, and weaken results.
- Conflicting or prescriptive government mandates about doing business with sensitive industries can lead to business restrictions, enforcement risks (including antitrust), reputational harm, strained regulator/client relationships, and criticism tied to perceived political alignments or participation in social/environmental initiatives.
- Broad macro and market factors materially affect performance: sentiment and confidence; inflation/deflation/recession; labor market tightness/unemployment; availability and cost of capital, liquidity and credit; levels and volatility in rates, spreads, FX, equities and commodities; geopolitical conflicts, terrorism, cyber events, climate and natural disasters, and health emergencies.
- Investment portfolio and market-making are exposed to losses from severe asset price declines, unexpected credit events, correlation breakdowns, ineffective hedges, and mispriced risks, which can cut profitability and constrain growth by reducing liquidity and capital.
- Consumer businesses are sensitive to income distribution, employment, interest rate regimes, housing prices, inflation, confidence, spending, and debt levels; adverse conditions reduce product demand and increase delinquencies, allowances, and charge-offs; consumer-focused policies (healthcare, education, immigration, employment, housing) and broader tax/regulatory changes can further pressure earnings.
- Wholesale businesses face lower fees and activity in weak markets, reduced investor participation in syndications/underwriting, potential losses on distributed credit commitments, and larger residual exposures, especially in leveraged lending.
- Sector-specific shocks (e.g., oil and gas price swings, commodity increases, lasting changes in consumer behavior) can weaken client credit profiles; commercial real estate stress can depress rents and valuations, raising delinquencies, defaults, charge-offs, and servicing costs.
- Asset management and custody revenues can fall with declining asset values, client outflows, and shifts to lower-fee products; large redemptions can hurt fund performance and trigger further outflows.
- Interest rate and credit spread risks: higher rates may lift net interest income but can curb loan originations, trigger underwriting losses and downgrades, drive deposit outflows, create AFS securities losses, tighten market liquidity, and raise funding costs; low/negative rates compress margins, alter depositor behavior, and reduce MSR values; wider credit spreads increase borrowing costs and affect fair-value earnings.
- Market valuation risk: volatility and illiquidity complicate pricing; subsequent revaluations or sales may realize losses; stress testing and hedging may not fully protect against extreme events.
- Credit and counterparty exposure: client/counterparty defaults, custodian failures, and disputes (including over derivatives and collateral) can cause losses, legal costs, and reputational harm; transactions with government entities carry enhanced sovereign, operational, and legal risks, including potential repudiation.
- Central counterparty (CCP) risk: CCP failures require costly contract replacement; members share in default and non-default losses (including from custodial, settlement, investment, or cyber incidents).
- Clearing, cash management, and custodial services create intra-day and collateral risks; client insolvencies can raise operational and litigation burdens, with collateral potentially insufficient.
- Collateral vulnerability in stress: declining values, unfavorable liquidation prices, counterparties’ inability to post collateral, and valuation disputes can amplify losses.

nodes.title: Credit
nodes.heading: 1.a.5 Credit
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase can be negatively affected by adverse changes in the financial condition of clients, counterparties, custodians and CCPs.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights market risk from extreme volatility and illiquidity that can reduce the fair value of instruments and acknowledges hedging and stress-testing may not fully mitigate losses.
- Details broad credit risk to clients, counterparties, custodians, and central counterparties (CCPs), including insolvency, fraud, legal failures, and resulting disputes and litigation.
- Explains CCP-related exposures: replacing contracts after a CCP default, mutualized losses from other members’ defaults, and bearing non-default losses (custodial, settlement, investment, cyber).
- Describes clearing and transaction services risks: client nonperformance, adequacy of collateral, intraday credit exposure, and losses/disputes arising from client bankruptcy or regulatory actions.
- Notes sovereign and public-sector risks, including repudiation of prior commitments, ultra vires claims, and legal/regulatory barriers that hinder dispute resolution and payment enforcement.
- Addresses derivatives disputes over terms, settlement, and collateral valuation that can lead to unexpected transaction, operational, legal costs, credit losses, and reputational harm.
- Warns of systemic and contagion risks from the failure or distress of significant market participants causing cascading market disruptions and amplified exposures.
- Emphasizes collateral risks in stressed markets: inability to realize fair value, liquidation shortfalls, counterparties’ failure to post collateral, and valuation disputes.
- Discusses concentration risks across industries, geographies, and similar business models that can amplify credit, liquidity, and market losses; may require higher credit loss allowances.
- Highlights consumer credit cycle vulnerabilities, including competitive easing of standards, lower margins, and higher defaults that can trigger charge-offs and broader economic weakness.
- Notes that inability to reduce positions during dislocations can raise market and credit risk, increase risk-weighted assets, and negatively affect capital, funding costs, and profitability.
- Outlines liquidity risk drivers: market-wide disruptions, regulatory-driven liquidity/capital needs, asset sale constraints, CCP/default events, unexpected outflows, deposit loss, commitment draws, and confidence shocks.
- Explains potential reliance on more expensive or limited alternative funding when traditional sources (e.g., deposits, FHLB) are constrained.
- Cites regulatory and resolution-related liquidity requirements (LCR, NSFR, liquidity pre-positioning) that can elevate funding costs and restrict flexibility.
- Concludes that ineffective liquidity management can constrain funding/investment in businesses and adversely affect results of operations.

nodes.title: Liquidity
nodes.heading: 1.a.6 Liquidity
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase’s ability to operate its businesses could be impaired if its liquidity is constrained.
nodes.summary:
- Exposure to losses during market stress due to volatility, illiquidity, and challenges realizing or valuing collateral.
- Significant credit and market risk from client/counterparty concentrations across similar industries, geographies, or business models, with contagion effects that can trigger fair value losses, higher allowances for credit losses, and limited ability to diversify or hedge.
- Consumer business risks from aggressive industry-wide expansion of consumer credit leading to margin compression, lending to weaker borrowers, higher defaults and charge-offs, and potential recessionary impacts on revenues.
- Market dislocations can impede position reduction, increasing market and credit risk, risk‑weighted assets, funding costs, and negatively affecting capital and profitability.
- Liquidity risks stemming from market-wide disruptions, regulatory changes, asset sale constraints, CCP or major participant defaults, unexpected cash/collateral outflows, deposit losses, and confidence shocks; potential reliance on more expensive alternative funding; constraints from LCR/NSFR, resolution planning, and subsidiary pre‑positioning; failure to manage liquidity can limit funding and investment in businesses.
- Holding company dependence on JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and the intermediate holding company (IHC) for cash flows; regulatory capital/liquidity restrictions (including SLR and internal thresholds) can limit dividends and intercompany payments, affecting the ability to service debt, pay dividends, repurchase/redemption of securities, and potentially accelerating resolution or bankruptcy proceedings.
- Credit rating downgrade risk: driven by profitability expectations, risk management, legal expenses, regulatory and macro/geopolitical factors; downgrades may occur amid broader instability and can reduce market access, raise funding and servicing costs, trigger collateral/funding needs, limit counterparties, widen credit spreads, and depress debt values.
- Benchmark transition risk: ongoing shift from LIBOR to alternative rates (e.g., SOFR) may not produce economic equivalents or achieve broad acceptance; inadequate transition readiness can cause market dislocation, pricing volatility, and suppressed capital markets activity; potential for litigation and disputes over fairness, disclosures, suitability, competition/benchmark conduct, and contractual determinations, leading to higher legal/operational costs and reputational harm.
- Capital requirements: subject to leverage- and risk-based rules plus GSIB surcharge, Stress Capital Buffer, and countercyclical buffers; requirements may rise due to regulatory actions, macro responses (e.g., COVID-19 impacts on deposits and leverage exposure), balance sheet/RWA shifts (market risk, delinquencies, downgrades), and higher Fed stress losses; consequences include limits on buybacks/dividends, required capital issuances or restricted redemptions, and curtailment of business activities.
- Operational risk context: reliance on effective financial, accounting, transaction execution, data processing, and other operational systems at JPMorgan Chase and across market participants.

nodes.title: Capital
nodes.heading: 1.a.7 Capital
nodes.start_phrase: Maintaining the required level and composition of capital may impact JPMorgan Chase’s ability to support business activities, meet evolving regulatory requirements and distribute capital to shareholders.
nodes.summary:
- Transition from U.S. dollar LIBOR to SOFR: While industry progress is significant, incomplete or ineffective implementation could cause market dislocation, pricing volatility across securities and derivatives, suppressed capital markets activity, and negatively affect JPMorgan Chase’s results and LIBOR-linked instruments it issues, funds, services, or holds.
- Legal and dispute risks from the benchmark transition: Potential claims of unfair treatment, client losses or higher costs, inadequate disclosures or conflicts, unsuitable product recommendations/sales, anti-competitive behavior or benchmark manipulation, and adverse contract interpretations—leading to higher legal and operational costs, potential payments, and reputational harm.
- Capital adequacy and regulatory requirements: As a GSIB, JPMorgan Chase must meet leverage- and risk-based capital rules and hold buffers (GSIB surcharge, Stress Capital Buffer, countercyclical buffer). Required capital can increase due to regulatory changes, systemic-event responses (e.g., COVID-19 impacts on deposits, leverage exposure, GSIB surcharge), balance sheet/RWA shifts (market risk, delinquencies, downgrades), and CCAR stress loss outcomes raising the SCB. Shortfalls or unfavorable changes could limit share repurchases, force or restrict capital instrument actions, constrain dividends, and curtail business activities.
- Operational reliance: The firm’s businesses depend on the effectiveness, accuracy, speed, and security of its own and other market participants’ financial, accounting, transaction processing, and data systems, supported by proper design, installation, maintenance, and training. (Section truncated.)

nodes.title: Operational
nodes.heading: 1.a.8 Operational
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase’s businesses are dependent on the effectiveness of its operational systems and those of other market participants.
nodes.summary:
- Benchmark transition risk: Ongoing move from U.S. dollar LIBOR to SOFR may cause market dislocation, pricing volatility, reduced capital markets activity, and adverse impacts on JPMC’s LIBOR-linked instruments and results; potential litigation over fairness, disclosures/conflicts, suitability, anti-competitive/benchmark conduct, and contractual determinations, leading to higher legal costs and reputational harm.
- Capital adequacy: Subject to leverage- and risk-based requirements plus GSIB, SCB and countercyclical buffers; required capital can rise due to regulatory changes, Federal Reserve/government actions, balance sheet/RWA shifts (market risk, delinquencies, downgrades), and stress test losses; consequences include constrained buybacks/dividends, required issuances or blocked redemptions of capital instruments, and curtailed business activity.
- Operational dependence: Heavy reliance on internal systems and third-party infrastructures (custodians, vendors, cloud/data/security providers, clearing/payment systems, CCPs, exchanges); failures or cyber incidents can delay services, disrupt settlements, cause erroneous/fraudulent transactions, trigger financial losses and higher costs, impede regulatory data collection, invite sanctions, and harm reputation.
- Growing complexity: Increasing transaction speed/volume/interconnectivity heightens risks from external fraud, human error, cascading system issues, software/hardware defects, and IP disputes; inability to maintain/upgrade systems to business and regulatory standards could materially harm the firm.
- Cybersecurity: Persistent, sophisticated attacks (malware, DDoS, ransomware) from criminals, hacktivists, and state-linked actors; absolute security is unattainable due to evolving techniques, insider/third-party risks, and lateral movement; risk amplified by mobile, cloud, acquisitions, and remote work; breaches can cause operational disruption, data theft/manipulation, delayed recovery, legal/privacy violations, financial/regulatory exposure, and reputational damage; investigations and remediation may be prolonged and uncertain.
- Change management risk: Introducing or modifying products, services, delivery platforms, or integrating acquisitions may introduce unrecognized operational risks, leading to liabilities, higher expenses, litigation/regulatory actions, reputational and liquidity impacts, and competitive weakness.
- External ecosystem risk: Breaches or failures at vendors, market infrastructures, retailers, processors, data aggregators, or customer-linked systems can increase fraud and loss exposure, remediation costs, and reputational harm; expanding interconnectivity raises potential for industry-wide disruptions and customer access restrictions.
- Workforce and conduct: Business performance depends on adequate staffing and the competence, integrity, and health/safety of employees at JPMC and key third parties; risks include poor execution/controls/training, labor shortages, health emergencies, misconduct or errors.
- Privacy/data protection: Complex, evolving global laws increase costs and operational complexity, may restrict cross-border data flows, data sharing, and product design; exposures arise from third parties lacking adequate controls; violations or mishandling can lead to fines, litigation, operational changes, and reputational damage amid heightened regulatory scrutiny and potential data localization mandates.
- Extraordinary events and resiliency: Cyber incidents, physical security breaches, power/telecom outages, tech failures/data loss, property damage/injuries, climate impacts, natural disasters/severe weather, accidents, health crises, civil unrest, hostilities/terrorism can disrupt operations; resiliency plans may be insufficient for simultaneous or concentrated events; outcomes include service disruption, losses, market infrastructure impacts, legal/regulatory exposure, and reputational harm.
- Vendor oversight: Enhanced regulatory standards for outsourcing and critical services increase costs; inadequate third-party risk management can harm clients, reduce revenue, raise expenses, trigger sanctions, and damage reputation.
- Risk management limitations: Framework, governance, data quality, models, and reporting may fail to capture all risks, especially during stress when correlations change; lapses can lead to poor decisions, non-compliance, losses, remedial costs, client harm, litigation/regulatory actions, and reputational damage.
- Model/estimate/judgment risk: Dependence on assumptions and historical trends for risk, capital, liquidity, stress testing, fair value, and credit loss allowances can result in errors due to incomplete data, illiquidity, tech issues, or review failures; unexpected losses and capital impacts may follow; regulatory non-approval of models can increase RWA and capital requirements.
- Disclosure and financial reporting controls: Material weaknesses or significant deficiencies could cause inaccurate reporting, constrain market access, increase remediation costs, and lead to legal/regulatory consequences and reputational harm.
- Strategic execution: Misjudging products, geography, client focus, acquisitions/investments, counterparties, and distribution channels—or failing to align with market, regulatory, and stakeholder (including ESG) expectations—can weaken franchise value and growth; risks include suboptimal capital allocation, weak due diligence/integration, slow response to market changes, and potential costs of exiting or disposing of properties.
- Competitive landscape: Intense and rising competition across U.S. and global financial services from banks, financial institutions, trading/advisory/investment management firms, and finance companies, amid regulatory change, technological advances, public scrutiny, and shifting economic conditions.

nodes.title: Strategic
nodes.heading: 1.a.9 Strategic
nodes.start_phrase: If JPMorgan Chase’s management fails to develop and execute effective business strategies, and to anticipate changes affecting those strategies, JPMorgan Chase’s competitive standing and results could suffer.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory/model risk: Use of internal models and estimations for Basel III market, credit and operational risk RWA requires regulator approval; non-approval could increase capital requirements, constrain growth, and hurt results.
- Disclosure and financial reporting controls: Lapses or weaknesses in disclosure controls or ICFR could cause inaccurate reporting, limit market access, increase remediation costs, trigger litigation/regulatory sanctions, damage reputation, and undermine investor confidence.
- Strategic execution risk: Performance depends on management’s ability to set and execute effective strategies across products/services, geographies, client segments, acquisitions/investments, counterparties, and distribution channels; poor choices, bad or incomplete information, or failure to adapt to regulation, markets, or stakeholder expectations (including ESG) could reduce franchise value and earnings.
- Capital and resource allocation: Risks from imprecise modeling or subjective judgments in capital allocation; need to control expenses, return capital, and build operational/technology/risk/financial/managerial capabilities; failures can impair growth.
- M&A and integration: Inadequate due diligence or weak integration of acquired businesses can create operational and conduct risks and harm performance.
- Real estate footprint: Disposing of excess properties, premises and facilities could entail material period-specific costs.
- Competitive pressures: Intensifying competition from banks, nonbanks, fintechs, big tech, trading/advisory firms, and finance companies may erode pricing, margins and market share; aggressive nonbank lending can amplify downturn instability affecting JPMorgan Chase.
- Technology disruption: E-commerce and digital innovations (e.g., electronic platforms, crypto, distributed ledgers, robo-advice, online lending and payments) can disintermediate traditional services, require higher investment to adapt, increase compliance costs, and reduce income; unexpected customer use or third‑party breaches heighten risks.
- Climate risk: Physical risks (acute weather events; chronic climate shifts) and transition risks (policy, technology, consumer preference changes) can depress asset values, disrupt operations, raise insurance and energy costs, create stranded assets, pressure business models, and pose reputational risk; inconsistent cross-border climate policies/regulations add complexity.
- Conduct risk: Employee misconduct (e.g., mis-selling, insider trading, market manipulation, government program fraud, improper tax/accounting structuring, fiduciary breaches, antitrust violations, unapproved communications use, discrimination/harassment, misreporting risk, misappropriation of assets/data) can harm clients and markets, invite litigation and enforcement, increase costs, force business curtailment, and damage reputation; risks can be heightened in newly acquired businesses despite conduct risk management efforts.
- Reputation risk: Loss of stakeholder trust can materially harm the firm’s ability to attract and retain clients, customers, investors and employees, impairing business performance.

nodes.title: Conduct
nodes.heading: 1.a.10 Conduct
nodes.start_phrase: Conduct failure by JPMorgan Chase employees can harm clients and customers, impact market integrity, damage JPMorgan Chase’s reputation and trigger litigation and regulatory action.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights climate-related regulatory risk, noting inconsistencies and conflicts across jurisdictions (including extraterritorial application) and potential misalignment with public policy or stakeholder preferences.
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s conduct risk framework, emphasizing adherence to the Code of Conduct and “How We Do Business” Principles, and integration of conduct expectations across recruiting, onboarding, training, performance management, promotion, and compensation.
- Acknowledges historical instances of employee misconduct that led to litigation and government actions (e.g., consent orders, deferred/non-prosecution agreements, sanctions) and notes no assurance against future incidents or violations.
- Lists examples of potential misconduct: improper product marketing/sales; insider trading, market manipulation, unauthorized trading; fraud in government relief programs; facilitating transactions for questionable tax/accounting/disclosure outcomes lacking clear economic substance; breaches of fiduciary duties; antitrust collusion; use of unapproved electronic communications; discrimination or harassment contrary to DEI goals; subordinating risk appetite to business/compensation goals; and misappropriation of property, confidential information, or technology.
- Outlines potential consequences of conduct failures: litigation, investigations, fines, penalties, or other sanctions; financial losses; increased operational and compliance costs; heightened regulatory scrutiny; mandated restructuring or cessation of activities; intensive management oversight; client/customer loss; and reputational damage.
- Notes conduct risks may be heightened in newly acquired businesses during integration.
- Introduces reputation risk, stressing that trust is critical to attracting and retaining clients, customers, investors, and employees, and that reputational damage can significantly harm the firm’s businesses.

nodes.title: Reputation
nodes.heading: 1.a.11 Reputation
nodes.start_phrase: Damage to JPMorgan Chase’s reputation could harm its businesses.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights climate-related risks arising from inconsistent and potentially extraterritorial climate policies and financial regulations across jurisdictions where JPMorgan Chase operates.
- Details conduct risk: employees are expected to adhere to the Code of Conduct and “first class business” principles; conduct risk management is embedded across recruiting, onboarding, training, performance, promotions, and compensation.
- Notes past instances of employee misconduct and warns such actions may recur or go undetected, potentially breaching prior regulatory resolutions.
- Enumerates examples of misconduct risks: improper sales/marketing; insider trading, market manipulation, or unauthorized trading; fraud in government relief programs; structuring for questionable tax/accounting disclosure outcomes; fiduciary breaches; antitrust violations; use of unapproved electronic communications; discrimination/harassment; misaligned risk management due to incentives; and misappropriation of property or confidential information.
- Outlines consequences of conduct failures: litigation, investigations, fines, penalties, sanctions; financial losses; higher operational/compliance costs; increased regulatory scrutiny; activity restrictions; management burdens; client/customer loss; and reputational harm—heightened for newly acquired businesses.
- Describes reputation risk drivers: employee misconduct; cyber/security breaches; data protection failures; poor risk management (including unpopular activities); missed ESG commitments; legal/regulatory non-compliance; operational failures; enforcement actions; actions during health emergencies; and third-party (including vendors, investees, JV partners, and acquisitions) non-compliance.
- Emphasizes the amplifying effect of rapid, pervasive negative publicity and social media on reputational damage.
- Notes rising activist scrutiny over ESG-related business practices (e.g., ties to industries perceived as harmful to health or the environment), including protests and shareholder proposals, potentially leading to regulatory scrutiny, client loss, talent challenges, divestment, and strategic business changes.
- Acknowledges industry-wide reputation spillovers from perceived unfair consumer treatment or inappropriate product sales practices.
- Addresses conflicts of interest and fiduciary risks: necessity to identify, disclose, and manage conflicts (including those involving third parties), ensure fair treatment and service standards, use data responsibly, meet fiduciary and privacy obligations; failures can trigger litigation, fines, higher costs, lost revenue, and reputational damage.
- Discusses geopolitical and country risks: outbreaks/escalation of hostilities or cyber aggression can cause global disruption, market volatility, asset sell-offs, currency depreciation/defaults, trade disruption, and loss of confidence; U.S. involvement may force operational curtailments and heighten cyber threats.
- Describes risks in certain countries with less developed or more volatile economies and heavier state influence: extreme currency moves, inflation, low/negative growth, sovereign distress; potential government actions such as price/capital/exchange controls, forced currency conversion, expropriation/nationalization (including IP), and adverse legal/regulatory changes, especially impactful in smaller, illiquid markets.
- Notes social instability risks in emerging and developed markets, including demonstrations, civil unrest, strikes, crime, and corruption, which can disrupt operations and clients.

nodes.title: Country
nodes.heading: 1.a.12 Country
nodes.start_phrase: An outbreak or escalation of hostilities between countries or within a country or region could have a material adverse effect on the global economy and on JPMorgan Chase’s businesses within the affected region or globally.
nodes.summary:
- Client and fiduciary obligations: Emphasis on identifying, addressing, and disclosing conflicts of interest (including third-party conflicts), delivering fair treatment and appropriate standards of service and care, responsible use of client/customer data, and proper handling of confidential information in compliance with laws. Failure could lead to customer dissatisfaction, litigation, fines, heightened regulatory scrutiny, higher costs, and reputational harm.
- Geopolitical and country risk: Potential adverse effects from hostilities, cyber attacks, and geopolitical instability, including global economic disruption, market volatility, asset sell-offs, currency depreciation and defaults, trade disruption, and reduced confidence. Possible curtailment of operations if the U.S. is involved in conflicts; increased cyber threats from adversaries.
- Emerging and less-developed market risks: Exposure to volatile economies, heavy government influence, extreme currency swings, inflation, low/negative growth, and sovereign stress. Potential for restrictive policies (capital/exchange controls, forced conversion), expropriation/nationalization (including IP), and abrupt legal/regulatory changes that can directly or indirectly suppress business.
- Social and political instability: Risks from demonstrations, civil unrest, strikes, crime and corruption, security issues, regime change, terrorism, and internal discord that can impair operations, revenues, and profitability locally and through cross-border contagion, including effects in the U.S.
- Talent and workforce: Dependence on attracting and retaining qualified, diverse employees and leadership successors amid intense competition. Risks tied to hybrid work models (potential performance/control degradation) or discontinuation (recruitment/retention challenges). Immigration/travel restrictions could hinder talent mobility and force less efficient, more costly operating adjustments.
- Legal and regulatory exposure: High likelihood of litigation, class actions, and formal/informal investigations with heightened, ongoing regulatory examinations. Potential for overlapping multi-jurisdiction actions triggered by industry-wide issues, leading to judgments, settlements, fines, sanctions, operational restructuring or product exits, reputational damage, increased costs, reduced profitability, and liabilities that may exceed reserves.

nodes.title: People
nodes.heading: 1.a.13 People
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase’s ability to attract and retain qualified and diverse employees is critical to its success.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines key risk factors for JPMorgan Chase: (1) geopolitical and security risks—such as hostilities, government overthrows, terrorism, and civil unrest—that can disrupt operations, revenues, and profitability globally and have cross-border effects, including in the U.S.; (2) people-related risks—intense competition for diverse talent, leadership succession challenges, potential performance and control weaknesses from hybrid work or, conversely, talent attraction/retention issues if hybrid is curtailed, and adverse impacts from restrictive immigration or travel policies that could degrade workforce quality or force less efficient, costlier operating model changes; and (3) legal and regulatory risks—ongoing and likely elevated litigation and investigations, heightened supervisory scrutiny, overlapping actions across jurisdictions, and potential outcomes including fines, penalties, sanctions, reputational harm, required restructuring or product/service exits, higher operational costs, reduced profitability, and exposures that may be unpredictable and exceed established reserves.

nodes.title: Legal
nodes.heading: 1.a.14 Legal
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase faces significant legal risks from litigation and formal and informal regulatory and government investigations.
nodes.summary:
- Geopolitical and country risk: Security and personal safety concerns, outbreaks of hostilities, geopolitical instability, government overthrows, terrorism, and internal discord can disrupt operations, revenues, growth, and profitability in affected countries, with spillover effects across borders, including the U.S.
- People and talent risk: Success depends on attracting and retaining qualified, diverse employees amid intense industry competition; challenges include leadership succession, potential performance/control degradation from hybrid work models (or retention risks if discontinued), and adverse impacts from restrictive immigration or travel policies that could dilute workforce quality or force less efficient, costlier operating model changes.
- Legal and regulatory risk: Significant exposure to litigation (including class actions) and frequent regulatory/government examinations and investigations, often overlapping across jurisdictions and triggered by industry events; potential outcomes include judgments, fines, penalties, sanctions, mandated restructuring or cessation of products/services, reputational harm, higher operational costs, reduced profitability, and liabilities that may be unpredictable and exceed established reserves.

nodes.title: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: 7.1 INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM), a financial holding company incorporated under Delaware law in 1968, is a leading financial services firm based in the United States of America (“U.S.”) , with operations worldwide.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and placement: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) for JPMorgan Chase covering the year ended December 31, 2022, included in both the Annual Report and the 2022 Form 10-K.
- Forward-looking statements: Cautionary language under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995; references to Forward-looking Statements (p. 154) and Risk Factors (Part I, Item 1A, pp. 9–32); statements speak only as of the filing date and are not updated.
- Glossary: Definitions of terms and acronyms available on pages 297–303.
- Company overview: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM), a Delaware-incorporated financial holding company (since 1968), with $3.7 trillion in assets and $292.3 billion in stockholders’ equity as of December 31, 2022.
- Business profile: A leading global financial services firm in investment banking, consumer and small business banking, commercial banking, transaction processing, and asset management; operates under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands serving U.S. consumers and global institutional clients.
- Organizational structure and key entities: Principal bank subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C.); principal nonbank subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; major non-U.S. operating subsidiaries J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.) and J.P. Morgan SE (Germany).
- Reportable segments: Four business segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment; references to Business Segment Results (pp. 61–80) and Note 32 for segment details.
- Regulatory filings and investor information: Firm’s website provides free access to SEC filings (Forms 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) and investor updates; SEC filings also available at sec.gov; website information is not incorporated by reference into the 2022 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW
nodes.heading: 7.2 EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW
nodes.start_phrase: This executive overview of the MD&A highlights selected information and does not contain all of the information that is important to readers of this 2022 Form 10-K.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 MD&A, summarizing firmwide performance, balance sheet trends, capital and liquidity, credit quality, business segment results, and credit provided/capital raised. Comparisons are 2022 versus 2021. Notes use of non-GAAP measures (e.g., pre-provision profit, ROTCE, TCE, TBVPS, NII/NIR excluding Markets, managed-basis revenue) with reconciliations referenced elsewhere.

- Firmwide results:
  - Net income $37.7B (down 22%); EPS $12.09; ROE 14%; ROTCE 18%.
  - Total net revenue $128.7B (up 6%): NII $66.7B (up 28%) driven by higher rates and loan growth; NII ex Markets $62.4B (up 40%). NIR $62.0B (down 11%) on lower Investment Banking fees, $2.4B Treasury & CIO securities losses, lower Home Lending production revenue and auto lease income, partially offset by stronger CIB Markets revenue and a $914MM gain on sale of Visa B shares.
  - Markets revenue $29.0B (up 6%): Fixed Income up 10%, Equity down 2%.
  - Noninterest expense $76.1B (up 7%) from higher structural costs and continued investment (compensation, technology, marketing), partly offset by lower volume/revenue-related costs.
  - Provision for credit losses $6.4B vs prior-year net benefit of $9.3B: includes $3.5B allowance build ($2.3B wholesale, $1.2B consumer) from loan growth and a weaker macro outlook, partly offset by reduced pandemic-related uncertainty; net charge-offs $2.9B.
  - Pre-provision profit $52.6B (up 4%).

- Credit quality and allowances:
  - Allowance for credit losses $22.2B; allowance to retained loans coverage 1.81% (vs 1.62%).
  - Nonperforming assets $7.2B, down $1.1B, driven by improved consumer credit and loan sales.

- Balance sheet trends:
  - Average loans $1.1T (up 6%) across lines of business.
  - Average deposits $2.5T (up 5%): growth in CCB (existing/new accounts) and AWM (residual effects of government actions), tempered by higher customer spending (CCB) and migration into investments (AWM); attrition in CIB and CB amid rising rates.

- Capital and liquidity:
  - CET1 capital $219B; CET1 ratios 13.2% (Standardized) and 13.6% (Advanced) reflecting CECL transition; SLR 5.6%.
  - Book value per share $90.29 (up 3%); TBVPS $73.12 (up 2%).
  - Liquidity: average eligible HQLA ≈ $733B and ≈$694B unencumbered marketable securities, totaling ≈$1.4T in liquidity sources.

- Managed-basis and other metrics:
  - Total net revenue (managed) $132.3B.
  - Notes references to detailed Consolidated Results and Balance Sheet analyses and non-GAAP reconciliations.

- Business segment highlights (full-year 2022):
  - Consumer & Community Banking (ROE 29%): average deposits up 10%; client investment assets down 10%; average loans up 1%; Card Services net charge-off rate 1.47%; debit/credit sales volume up 14%; active mobile customers up 9%.
  - Corporate & Investment Bank (ROE 14%): #1 in Global Investment Banking fees with 8.0% wallet share; Total Markets revenue $29.0B (up 6%).
  - Commercial Banking (ROE 16%): gross Investment Banking revenue $3.0B (down 42%); average deposits down 2%; average loans up 9%.
  - Asset & Wealth Management (ROE 25%): AUM $2.8T (down 11%); average deposits up 14%; average loans up 9%.

- Credit provided and capital raised in 2022:
  - Total $2.4T across clients (loans, commitments, and capital raised).
  - $250B to consumers; $33B to U.S. small businesses; $1.1T to corporations; $1.0T capital raised for corporate and non-U.S. government entities; $65B for nonprofits and U.S. government entities.

nodes.title: Business Developments
nodes.heading: 7.3 Business Developments
nodes.start_phrase: The duration and potential outcomes of the war in Ukraine remain uncertain.
nodes.summary:
- Business Developments — War in Ukraine: The firm is reducing positions and certain business activities tied to Russia, helping clients manage pre-existing obligations and Russia-related risks. While direct exposure to Russia and Russia-associated clients/counterparties is not material, the firm is monitoring potential secondary impacts (market volatility, inflation, sanctions effects) and operational risks (sanctions compliance, heightened cyber risk). It defines “Russia” and “Russia-associated” within its internal country risk framework and references detailed risk and portfolio sections elsewhere in the 10-K.

- Interbank Offered Rate (IBOR) Transition: The firm is in the final stages of transitioning away from LIBOR in line with IOSCO standards, with U.S. dollar LIBOR ceasing June 30, 2023. As of December 31, 2022, it had significantly reduced USD LIBOR-linked exposure across derivatives, loans, securities, and issuances, is on track with internal/industry milestones, and continues client engagement. Remaining exposure is mostly in derivatives; central counterparty conversions in Q2 2023 are expected to remediate about 40% of remaining USD LIBOR derivatives, with most of the rest addressed via contractual fallbacks.

- Legislative/Regulatory Support and Systems Readiness: The U.S. LIBOR Act (March 15, 2022) provides a framework for legacy contracts; the UK FCA proposes “synthetic” USD LIBOR for 1-, 3-, and 6-month tenors through September 30, 2024 for contracts outside the Act’s scope, both measures intended to ease transition and reduce dispute/litigation risk. The firm is updating risk, operational systems, and models, and monitoring market, client, regulatory, and legislative developments, with additional references to risk factors and accounting/reporting updates.
