nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.heading: 7.4 CONSOLIDATED RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.start_phrase: This section provides a comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s Consolidated Results of Operations on a reported basis for the two-year period ended December 31, 2022 , unless otherwise specified.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results of operations for the two years ended December 31, 2022, with cross-references to the 2021 Form 10-K for 2021 vs. 2020 comparisons and to the firm’s critical accounting estimates.
- Revenue overview (2020–2022): Detailed table of noninterest revenue components and net interest income (NII), showing 2022 total net revenue of $128.7B (up from $121.6B in 2021), driven by higher NII ($66.7B vs. $52.3B) offset by lower noninterest revenue ($62.0B vs. $69.3B). Breakouts include investment banking fees, principal transactions, lending- and deposit-related fees, asset management/administration/commissions, investment securities gains/losses, mortgage fees, card income, and other income.
- Footnote details: Other income includes operating lease income ($3.7B in 2022; $4.9B in 2021; $5.5B in 2020) and losses on tax-oriented investments; references to Note 6.
- 2022 vs. 2021 key drivers by line item:
  - Investment banking fees: Declined in CIB due to volatile markets leading to lower equity and debt underwriting activity and lower advisory from fewer announced deals.
  - Principal transactions: Increased overall, reflecting stronger Fixed Income Markets performance (notably Currencies & Emerging Markets and Rates) and higher Equity Derivatives and Prime Finance revenue, partially offset by:
    - Credit Adjustments & Other loss of $836MM vs. a $250MM gain in 2021 (driven by funding spread widening and losses tied to commodities and Russia-related exposures).
    - Q2 2022 net markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (primarily unfunded commitments) in CIB and CB.
    - Higher net losses on certain legacy private equity investments in Corporate.
    - Net losses in Treasury and CIO related to cash deployment transactions, more than offset by associated NII.
    - Note that principal transactions can be offset in other revenue lines; CIB Markets performance is assessed on a total revenue basis.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: Increased on higher service fee volume in CCB, largely offset by lower cash management fees in CB and CIB due to higher client earnings credits.
  - Asset management, administration and commissions: Decreased due to lower AWM asset management fees from weaker average market levels (partly offset by removal of most money market fund fee waivers and net long-term inflows), lower custody fees in Securities Services from lower average AUC, and lower brokerage commissions in AWM, partially offset by higher travel-related services and annuity commissions in CCB.
- Cross-references: Segment-level details cited for CCB, CIB, CB, AWM, and Note 6 for additional information.

nodes.title: Revenue
nodes.heading: 7.4.1 Revenue
nodes.start_phrase:
Investment banking fees decreased in CIB, as volatile 
market conditions resulted in:
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results of operations for 2022 versus 2021, with references to prior-year analysis and critical accounting estimates.
- Revenue overview: Presents a three-year revenue table (2020–2022) detailing noninterest revenue components and net interest income; total net revenue rose to $128.7B in 2022 (noninterest revenue $62.0B; net interest income $66.7B).
- Investment banking fees: Declined due to volatile markets leading to lower equity/debt underwriting and advisory activity in CIB.
- Principal transactions: Increased on strong Fixed Income Markets (notably Currencies & Emerging Markets and Rates) and Equity Derivatives/Prime Finance; partially offset by:
  - $836M loss in Credit Adjustments & Other (funding spread widening; Russia/commodities exposures),
  - Net markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (CIB and CB),
  - Higher losses on legacy private equity (Corporate),
  - Net losses in Treasury & CIO tied to cash deployment (offset by related NII).
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Up on higher service fee volume in CCB, mostly offset by greater client earnings credits reducing cash management fees in CB and CIB.
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Down due to lower AWM management fees (market declines), lower custody fees (Securities Services), and lower brokerage commissions; partially offset by higher travel-related and annuity commissions in CCB and reduced money market fund fee waivers plus net inflows.
- Investment securities gains/losses: Larger net losses from sales of MBS and U.S. Treasuries due to portfolio repositioning in Treasury & CIO.
- Mortgage fees and related income: Down on lower production margins and volumes; largely offset by higher servicing income (no prior-year MSR risk-management loss and more third-party loans serviced).
- Card income: Down due to higher amortization of new account origination costs; partly offset by higher annual fees and increased commercial card payments revenue in CIB and CB.
- Other income: Down on lower auto operating lease income and investment losses in CIB/AWM; offsets included a $914M gain on sale of Visa B shares, other investment gains, insurance settlement proceeds, a gain on an equity-method investment in CB, favorable FX impacts on net investment hedges (Treasury & CIO), and absence of prior-year weather-related write-downs.
- Net interest income: Increased on higher rates and loan growth, partially offset by lower Markets NII. Average interest-earning assets were ~$3.3T with a 2.78% yield; net yield 2.00% (up 36 bps); net yield excluding Markets 2.60% (up 69 bps).
- Notes: CIB Markets performance assessed on a total revenue basis; references provided to segment discussions, non-GAAP reconciliations, and detailed schedules.

nodes.title: Provision for credit losses
nodes.heading: 7.4.2 Provision for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase:
The provision for credit losses was $6.4 billion, reflecting a 
net addition of $3.5 billion to the allowance for credit 
losses and $2.9 billion of net charge-offs.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Summary of JPMorgan Chase’s provision for credit losses for 2022, with comparisons to 2021 and 2020, drivers of changes, and segment-level references.

- Key figures (in millions):
  - Total provision for credit losses: 2022 $6,389; 2021 $(9,256); 2020 $17,480.
  - By category (2022 / 2021 / 2020):
    - Consumer, excluding credit card: $506 / $(1,933) / $1,016
    - Credit card: $3,353 / $(4,838) / $10,886
    - Total consumer: $3,859 / $(6,771) / $11,902
    - Wholesale: $2,476 / $(2,449) / $5,510
    - Investment securities: $54 / $(36) / $68

- 2022 vs. 2021 drivers:
  - 2022 provision of $6.4B reflects:
    - Net addition to allowance for credit losses of $3.5B, comprised of:
      - $2.3B in wholesale, driven by a deteriorating macroeconomic outlook and loan growth (predominantly in CB and CIB).
      - $1.2B in consumer, predominantly Card Services, due to higher outstanding balances and a weaker macro outlook, partially offset by reduced uncertainty as pandemic effects recede.
    - Net charge-offs of $2.9B, flat year-over-year.
  - 2021 included a $12.1B net reduction in the allowance for credit losses.

- Macroeconomic context:
  - Deterioration in the Firm’s outlook, with the Q4 2022 central scenario reflecting a mild recession.
  - Increased weighting of adverse scenarios beginning Q1 2022 due to higher inflation, monetary policy shifts, and geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine.

- Net charge-offs detail (2022 vs. 2021):
  - Card Services: $309M decrease, reflecting continued U.S. consumer strength; median deposit balances declined in H2 2022 amid higher spending.
  - Auto and Banking & Wealth Management: $190M increase as prior-year results benefited from government stimulus and payment assistance.
  - CIB: $76M increase.

- References: Further detail indicated in segment discussions (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM), Allowance for Credit Losses section, and Notes 1, 10, and 13 of the 2022 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Noninterest expense
nodes.heading: 7.4.3 Noninterest expense
nodes.start_phrase:
Compensation expense increased driven by additional 
headcount, primarily in technology and operations, as well 
as front office, and the impact of inflation , partially offset 
by lower revenue-related compensation in CIB.
nodes.summary:
- Presents noninterest expense details for 2022, 2021, and 2020, totaling $76,140m, $71,343m, and $66,656m, respectively.
- Compensation expense rose to $41,636m in 2022, driven by headcount growth (technology, operations, front office) and inflation, partially offset by lower revenue-related compensation in CIB.
- Noncompensation expense totaled $34,504m in 2022; key categories include occupancy, technology/communications/equipment, professional and outside services, marketing, and other.
- 2022 vs. 2021 noncompensation drivers: higher business investments (marketing and technology) and higher structural costs (travel and entertainment, regulatory assessments, occupancy from higher utilities and lease exit costs, and other employee-related expense); partially offset by lower volume-related costs (lower depreciation from reduced Auto lease assets and lower AWM distribution fees), higher operating losses and outside services in CCB, and lower legal expense.
- Notes: technology/communications/equipment includes depreciation on auto operating lease assets; “Other” includes firmwide legal expense of $266m (2022), $426m (2021), and $1.1b (2020). 2021 included a $550m contribution to the Firm’s Foundation.
- Income tax section provides income before tax ($46,166m in 2022; $59,562m in 2021; $35,815m in 2020), income tax expense ($8,490m; $11,228m; $6,684m), and effective tax rates (18.4%; 18.9%; 18.7%).
- 2022 effective tax rate decreased vs. 2021 due to tax audit settlement benefits, largely offset by other tax adjustments and changes in the level and mix of income and expenses across jurisdictions.

The effective tax rate decreased driven b y incom e tax 
benefits compared with income tax expense in the prior 
year related to tax audit settlements, largely offset by other 
tax adjustments a nd a change in the level and mix of 
income and expenses subject to U.S. federal and state and

nodes.summary:
- Presents a three-year breakdown (2020–2022) of noninterest expense, totaling $76.1B in 2022, $71.3B in 2021, and $66.7B in 2020, split into compensation and noncompensation categories.
- Details noncompensation components: occupancy; technology, communications and equipment (includes depreciation on auto operating lease assets); professional and outside services; marketing; and other.
- Discloses Firmwide legal expense included in “Other”: $266M (2022), $426M (2021), $1.1B (2020).
- Explains 2022 vs. 2021 changes:
  - Compensation expense increased due to higher headcount (technology, operations, front office) and inflation, partly offset by lower revenue-related compensation in CIB.
  - Noncompensation expense rose from increased business investments (marketing, technology) and higher structural costs (travel and entertainment, regulatory assessments, occupancy from higher utilities and lease exit costs, other employee-related expenses).
  - Offsets included lower volume-related costs (reduced depreciation from lower Auto lease assets; lower AWM distribution fees), partially offset by higher operating losses and outside services in CCB, and lower legal expense.

- Summarizes income tax results for 2020–2022: pretax income of $46.2B (2022), $59.6B (2021), $35.8B (2020); tax expense of $8.5B, $11.2B, $6.7B; effective tax rates of 18.4%, 18.9%, and 18.7%, respectively.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEETS AND CASH FLOWS ANALYSIS
nodes.heading: 7.5 CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEETS AND CASH FLOWS ANALYSIS
nodes.start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 .
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Analysis of significant year-over-year changes in JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated balance sheet between December 31, 2022 and 2021, with selected data and drivers.
- Overall size: Total assets decreased 2% to $3.666 trillion.
- Liquidity and cash:
  - Cash and due from banks increased 5%; deposits with banks fell 24% due to lower deposits across lines of business and loan growth; excess cash placements at central banks noted.
- Securities financing and trading:
  - Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements rose 21% from lower netting, higher demand to cover shorts in Fixed Income Markets, and increased Treasury/CIO cash deployment.
  - Securities borrowed fell 10% on lower client-driven activity and reduced demand to cover equity shorts.
  - Trading assets increased 5% on higher FX derivative receivables and Treasury/CIO cash deployment.
- Investment securities:
  - Net investment securities declined 6%: AFS down 33% (paydowns and unrealized losses in AOCI, partly offset by net purchases); HTM up 17% driven by $78.3 billion transfer from AFS to HTM for capital management and additional purchases (partly offset by paydowns).
- Loans and credit quality:
  - Loans increased 5% driven by higher Card Services balances (spending and originations), increased originations and revolver utilization in Commercial Banking, and higher wholesale loans in CIB; partially offset by lower Home Lending mortgage warehouse loans (sales outpacing originations amid higher rates) and PPP loan forgiveness.
  - Allowance for loan losses rose 20% (net addition of $3.3 billion): $2.1 billion in wholesale (worsened macro outlook and growth in CB/CIB) and $1.2 billion in consumer (mainly Card Services; higher balances and softer outlook), partially offset by reduced pandemic-related uncertainty. Additional $121 million added to the allowance for lending-related commitments (other liabilities).
- Other notable line items:
  - Accrued interest and accounts receivable up 22%; goodwill/MSRs/intangibles up 7%; premises and equipment up 2%; other assets up 1%.

nodes.title: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
nodes.heading: 7.5.1 Consolidated balance sheets analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 .
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Year-over-year analysis of consolidated balance sheets (Dec 31, 2022 vs. 2021), highlighting major drivers across assets, liabilities, and equity.

- Total assets: Down 2% to $3.666T.
  - Cash and deposits with banks: Declined due to lower deposits across lines of business and loan growth; excess cash placements at central banks decreased.
  - Federal funds sold/resale agreements: Up on lower netting, higher demand to cover shorts in Fixed Income Markets, and greater cash deployment in Treasury/CIO.
  - Securities borrowed: Down on lower client activity and reduced demand to cover equity shorts.
  - Trading assets: Up, driven by higher FX derivative receivables and Treasury/CIO cash deployment.
  - Investment securities: Down overall; AFS declined (paydowns, unrealized losses in AOCI), HTM increased (purchases and a $78.3B transfer from AFS to HTM for capital management).
  - Loans: Up 5%, led by Card (spend and originations), CB originations/revolver utilization, and CIB wholesale loans; offset by lower Home Lending mortgage warehouse balances (rate-driven) and PPP forgiveness.
  - Allowance for loan losses: Up 20% to $19.7B; net build of $3.3B (wholesale $2.1B on weaker macro and growth; consumer $1.2B mainly Card and macro), partly offset by reduced pandemic-related uncertainty; plus $121M build for lending-related commitments and $54M for investment securities.
  - Accrued interest/receivables: Up on client-driven Markets activity and Payments timing (year-end weekend).
  - Goodwill/MSRs/intangibles: Up due to higher MSRs (rates) and acquisitions (Renovite, Global Shares, Figg, Frosch, Volkswagen Payments).
  - Other assets: Up from securities financing activities, partly offset by lower auto operating lease assets.

- Total liabilities: Down 2% to $3.373T.
  - Deposits: Down 5%; CB/CIB attrition (notably non-operating), outflows to AWM amid rising rates, and CCB balance declines from higher spending (partly offset by inflows to new accounts).
  - Federal funds purchased/repurchase agreements: Up on higher secured financing of trading assets in Markets, partly offset by lower secured financing of AFS in Treasury/CIO.
  - Short-term borrowings: Down on reduced Markets financing needs.
  - Trading liabilities: Up on client-driven market-making and higher short positions.
  - Accounts payable/other liabilities: Up on higher client payables (Markets, Prime Finance) and Payments timing (year-end weekend).
  - Beneficial interests in consolidated VIEs: Up on higher commercial paper issuance tied to increased conduit loan balances.
  - Long-term debt: Down; fair value hedge adjustments (higher rates) and lower FV of structured notes offset by net issuances of senior debt and structured notes.

- Stockholders’ equity: Down 1% to $292.3B, reflecting net unrealized AOCI losses from higher rates impacting AFS securities and cash flow hedges in Treasury/CIO.

- Themes: Balance sheet mix shift toward HTM from AFS; rate environment pressured AOCI; increased repo-style activity and trading-related balances; credit reserve builds on macro deterioration and portfolio growth; timing effects from year-end weekend influenced receivables/payables.

nodes.title: Consolidated cash flows analysis
nodes.heading: 7.5.2 Consolidated cash flows analysis
nodes.start_phrase:
The following is a discussion of cash flow activities during 
the years ended D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 .
nodes.summary:
Summary of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated cash flows analysis for 2022 and 2021, with comparative table including 2020:

- Operating activities: Provided $107.1B in 2022 (vs. $78.1B in 2021; used $79.9B in 2020). 2022 inflows driven by higher accounts payable/other liabilities, lower securities borrowed, and net proceeds from sales, securitizations, and paydowns of loans held-for-sale, partially offset by higher trading assets. 2021 inflows driven by lower trading assets and higher payables/other liabilities, partially offset by higher securities borrowed and lower trading liabilities. The Firm notes operating assets/liabilities can vary significantly with client activity, risk management, and markets, and believes liquidity sources are sufficient for operating needs.

- Investing activities: Used $137.8B in 2022 (vs. $129.3B in 2021; $261.9B in 2020). 2022 outflows from net loan originations and higher securities purchased under resale agreements, partially offset by net proceeds from investment securities. 2021 outflows from net purchases of investment securities and higher net loan originations, partially offset by lower securities purchased under resale agreements.

- Financing activities: Used $126.3B in 2022 (vs. provided $276.0B in 2021; $596.6B in 2020). 2022 outflows reflect lower deposits, partially offset by net proceeds from long- and short-term borrowings. 2021 inflows reflect higher deposits and net borrowing proceeds, partially offset by a decrease in securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements. In both periods, cash was used for share repurchases and dividends on common and preferred stock.

- Effect of exchange rate changes on cash: $(16.6)B in 2022 vs. $(11.5)B in 2021 (vs. $9.2B in 2020).

- Net change in cash and due from banks and deposits with banks: Decrease of $173.6B in 2022 vs. increase of $213.2B in 2021 (vs. $264.0B in 2020).

- Cross-references provided to related sections: Consolidated Balance Sheets Analysis, Capital Risk Management, Liquidity Risk Management, and the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows.

nodes.title: EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
nodes.heading: 7.6 EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm prepares its Consolidated Financial Statements in 
accordance with U.S. GAAP; these financial statements 
appear on pages 159-163 .
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Explains the firm’s use of non-GAAP financial measures and provides a reconciliation from U.S. GAAP (“reported”) results to “managed” basis results.
- Reported vs. managed basis:
  - Reported basis follows U.S. GAAP and is comparable year-to-year and across companies.
  - Managed basis is a non-GAAP view used by management at the firm and business-segment levels (including the overhead ratio). It starts with GAAP results and applies fully taxable-equivalent (FTE) reclassifications so revenue from tax-exempt items is comparable to taxable revenue.
- Mechanics of FTE adjustments:
  - Revenue from tax-exempt securities and tax-credit investments is grossed up to a taxable-equivalent basis.
  - The offsetting tax impact is recorded in income tax expense.
  - These adjustments do not affect net income for the firm or the lines of business (LOBs).
- Rationale: Managed non-GAAP measures help management and investors assess underlying operational performance and trends and facilitate comparisons with competitors, though such measures may not be comparable to similarly labeled metrics used by other companies.
- Reconciliation highlights (years ended December 31):
  - 2022: FTE adjustments add $3.6B to total net revenue (from $128.7B reported to $132.3B managed); overhead ratio improves from 59% (reported) to 58% (managed); income tax expense increases by $3.6B; net income unchanged at $37.7B.
  - 2021: FTE adjustments add $3.7B (from $121.6B to $125.3B); overhead ratio improves from 59% to 57%; income tax expense increases by $3.7B; net income unchanged at $48.3B.
  - 2020: FTE adjustments add $3.0B (from $120.0B to $122.9B); overhead ratio improves from 56% to 54%; income tax expense increases by $3.0B; net income unchanged at $29.1B.
- Line-item effects:
  - FTE adjustments affect other income, total noninterest revenue, net interest income, total net revenue, pre-provision profit, income before tax, and income tax expense.
  - Provision for credit losses and total noninterest expense are unchanged by FTE adjustments.
- Segment note: FTE adjustments are predominantly recognized in CIB, CB, and Corporate; the firm also reviews LOB results on a managed basis.
- Cross-references: GAAP financial statements appear on pages 159–163; additional non-GAAP segment information is in Business Segment Results on pages 61–80.

nodes.title: Non-GAAP financial measures
nodes.heading: 7.6.1 Non-GAAP financial measures
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm prepares its Consolidated Financial Statements in 
accordance with U.S. GAAP; these financial statements 
appear on pages 159-163 .
nodes.summary:
- The firm reports results under U.S. GAAP (“reported” basis) and also presents non-GAAP “managed” basis results used by management to assess performance, including the overhead ratio.
- Managed basis starts with GAAP results and applies fully taxable-equivalent (FTE) reclassifications so tax-exempt revenues are comparable to taxable revenues; the offsetting tax impact is recorded in income tax expense.
- These FTE adjustments change revenue, pre-provision profit, and income tax expense but have no impact on net income for the firm or lines of business (LOBs).
- Management also uses other non-GAAP measures at the firm and segment level to evaluate underlying operational trends and compare with competitors; such measures may not be comparable to similarly named metrics at other companies.
- References: Consolidated Financial Statements (pages 159–163) and Business Segment Results (pages 61–80) for more detail on non-GAAP measures.
- A reconciliation table (2022, 2021, 2020) bridges reported to managed basis, showing:
  - FTE adjustments that increase total net revenue by $3.6B (2022), $3.7B (2021), and $3.0B (2020), primarily recognized in CIB, CB, and Corporate.
  - Total noninterest expense and provision for credit losses unchanged by these adjustments.
  - Income tax expense increased by the same FTE amounts, leaving net income unchanged.
  - Overhead ratio slightly lower on a managed basis (e.g., 58% vs. 59% in 2022; 57% vs. 59% in 2021; 54% vs. 56% in 2020); FTE column for the ratio is not meaningful (NM).

nodes.title: Net interest income, net yield, and noninterest revenue excluding CIB Markets
nodes.heading: 7.6.2 Net interest income, net yield, and noninterest revenue excluding CIB Markets
nodes.start_phrase:
In addition to reviewing net interest income, net yield, and 
noninterest revenue on a managed basis, management also 
reviews these metrics excluding CIB Markets, as shown 
below.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the section: Management’s use of non-GAAP metrics that exclude CIB Markets (Fixed Income and Equity Markets) to evaluate JPMorgan Chase’s core lending, investing/ALM, and deposit-raising activities without Markets-driven volatility. CIB Markets performance is assessed on a total revenue basis. These alternative views are intended to help investors analyze revenue trends.

- Reported vs managed basis: Net interest income (NII) and noninterest revenue are presented on both a reported and fully taxable-equivalent (FTE) managed basis; interest includes hedge effects.

- Key 2022–2020 metrics:
  - NII (managed): $67.1B (2022), $52.7B (2021), $55.0B (2020).
  - Markets NII: $4.8B (2022), $8.2B (2021), $8.4B (2020).
  - NII excluding Markets: $62.4B (2022), $44.5B (2021), $46.6B (2020).
  - Average interest-earning assets excluding Markets: $2.40T (2022), $2.33T (2021), $2.03T (2020).
  - Net yield (managed): 2.00% (2022), 1.64% (2021), 1.98% (2020).
  - Net yield on Markets assets: 0.50% (2022), 0.93% (2021), 1.11% (2020).
  - Net yield excluding Markets: 2.60% (2022), 1.91% (2021), 2.30% (2020).
  - Noninterest revenue (managed): $65.1B (2022), $72.6B (2021), $67.9B (2020).
  - Markets noninterest revenue: $24.2B (2022), $19.2B (2021), $21.1B (2020).
  - Noninterest revenue excluding Markets: $40.9B (2022), $53.4B (2021), $46.8B (2020).
  - Memo: Total Markets net revenue: $29.0B (2022), $27.4B (2021), $29.5B (2020).

- Observed trends: In 2022, NII and net yield excluding Markets rose notably versus 2021, while Markets NII and Markets yield declined; noninterest revenue excluding Markets decreased year over year; total Markets net revenue increased versus 2021.

- Definitions of GAAP and non-GAAP performance measures:
  - BVPS = common stockholders’ equity / common shares at period-end.
  - Overhead ratio = total noninterest expense / total net revenue.
  - ROA = reported net income / total average assets.
  - ROE = net income applicable to common equity / average common stockholders’ equity.
  - ROTCE = net income applicable to common equity / average tangible common equity.
  - TBVPS = tangible common equity / common shares at period-end.

- Additional non-GAAP measures reviewed:
  - Adjusted expense: noninterest expense excluding Firmwide legal expense.
  - Pre-provision profit: total net revenue less total noninterest expense.
  - Allowance for loan losses to period-end loans retained excluding trade finance and conduits, to better assess CIB’s allowance coverage ratio.

nodes.title: Calculation of certain U.S. GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures
nodes.heading: 7.6.2.1 Calculation of certain U.S. GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures
nodes.start_phrase:
Certain U.S. GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures are calculated as 
follows:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Presentation of net interest income, net yield, and noninterest revenue on a managed basis and explicitly excluding CIB Markets (Fixed Income and Equity Markets) to isolate core lending, investing/ALM, and deposit activities from Markets-related volatility. These exclusions are non-GAAP measures.

- Management’s approach: 
  - Reviews the above metrics both including and excluding CIB Markets; evaluates CIB Markets primarily on total revenue due to offsets across revenue lines.
  - Uses taxable-equivalent (FTE) adjustments and includes hedge effects in interest.
  - Believes these alternative measures help investors analyze revenue trends and firm performance.

- 2020–2022 highlights (in millions, except rates):
  - Net interest income (managed) increased to $67,144 in 2022 (from $52,741 in 2021); excluding Markets rose to $62,355 in 2022 (from $44,498).
  - Average interest-earning assets excluding Markets grew to $2,395,884 in 2022.
  - Net yield on average interest-earning assets excluding Markets improved to 2.60% in 2022 (from 1.91% in 2021), while Markets yield declined to 0.50%.
  - Noninterest revenue (managed) declined to $65,133 in 2022 (from $72,563); excluding Markets fell to $40,938 (from $53,412), while Markets noninterest revenue rose to $24,195.
  - Memo: Total Markets net revenue was $28,984 in 2022.

- Footnotes/references: Interest includes hedge effects; FTE used where applicable; additional CIB Markets details referenced on pages 70–71.

- Defined GAAP and non-GAAP metrics:
  - BVPS, TBVPS, ROA, ROE, ROTCE, and Overhead ratio (formulas provided).
  - Adjusted expense (excludes Firmwide legal expense).
  - Pre-provision profit (total net revenue less total noninterest expense).

- Additional non-GAAP review: Allowance for loan losses to period-end loans retained excluding trade finance and conduits to provide a more meaningful CIB allowance coverage ratio.

nodes.title: TCE, ROTCE and TBVPS
nodes.heading: 7.6.3 TCE, ROTCE and TBVPS
nodes.start_phrase: TCE, ROTCE and TBVPS are each non-GAAP financial measures.
nodes.summary:
- Defines three non-GAAP measures used to assess the Firm’s use of equity: Tangible Common Equity (TCE), Return on Tangible Common Equity (ROTCE), and Tangible Book Value per Share (TBVPS).
- TCE is calculated as common stockholders’ equity minus goodwill and identifiable intangible assets (other than MSRs), plus related deferred tax liabilities.
- ROTCE measures net income applicable to common equity as a percentage of average TCE.
- TBVPS equals TCE at period-end divided by common shares at period-end.
- Provides a reconciliation from common stockholders’ equity to TCE for period-end Dec 31, 2022 and Dec 31, 2021, and averages for 2022, 2021, and 2020:
  - Common stockholders’ equity: $264,928m (2022 PE), $259,289m (2021 PE); averages $253,068m (2022), $250,968m (2021), $236,865m (2020)
  - Less goodwill: $51,662m; $50,315m; averages $50,952m; $49,584m; $47,820m
  - Less other intangibles: $1,224m; $882m; averages $1,112m; $876m; $781m
  - Add certain deferred tax liabilities: $2,510m; $2,499m; averages $2,505m; $2,474m; $2,399m
  - Resulting TCE: $214,552m; $210,591m; averages $203,509m; $202,982m; $190,663m
- Reports ROTCE of 18% (2022), 23% (2021), and 14% (2020); TBVPS of $73.12 (Dec 31, 2022) and $71.53 (Dec 31, 2021).
- Notes that the deferred tax liabilities added back are related to tax-deductible goodwill and identifiable intangibles created in nontaxable transactions and are netted against those assets when calculating TCE.

nodes.title: BUSINESS SEGMENT RESULTS
nodes.heading: 7.7 BUSINESS SEGMENT RESULTS
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and structure: JPMorgan Chase reports results on a line‑of‑business (LOB) managed basis with four major reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment. In Q4 2022, Consumer & Business Banking was renamed Banking & Wealth Management (BWM) within CCB, and Card & Auto was renamed Card Services & Auto.
- Segment scope and activities:
  - CCB: Banking & Wealth Management (Consumer Banking, J.P. Morgan Wealth Management, Business Banking), Home Lending (Production, Servicing, Real Estate Portfolios), and Card Services & Auto.
  - CIB: Investment Banking, Payments, Lending, Markets (Fixed Income and Equity), Securities Services, and Credit Adjustments & Other.
  - CB: Middle Market Banking, Corporate Client Banking, and Commercial Real Estate Banking.
  - AWM: Asset Management and Global Private Bank.
- Segment reporting methodology: Results are presented as if each segment were a stand‑alone business, with allocations of certain income and expenses, and an assessed equity (capital) level for each LOB. Assumptions and methodologies are periodically reassessed and may be refined.
- Revenue sharing: Revenue from joint client activities is recognized in the segment responsible for the product/service and allocated to participating segments under revenue‑sharing agreements.
- Expense allocation: Costs for services provided by corporate support units or other segments are generally allocated based on actual cost and usage. Certain corporate support, technology, and operations costs not currently utilized by LOBs are retained in Corporate.
- Funds transfer pricing (FTP): Allocates interest income/expense to LOBs and transfers primary interest rate and liquidity risk to Treasury and CIO. Methodologies are updated periodically. In 2022’s rising rate environment, asset funding costs increased and deposit margins expanded.
- Foreign exchange risk: Certain FX risks from LOBs and Other Corporate are centralized in Treasury and CIO; related P&L from FX rate movements is reported there.
- Debt expense and preferred stock dividends: Nearly all credit spread costs of unsecured long‑term debt and preferred dividends are allocated to LOBs based on regulatory capital alignment and funding needs; debt cost flows through segment net interest income; preferred dividends reduce net income applicable to common equity.
- Capital allocation: Equity assigned to segments reflects Basel III Standardized and Advanced RWA, the GSIB surcharge, and severe‑stress simulations. Allocations are reassessed at least annually; updates as of January 1, 2023 reflect changes in firm capital requirements and LOB RWA.
- Segment results (managed basis) for 2022–2020: Tables present total net revenue, noninterest expense, pre‑provision profit, provision for credit losses, net income/(loss), and ROE by segment and in total.
  - 2022 highlights: Firm total net revenue $132.3B; net income $37.7B; ROE 14%. CCB: revenue $55.0B, net income $14.9B, ROE 29%. CIB: revenue $47.9B, net income $15.0B, ROE 14%. CB: revenue $11.5B, net income $4.2B, ROE 16%. AWM: revenue $17.7B, net income $4.4B, ROE 25%. Corporate: net loss $0.7B.
- Selected firmwide metrics:
  - Wealth Management (Global Private Bank in AWM and J.P. Morgan Wealth Management in CCB): client assets $2.44T; 8,166 client advisors (2022).
  - J.P. Morgan Payments (activities in CIB and CB): total net revenue $13.9B; merchant processing volume $2.16T; average deposits $779B (2022).
- The section sets up a comparative discussion of segment results for the years ended December 31, 2022 and 2021.

nodes.title: CONSUMER & COMMUNITY BANKING
nodes.heading: 7.7.1 CONSUMER & COMMUNITY BANKING
nodes.start_phrase:
Consumer & Community Banking offers products and 
services to consumers and small businesses through 
bank branches, ATMs, digital (including mobile and 
online) and telephone banking.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and structure of JPMorgan Chase’s Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) segment, including distribution channels (branches, ATMs, digital, phone) and organization into Banking & Wealth Management (BWM), Home Lending, and Card Services & Auto, with a summary of each unit’s offerings (deposits, investments, lending, cash management, payments, mortgages, credit cards/travel, auto loans and leases).
- Segment financials for 2020–2022: revenue composition (net interest income vs. noninterest revenue), total net revenue ($55.0B in 2022), provision for credit losses, noninterest expense, pretax income, income taxes, and net income ($14.9B in 2022).
- Revenue by line of business in 2022: BWM $30.3B, Home Lending $3.7B, Card Services & Auto $21.1B; mortgage fees detail (production vs. net servicing, including MSR risk management impacts).
- Key ratios: return on equity (29% in 2022) and overhead ratio (57%).
- 2022 vs. 2021 performance drivers:
  - Net income down 29% driven by higher provision for credit losses (vs. a prior-year net benefit).
  - Net revenue up 10%; net interest income up 22% from margin expansion on higher rates, BWM deposit growth, and higher revolving balances in Card; partially offset by PPP forgiveness impacts in BWM and tighter Home Lending spreads.
  - Noninterest revenue down 13% on lower mortgage production margins/volume, lower auto operating lease income, and higher amortization of new card account origination costs; partially offset by higher net mortgage servicing revenue (absence of prior-year MSR losses), higher travel-related commissions and annuity sales, and higher deposit-related fees.
  - Noninterest expense up 8% on investments and higher compensation, technology, and marketing; partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation; higher operating losses noted.
  - Provision for credit losses of $3.8B: net charge-offs of $2.7B (down y/y, with Card lower, offset by higher Auto and BWM), and a $1.1B allowance build (primarily Card on higher balances and a weaker macro outlook, plus Home Lending), versus a $9.8B allowance release in 2021.
- Balance sheet metrics (period-end and average): total assets (~$514B period-end 2022), loans by business (BWM, Home Lending, Card, Auto), deposits (~$1.13T period-end; ~$1.16T average), equity ($50B), and headcount (135K).
- Credit quality and allowances: nonaccrual loans ($3.9B); net charge-offs by business (Card $2.4B, etc.) and total NCO rate (0.62%); delinquency metrics (Home Lending, Card, Auto); allowance for loan losses by business (total $13.5B), with notes on exclusions for government-insured/guaranteed and PPP loans and COVID-related deferrals.
- Customer and activity metrics: CCB households (69.3M), branches (4,787), active digital (63.1M) and mobile (49.7M) customers, debit/credit sales volume ($1.56T), and total payments transaction volume ($5.6T).
- Banking & Wealth Management specifics: average deposits ($1.15T) and deposit margin (1.71%); Business Banking average loans ($22.3B) and originations ($4.3B, reflecting PPP wind-down); client investment assets ($647B) and advisor count.
- Home Lending specifics: sharp decline in originations to $65.4B (retail $38.5B, correspondent $26.9B), higher third‑party servicing ($584B), and higher MSR carrying value ($8.0B).
- Card Services specifics: higher sales volume ($1.06T), net revenue rate (9.87%) and net yield (9.77%), and increased new accounts (9.6M).
- Auto specifics: lower loan/lease originations ($30.4B) and reduced average operating lease assets ($14.3B), reflecting normalization from prior peaks.
- Notable footnotes and changes: segment renamings in 4Q22 (Consumer & Business Banking to Banking & Wealth Management; Card & Auto to Card Services & Auto); disclosure of operating lease income and depreciation trends; PPP loan balances and guarantees; MSR risk management results.

nodes.title: CORPORATE & INVESTMENT BANK
nodes.heading: 7.7.2 CORPORATE & INVESTMENT BANK
nodes.start_phrase:
The Corporate & Investment Bank, which consists of 
Banking and Markets & Securities Services, offers a 
broad suite of investment banking, market-making, 
prime brokerage, lending, and treasury and securities 
products and services to a global client base of 
corporations, investors, financial institutions, 
merchants, government and municipal entities.
nodes.summary:
- Scope of business: Describes JPMorgan Chase’s Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB) and its two pillars—Banking (Investment Banking, Payments, Lending) and Markets & Securities Services. Outlines services including M&A and capital markets advisory, equity/debt underwriting, loan origination and syndication, cross-border financing, payments and treasury, global market-making in cash and derivatives, risk management solutions, prime brokerage, research, custody, fund accounting/administration, and securities lending for global corporates, financial institutions, investors, governments and municipalities.

- 2022 vs. 2021 performance highlights:
  - Net income $15.0B, down 29%; total net revenue $47.9B, down 7%.
  - Banking revenue $15.3B, down 23%:
    - Investment Banking $6.5B, down 48% on lower fees across products amid volatile markets; $251MM markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions; still ranked #1 for Global IB fees (Dealogic).
      - Equity underwriting $1.0B, down 74%; debt underwriting $2.8B, down 43%; advisory $3.1B, down 30%.
    - Payments $7.4B, up 18%; excluding net impact of equity investments, $7.8B, up 33% on deposit margin expansion and higher fee volumes.
    - Lending $1.4B, up 38% on higher net interest income from loan growth and gains on hedges (vs. prior-year losses).
  - Markets & Securities Services revenue $32.6B, up 2%; Markets $29.0B, up 6%:
    - Fixed Income Markets $18.6B, up 10% (strength in Currencies & Emerging Markets and Rates; weaker Securitized Products).
    - Equity Markets $10.4B, down 2% (lower Cash Equities, offset by Equity Derivatives).
    - Securities Services $4.5B, up 4% (deposit margin expansion and fee growth, offset by lower average AUC market values and deposits).
    - Credit Adjustments & Other: loss of $836MM (funding spread widening; exposures related to commodities and Russia), vs. $250MM gain in 2021.
  - Noninterest expense $27.1B, up 7% (structural expense and investments, higher compensation; partly offset by lower revenue-related comp and legal expense).
  - Provision for credit losses $1.2B (net addition driven by macro deterioration and loan growth) vs. prior-year net benefit of $1.2B.

- Income statement detail (2022/2021/2020):
  - Noninterest revenue $36.0B/$38.2B/$35.1B; net interest income $11.9B/$13.5B/$14.2B.
  - Compensation expense $13.9B/$13.1B/$11.6B; noncompensation expense $13.2B/$12.2B/$11.9B.
  - Footnotes: card income ~$1.0B/$910MM/$840MM; tax-equivalent adjustments tied to alternative energy credits, affordable housing investments, and tax-exempt municipal bond income ~$3.0B/$3.0B/$2.4B.

- Financial ratios (2022/2021/2020):
  - Return on equity: 14%/25%/20%.
  - Overhead ratio: 57/49/48.
  - Compensation expense as % of total net revenue: 29%/25%/24%.

- Revenue by business (2022/2021/2020):
  - Banking: $15.263B/$19.777B/$15.577B (Investment Banking $6.510B/$12.506B/$8.871B; Payments $7.376B/$6.270B/$5.560B; Lending $1.377B/$1.001B/$1.146B).
  - Markets & Securities Services: $32.636B/$31.972B/$33.707B (Fixed Income $18.617B/$16.865B/$20.878B; Equity $10.367B/$10.529B/$8.605B; Securities Services $4.488B/$4.328B/$4.253B; Credit Adjustments & Other $(836)MM/$250MM/$(29)MM). Notes on centrally managed CVA/FVA and valuation adjustments.

- Balance sheet and operating metrics:
  - Period-end (2022): total assets $1.334T; total loans $229.9B (retained $187.6B; held-for-sale/fair value $42.3B); equity $103B.
  - Averages (2022): total assets $1.406T; trading assets—debt/equity $405.9B; derivative receivables $77.8B; total loans $219.5B.
  - Headcount: 73,452 (vs. 67,546 in 2021; 61,733 in 2020).

- Credit quality (2022/2021/2020):
  - Net charge-offs/(recoveries): $82MM/$6MM/$370MM; NCO rate 0.05%/~0%/0.27% (excludes HFS/fair value loans).
  - Nonperforming assets: $1.95B/$1.84B/$2.81B; nonaccrual loans $1.57B/$1.43B/$2.67B (excludes certain government-insured mortgages).
  - Allowance for credit losses: $3.74B ($2.29B loans; $1.45B lending-related commitments) vs. $2.72B/$3.90B.
  - Coverage/quality ratios: ALL to loans retained 1.22% (1.77% in 2020); to loans retained ex trade finance/conduits 1.67%; ALL to nonaccrual loans retained 319%; nonaccrual loans to total loans 0.68%.

- Investment banking fees breakdown (2022/2021/2020):
  - Advisory $3.051B/$4.381B/$2.368B; Equity underwriting $1.034B/$3.953B/$2.758B; Debt underwriting $2.844B/$5.025B/$4.351B; total $6.929B/$13.359B/$9.477B (long-term debt includes loan syndications).

- League table standings (Dealogic):
  - 2022 ranks: #1 Global investment banking fees (8.0% share); #2 Global M&A (8.2%); #1 Global equity & equity-related; #1 Global long-term debt; #1 Global loan syndications; consistently top-ranked in U.S. across categories.

- Markets revenue methodology:
  - Markets performance assessed on total revenue (principal transactions, fees/commissions/other income, net interest income) due to offsets across line items.
  - Defines principal transactions revenue and “inventory-related revenue”; notes drivers including client activity, bid-offer spreads, market liquidity and volatility, and macro factors (rates, FX, credit spreads, equity/commodity prices).

nodes.title: COMMERCIAL BANKING
nodes.heading: 7.7.3 COMMERCIAL BANKING
nodes.start_phrase:
Commercial Banking provides comprehensive financial 
solutions, including lending, payments, investment 
banking and asset management products across three 
primary client segments: Middle Market Banking, 
Corporate Client Banking and Commercial Real Estate 
Banking.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s Commercial Banking segment, its comprehensive financial solutions (lending, payments, investment banking, asset management), and its primary client segments:
  - Middle Market Banking (small/midsized companies, local governments, nonprofits)
  - Corporate Client Banking (large corporations)
  - Commercial Real Estate Banking (investors, developers, and owners across multifamily, office, retail, industrial, affordable housing)
  - “Other” for amounts not aligned with a primary segment
- Selected income statement data for 2020–2022, detailing:
  - Noninterest revenue, net interest income, total net revenue
  - Provision for credit losses
  - Noninterest expense (compensation and noncompensation)
  - Income before tax, income tax expense, and net income
- Footnotes:
  - Card income amounts for 2022, 2021, 2020
  - Tax-equivalent adjustments related to tax credits and tax‑exempt income from municipal financing
- 2022 vs. 2021 performance commentary:
  - Net income of $4.2B, down 20%, driven by a swing to a higher provision for credit losses versus a prior-year net benefit
  - Total net revenue of $11.5B, up 15%
  - Net interest income of $8.2B, up 35%, benefiting from higher rates (deposit margin expansion) and loan growth, partially offset by higher funding costs and lower deposits
  - Noninterest revenue of $3.3B, down 15%, on lower investment banking revenue and net markdowns on held-for-sale positions in the bridge financing portfolio; partially offset by a gain on an equity method investment received in partial satisfaction of a loan
  - Noninterest expense of $4.7B, up 17%, due to higher volume/revenue-related costs, structural expense (including compensation), and payments growth
  - Provision for credit losses of $1.3B reflecting allowance build from a deteriorating macro outlook and loan growth, versus a $947MM net benefit in 2021

nodes.title: CB product revenue consists of the following:
nodes.heading: 7.7.3.1 CB product revenue consists of the following:
nodes.start_phrase:
Lending includes a variety of financing alternatives, 
which are primarily provided on a secured basis; 
collateral includes receivables, inventory, equipment, 
real estate or other assets.
nodes.summary:
- Defines Commercial Banking (CB) product revenue categories and what they include:
  - Lending: secured financing (term loans, revolvers, bridge, ABL, leases, standby LCs) backed by receivables, inventory, equipment, real estate, or other assets.
  - Payments: cash management, payments/receipts solutions, and fund investment/management used by CB clients globally.
  - Investment banking: advisory, loan syndications, capital-raising (equity/debt), and risk management solutions; includes fees and markets revenue serving CB clients.
  - Other revenue: tax-equivalent adjustments from Community Development Banking and principal transaction activity.
- Presents selected income statement data for 2020–2022:
  - Revenue by product (Lending, Payments, Investment banking, Other) and total net revenue for each year.
  - Investment banking revenue, gross (a firmwide metric before revenue sharing).
- Provides revenue by client segment for 2020–2022:
  - Middle Market Banking, Corporate Client Banking, Commercial Real Estate Banking, and Other, with total net revenue.
- Shows key financial ratios:
  - Return on equity and overhead ratio for each year.
- Notes presentation changes and revenue sharing:
  - 4Q22 reclassification of certain CIB Markets revenue from investment banking to payments with prior periods revised.
  - CB’s share of investment banking revenue sold through CIB and firmwide revenue-sharing arrangements.
- Includes selected balance sheet and operating metrics (period-end and average) for 2020–2022:
  - Total assets, total loans (retained; held-for-sale/fair value), equity.
  - Client deposits and other third‑party liabilities (average).
  - Loans by client segment (period-end and average).
  - Headcount.
- Discloses PPP loan balances at period-end, primarily within Middle Market Banking, and references to further PPP discussion.
- Provides credit quality data and related ratios for 2020–2022:
  - Net charge-offs/(recoveries).
  - Nonperforming assets (nonaccrual loans retained; held-for-sale/fair value; assets acquired in loan satisfactions).
  - Allowance for credit losses (loan losses and lending-related commitments).
  - Ratios: net charge-off rate, allowance to period-end loans, allowance to nonaccrual loans, and nonaccrual loans to total loans.
  - Footnotes on allowance held against nonaccrual loans, exclusion of certain SBA‑guaranteed PPP loans from nonaccrual, and methodology notes.

nodes.title: ASSET & WEALTH MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.7.4 ASSET & WEALTH MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Asset & Wealth Management, with client assets of $4.0 
trillion , is a global leader in investment and wealth 
management.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: JPMorgan Chase’s Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) manages $4.0 trillion in client assets, with a majority in actively managed portfolios, positioning it as a global leader in investment and wealth management.

- Business lines:
  - Asset Management: Provides multi-asset investment solutions across equities, fixed income, alternatives, and money market funds to institutional and retail clients.
  - Global Private Bank (GPB): Delivers retirement products, brokerage, custody, estate planning, lending, deposits, and investment management for high net worth clients.

- 2022 financial performance (vs. 2021):
  - Total net revenue: $17.7B, up 5% (Net interest income $5.24B, up 35%; Noninterest revenue $12.51B, down 4%).
  - Expenses: Total noninterest expense $11.83B, up 8% (driven largely by higher compensation and structural investments).
  - Provision for credit losses: $128M net addition (vs. $227M net benefit in 2021).
  - Net income: $4.37B, down 8%.

- Revenue by line of business (2022):
  - Asset Management: $8.82B, down 5%, due to net investment valuation losses versus prior-year gains and lower management fees from market declines and net liquidity outflows, partially offset by the removal of most money market fund fee waivers.
  - Global Private Bank: $8.93B, up 16%, driven by margin expansion on higher rates and higher average deposits, and to a lesser extent higher average loans and wider spreads; partially offset by lower brokerage/placement fees and lower management fees.

- Key ratios (2022):
  - Return on equity: 25% (vs. 33% in 2021; 28% in 2020).
  - Overhead ratio: 67 (vs. 64 in 2021; 70 in 2020).
  - Pre-tax margin: AWM 33% (vs. 37%); Asset Management 30% (vs. 35%); GPB 35% (vs. 39%).

nodes.title: Asset Management has two high-level measures of its overall fund performance.
nodes.heading: 7.7.4.1 Asset Management has two high-level measures of its overall fund performance.
nodes.start_phrase:
Mutual fund rating services rank funds based on 
their risk adjusted performance over various periods.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How Asset Management evaluates overall fund performance and key operating/financial metrics for 2020–2022 (with certain items specific to the Global Private Bank).
- Performance measures:
  - Percentage of mutual fund AUM in 4- or 5-star funds.
    - Explains industry star rating scales (1–5) based on risk‑adjusted performance; Morningstar overall rating weighted across 3/5/10 years; Nomura uses 3‑year risk‑adjusted performance for Japan.
    - Methodology notes: ratings and peer groups sourced from providers; U.S. funds assessed at share‑class level; non‑U.S. generally at “primary share class” (fund level for Japan); assets redenominated to USD as applicable; funds with <3 years not rated; exclusions include money market funds, Undiscovered Managers Fund, and Brazil‑domiciled funds; past performance disclaimer.
  - Percentage of mutual fund AUM ranked in 1st or 2nd quartile over 1, 3, and 5 years.
    - Quartiles based on net‑of‑fee absolute returns; rankings and peer groups sourced from providers (Morningstar, Lipper, Nomura) and subject to the same share‑class/primary share class methodology and exclusions as above; assets redenominated to USD as applicable; past performance disclaimer.
  - “Primary share class” defined as: C share for European funds; Acc share for Hong Kong SAR and Taiwan; if unavailable, the oldest share class is used.
- Reported results (as of/for years ended Dec 31):
  - Share of JPM mutual fund AUM rated 4- or 5‑star: 2022: 73%; 2021: 69%; 2020: 63%.
  - AUM ranked in 1st/2nd quartile:
    - 1‑year: 2022: 65%; 2021: 53%; 2020: 63%.
    - 3‑year: 2022: 75%; 2021: 72%; 2020: 69%.
    - 5‑year: 2022: 81%; 2021: 80%; 2020: 72%.
- Selected balance sheet data (period‑end) and averages (note: loans, deposits, and related credit data pertain to the Global Private Bank):
  - Period‑end (USD millions): Total assets 232,037 (2022), 234,425 (2021), 203,384 (2020); Loans 214,006; Deposits 233,130; Equity 17,000 (with prior‑year comparatives shown).
  - Average (USD millions): Total assets 232,438 (2022), 217,187 (2021), 181,432 (2020); Loans 215,582; Deposits 261,489; Equity 17,000 (with prior‑year comparatives shown).
- Workforce:
  - Headcount: 26,041 (2022), 22,762 (2021), 20,683 (2020).
  - Global Private Bank client advisors: 3,137 (2022), 2,738 (2021), 2,462 (2020).
- Credit data and quality statistics (Global Private Bank):
  - Net charge‑offs/(recoveries): $(7) million (2022), $26 million (2021), $(14) million (2020); net charge‑off/(recovery) rate ~0.00%, 0.01%, and (0.01)% respectively.
  - Nonaccrual loans: $459 million (2022), $708 million (2021), $964 million (2020).
  - Allowance for credit losses: $514 million total in 2022 ($494 million loan losses; $20 million lending‑related commitments), with prior‑year comparatives shown.
  - Key ratios (2022): allowance for loan losses to period‑end loans 0.23%; allowance for loan losses to nonaccrual loans 108%; nonaccrual loans to period‑end loans 0.21%.

nodes.title: Client assets
nodes.heading: 7.7.4.2 Client assets

- Summary of client assets and assets under management (AUM) for 2022 versus 2021: total client assets were $4.0 trillion (down 6%) and AUM were $2.8 trillion (down 11%), driven by lower market levels and net outflows from liquidity products, partially offset by continued net inflows into long-term products.

Footnote notes inclusion of certain CCB client investment assets managed by AWM.
