nodes.title: CORPORATE
nodes.heading: 7.7.5 CORPORATE
nodes.start_phrase:
The Corporate segment consists of Treasury and Chief 
Investment Office (“CIO”) and Other Corporate.
nodes.summary:
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s Corporate segment, which comprises Treasury and Chief Investment Office (CIO) and Other Corporate. Treasury and CIO manage firmwide liquidity, funding, capital, and structural interest rate and foreign exchange risks. Other Corporate houses centrally managed staff functions (Real Estate, Technology, Legal, Corporate Finance, HR, Internal Audit, Risk Management, Compliance, Control Management, Corporate Responsibility and other groups) and firmwide initiatives not tied to a specific line of business.
- Presents three-year selected financials (2020–2022) for the segment, including revenue components, provision for credit losses, noninterest expense, pretax results, tax expense/benefit, net income/loss, assets, loans, deposits, and headcount, with tax-equivalent adjustments disclosed.
- 2022 vs. 2021 performance highlights: net loss narrowed to $743 million from $3.7 billion; total net revenue improved to $80 million from a $3.5 billion loss, driven by higher net interest income from rising rates, partially offset by lower noninterest revenue.
- Drivers of lower 2022 noninterest revenue: larger investment securities losses from MBS and U.S. Treasury sales tied to portfolio repositioning; adverse FX impacts from dollar strength; losses on cash deployment transactions (offset by related NII); losses (including hedge costs) tied to international consumer growth initiatives; and losses on legacy private equity. Offsets included a gain on the sale of Visa B shares (with a derivative retaining conversion-rate risk), higher gains on certain Other Corporate investments, and insurance settlement proceeds.
- 2022 noninterest expense decreased by $768 million to $1.0 billion due to FX-driven lower structural expenses, reduced retained technology expense, and a smaller contribution to the Firm’s Foundation, partially offset by higher investments in international consumer growth initiatives.
- Tax: 2022 reflected a net tax benefit from audit settlements and other adjustments, alongside changes in the mix of income/expenses affecting tax reserves.
- Other Corporate includes international consumer growth initiatives: Chase U.K. (digital retail bank), Nutmeg (U.K. digital wealth manager), and a 40% stake in Brazil’s C6 Bank (acquired in 1Q22).
- Treasury and CIO overview: executes asset-liability management primarily through high-quality investment securities and derivatives; manages cash via central bank deposits and short-term instruments; and oversees interest rate and FX risks.
- Investment securities portfolio details: $629.3 billion net of allowance at 12/31/22 with an average AA+ rating; composition includes U.S. and non-U.S. government securities, GSE/agency and nonagency MBS, CLOs, municipal obligations, and other ABS. Includes data on AFS/HTM averages and period-end balances, net losses on investment securities in 2022, allowance for credit losses levels, and notable transfers from AFS to HTM for capital management in 2020–2022.
- Segment breakouts: in 2022, Treasury and CIO recorded a net loss of $197 million and Other Corporate a net loss of $546 million; total assets declined versus 2021, deposits rose mainly due to international consumer initiatives, and headcount increased.
- References to related notes and risk management sections for further detail (derivatives, investment securities, allowance for credit losses, liquidity, market risk, and Visa B share sale).

nodes.title: Treasury and CIO overview
nodes.heading: 7.7.5.1 Treasury and CIO overview
nodes.start_phrase:
Treasury and CIO is predominantly responsible for 
measuring, monitoring, reporting and managing the Firm’s 
liquidity, funding, capital, structural interest 
rate and foreign exchange risks.
nodes.summary:
- References: Points to Note 10 (investment securities portfolio) and Note 13 (allowance for credit losses), and Note 5 (derivatives), plus sections on Liquidity Risk Management and Market Risk Management.
- Taxes: Current-period income tax benefit driven by tax audit settlements and other adjustments; partially offset by changes in the level/mix of income and expenses across U.S. federal, state, and local taxes, affecting tax reserves.
- Other Corporate: International consumer growth initiatives include Chase U.K. (digital bank), Nutmeg (U.K. digital wealth manager), and a 40% stake in Brazil’s C6 Bank (closed Q1 2022).
- Treasury and CIO overview: Manages firmwide liquidity, funding, capital, and structural interest rate and FX risks arising from the business segments; executes asset-liability management primarily via high-quality investment securities and derivatives; manages cash through central bank deposits and short-term instruments.
- Investment securities portfolio: Composed mainly of U.S./non-U.S. government securities, U.S. GSE and agency/nonagency MBS, CLOs, municipal obligations, and other ABS. As of Dec 31, 2022, portfolio net of ACL was $629.3 billion; average credit rating AA+.
- Financial highlights (2020–2022):
  - Investment securities gains/(losses): 2022 $(2,380)M; 2021 $(345)M; 2020 $795M.
  - Shift from AFS to HTM: AFS balances declined while HTM increased; average AFS from $413.4B (2020) to $239.9B (2022); average HTM from $94.6B (2020) to $412.2B (2022).
  - Period-end AFS fell to $204.0B (2022) from $306.4B (2021); HTM rose to $425.3B (2022) from $363.7B (2021).
  - Portfolio net of ACL at period-end: $629.3B (2022) vs. $670.1B (2021) and $587.9B (2020).
  - Transfers from AFS to HTM for capital management: $78.3B (2022), $104.5B (2021), $164.2B (2020).
  - ACL on investment securities: $67M (2022), $42M (2021), $78M (2020).

nodes.title: FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.8 FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Risk is an inherent part of JPMorgan Chase’s business 
activities.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes JPMorgan Chase’s firmwide risk management philosophy: risk is inherent across activities, and the objective is to balance client, customer and investor interests with the Firm’s safety and soundness.
- Outlines core risk management principles: individual accountability for identifying and escalating risks; ownership of risk identification, data and management within each line of business (LOB) and Corporate; and a firmwide governance and oversight structure.
- Links compensation to risk: a disciplined compensation framework with strong governance integrates risk and control outcomes into performance evaluations and incentives.
- Defines the risk governance framework across three dimensions:
  - Drivers of risk (e.g., economic conditions, regulation, market evolution, business decisions, process errors, misconduct, market dysfunction, natural disasters).
  - Types of risk: strategic; credit and investment (consumer, wholesale, investment portfolio); market; and operational (including compliance, conduct, legal, estimation and model risk).
  - Impacts of risk: quantitative (earnings, capital, liquidity, fines/penalties) and qualitative (reputation, client loss, regulatory actions).
- Describes the Independent Risk Management (IRM) function—Risk Management and Compliance—led by a CRO appointed by the CEO and approved by the Board Risk Committee, with authority delegated to Firmwide Risk Executives, LOB CROs, and the Chief Compliance Officer to set policies, standards, and oversee implementation.
- Details the “three lines of defense” model:
  - First line: LOBs, Treasury/CIO, and aligned Operations/Technology/Control Management own risk identification and control execution, adhering to IRM frameworks.
  - Second line: IRM independently assesses and challenges first-line practices and sets policies/standards for its processes.
  - Third line: Internal Audit independently assesses the adequacy and effectiveness of processes, controls, governance and risk management, reporting to the Audit Committee.
- Notes other control-contributing functions (Finance, HR, Legal) that identify risks and implement IRM frameworks.
- Explains risk identification and ownership: LOBs/Corporate identify and control risks; a firmwide framework catalogs material risks in a central repository; IRM reviews/challenges and reports consolidated results to the Firmwide Risk Committee (FRC) and Board Risk Committee.
- Covers risk appetite: quantitative and qualitative frameworks set by senior management and approved by the Board Risk Committee; capacity and adherence are monitored and reported to the Board.
- Presents the governance and oversight structure and escalation channels:
  - Operating Committee (CEO, CRO, CFO, General Counsel, LOB CEOs, others) escalates to the Board.
  - Board oversight via principal committees:
    - Board Risk Committee: oversees the global risk framework, approves primary risk policies, reviews frameworks and analysis, and addresses appetite breaches and significant risk issues (including capital/liquidity).
    - Audit Committee: oversees internal controls, financial reporting integrity, compliance, external auditor, and Internal Audit.
    - Compensation & Management Development Committee: oversees compensation programs, executive performance and pay, culture and conduct.
    - Public Responsibility Committee: oversees community investment, fair lending, sustainability, consumer practices, and public policy with reputational impact.
    - Corporate Governance & Nominating Committee: oversees Board governance, nominations, and self-evaluation framework.
- Identifies key senior management committees:
  - Firmwide Risk Committee (highest management-level risk forum).
  - Firmwide Control Committee (operational risk escalation and significant events).
  - LOB and Regional Risk Committees (governance, limits, and control oversight with remediation focus).
  - LOB/Corporate Function Control Committees (operational risk and control environment, indicators, issues, and remediation).
  - Asset and Liability Committee (ALM, liquidity, interest rate, and capital risk).
  - Valuation Governance Forum (valuation risk oversight).
- Lists the risk governance and oversight topics covered in subsequent sections: Strategic, Capital, Liquidity, Reputation, Consumer Credit, Wholesale Credit, Investment Portfolio, Market, Country, Climate, Operational, Compliance, Conduct, Legal, and Estimations & Model Risk.

nodes.title: STRATEGIC RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.8.1 STRATEGIC RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Strategic risk is the risk to earnings, capital, liquidity or 
reputation associated with poorly designed or failed 
business plans or inadequate response s to changes in the 
operating environment.
nodes.summary:
- Defines strategic risk as potential adverse impacts on earnings, capital, liquidity, or reputation arising from flawed business plans or inadequate responses to environmental changes.
- Governance and oversight: The Operating Committee and LOB/Corporate senior leaders manage major strategic risks; Independent Risk Management (IRM) participates in strategic discussions, business reviews, risk/control committees, governance forums, and acquisition/new business initiative reviews. The Board oversees strategic decisions, and the Board Risk Committee oversees IRM and the risk governance framework.
- Risk identification and appetite: LOB/Corporate management identify risks tied to business plans and integrate them into the Firmwide Risk Identification framework and risk appetite; IRM performs qualitative assessments of strategic initiatives’ impact on the Firm’s risk profile.
- Strategic planning process: The Firm’s strategic plan sets the strategic framework and initiatives, including budget, risk appetite, capital, earnings, and asset-liability management objectives. Guided by “How We Do Business” principles, leadership periodically reviews performance versus prior-year initiatives, assesses the operating environment, and refines or develops strategies.
- Board engagement and budgeting: The strategic plan and IRM’s assessment are provided to the Board for review and approval, and the plan is reflected in the Firm’s budget.
- Balance sheet strategy: Managing strategic risk also relies on a balance sheet strategy focused on risk-adjusted returns, strong capital, and robust liquidity, with references to detailed sections on capital, liquidity, and reputation risk.

nodes.title: CAPITAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.8.2 CAPITAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Capital risk is the risk the Firm has an insufficient level or 
composition of capital to support the Firm’s business 
activities and associated risks during normal economic 
environments and under stressed conditions.
nodes.summary:
- Defines capital risk as the risk of having insufficient level or composition of capital to support activities in normal and stressed conditions, and emphasizes a “fortress balance sheet” philosophy focused on risk‑adjusted returns, strong capital, and robust liquidity.
- Describes the Capital Risk Management function’s independent oversight, including setting and monitoring capital risk metrics, limits and appetite; breach management; assessing capital management activities (including the Contingency Capital Plan); and ensuring compliance with regulatory capital rules.
- Outlines capital management led by Treasury and CIO with objectives to: maintain sufficient capital through cycles and stress; preserve flexibility for investments; serve as a source of strength to subsidiaries; operate above minimums and maintain well‑capitalized status for the firm and IDIs; meet distribution goals; and hold resources to operate through a resolution period.
- Explains how objectives are met via internal minimum capital requirements and strong governance, flexibility to respond to events, and regular monitoring with escalation protocols at firm and material legal entity levels.
- Details governance bodies overseeing capital: Capital Governance Committee, Firmwide ALCO, LOB/regional ALCOs, and the CTC Risk Committee; Board Risk Committee periodically reviews capital risk tolerance.
- Summarizes capital planning and stress testing under the Federal Reserve’s CCAR, which assesses capital adequacy, ICAAP, and capital distributions; the SCB is set from the severely adverse scenario. Notes 2022 outcomes: SCB at 4.0% and a 12.0% standardized CET1 requirement effective Oct 1, 2022–Sep 30, 2023.
- Describes the ICAAP as an annual, board‑informed process integrating firmwide stress testing with capital planning; Audit Committee reviews/approves the framework; scenarios cover macroeconomic factors, global market shocks, and idiosyncratic operational risks, with tailored stresses and sensitivity analyses as needed.
- Presents the Contingency Capital Plan, defining capital targets and minimums in normal and stressed environments, monitoring distribution appropriateness, and outlining staged contingency actions at specified capital depletion levels.
- Reviews regulatory capital requirements set by the Federal Reserve and OCC aligned to Basel III, including calculation of RWA under Standardized and Advanced approaches; Standardized is currently more binding. Covers credit, market (and under Advanced, operational) risk RWA, management overlays, and the SLR requirement for Advanced Approaches firms.
- Notes key regulatory developments related to CECL capital transition: post‑COVID delay ended Dec 31, 2021; beginning Jan 1, 2022, benefits phase out 25% per year over three years; as of Dec 31, 2022, CET1 reflected a remaining $2.2 billion benefit, with phased impacts also to Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA.

nodes.title: Basel III Overview
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.1 Basel III Overview
nodes.start_phrase:
The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital 
ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and 
internationally active U.S. BHCs and banks, including the 
Firm and its IDI subsidiaries, including JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines governance of capital planning, noting Board oversight of capital actions and Audit Committee approval of the capital planning framework.
- Describes the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), prepared annually to assess capital sources/uses and compliance with supervisory expectations, integrating firmwide stress testing with capital planning.
- Details stress testing methodology: centrally defined economic scenarios applied across businesses, covering macroeconomic drivers, global market shocks, and idiosyncratic operational risks; includes CCAR and additional tailored scenarios and sensitivity analyses.
- Explains the Contingency Capital Plan, which sets capital management principles for normal and stressed conditions, calibrates target capital levels vs. minimums, monitors capital distributions, and outlines phased contingency actions at different depletion levels.
- Summarizes U.S. regulatory capital requirements set by the Federal Reserve (consolidated holding company) and OCC (IDI subsidiaries), aligned with Basel standards.
- Provides a Basel III overview: capital adequacy determined via risk-weighted assets (RWA) under two approaches—Standardized and Advanced—with the firm evaluated against the more binding result (currently Standardized). Credit risk RWA differs (internal models under Advanced vs. supervisory risk weights under Standardized); market risk RWA is broadly consistent across approaches. The firm may supplement RWA based on management judgment and regulatory feedback. Advanced approaches also require the supplementary leverage ratio (SLR).
- Notes key regulatory development on CECL capital transition: a pandemic-related two-year delay through Dec 31, 2021, followed by a three-year phase-out at 25% per year beginning Jan 1, 2022. A $2.9 billion CET1 benefit is being phased out; $2.2 billion remained as of Dec 31, 2022. Other CECL transition effects also phased out 25% in 2022 across Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA.
- Includes cross-references to related sections on capital actions and SLR for further detail.

nodes.title: Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.2 Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk
nodes.start_phrase:
On 
January 1, 2022, the Firm adopted “Standardized Approach 
f o r C o u n t e r p a r t y C r e d i t R i s k ” ( “ S A - C C R ” ) , w h i c h r e p l a c e d 
the Current Exposure Method used to measure derivatives 
counterparty exposure under the Standardized and 
Advanced approach RWA where internal models are not 
used, as well as leverage exposure used to calculate the SLR 
in the regulatory capital framework.
nodes.summary:
- The firm adopted the Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR) on January 1, 2022, replacing the Current Exposure Method for measuring derivatives counterparty exposure under both Standardized and Advanced RWA where internal models are not used, and for leverage exposure in the SLR calculation.
- SA-CCR implementation follows a November 2019 rule by U.S. banking regulators applicable to Basel III Advanced Approaches institutions, including the firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
- Adoption effects (based on 12/31/2021 derivatives exposure): approximately $40 billion increase in Standardized RWA; about 30 bps reduction in the CET1 capital ratio; modest decrease in total leverage exposure; increase in Advanced RWA, though less than the increase in Standardized RWA.

nodes.title: Risk-based Capital Regulatory Requirements
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.3 Risk-based Capital Regulatory Requirements
nodes.start_phrase: The following chart presents the Firm’s Basel III CET1 capital ratio requirements under the Basel III rules currently in effect.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s risk-based and leverage-based regulatory capital framework under Basel III. It explains the minimum CET1 requirement of 4.5% of risk-weighted assets and the capital conservation buffer structure, which includes a GSIB surcharge, a discretionary countercyclical buffer (0–2.5%), and either a fixed 2.5% buffer under the Advanced approach or a variable Stress Capital Buffer (floored at 2.5%) under the Standardized approach. The Firm’s GSIB surcharge is determined annually using the higher of two methods: Method 1 (FSB/Basel criteria) and Method 2 (replaces substitutability with short-term wholesale funding and applies a multiplication factor). Reported GSIB surcharges were: 2021—M1 2.0%, M2 3.5%; 2022—M1 2.0%, M2 3.5%; 2023—M1 2.5%, M2 4.0%, with Method 2 expected to rise to 4.5% effective January 1, 2024. The U.S. countercyclical capital buffer was 0% as of December 31, 2022, but can be increased up to 2.5% of RWA with a 12‑month phase-in. Failure to meet minimums plus buffers limits dividends, share repurchases, and certain executive bonuses. The Firm targets a Basel III Standardized CET1 ratio of 13.0% for Q1 2023 and 13.5% for Q1 2024 (reflecting the anticipated GSIB surcharge increase and assuming no SCB change), noting quarterly variability. It also summarizes TLAC requirements for GSIBs (external TLAC and eligible long-term debt), the Supplementary Leverage Ratio rules (minimum 3.0% plus a 2.0% buffer for certain firms) and its calculation, and states that the Firm and its insured depositories must also satisfy “well-capitalized” standards and PCA requirements, with further details referenced in Note 27 and Pillar 3 disclosures.

nodes.title: Risk-based Capital Targets
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.4 Risk-based Capital Targets
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s current target for its Basel III Standardized CET1 capital ratio is 13.0% for the first quarter of 2023, increasing to 13.5% for the first quarter of 2024 with consideration for an increase in the GSIB surcharge in 2024, and assuming no change in the Stress Capital Buffer.
nodes.summary:
- GSIB surcharge levels: For 2023, the Firm’s effective GSIB surcharge rose to 2.5% (Method 1) and 4.0% (Method 2), versus 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022 and 2021. The FSB’s November 21, 2022 list confirmed a 2.5% Method 1 surcharge effective January 1, 2023. Method 2 calculated at 4.5% using 2021 and 2022 data is expected to raise the Firm’s effective GSIB surcharge to 4.5% on January 1, 2024.
- Countercyclical capital buffer: As of December 31, 2022, the U.S. buffer remained at 0%. The Federal Reserve (with the FDIC and OCC) reviews it at least annually and can raise it up to 2.5% of RWA with a 12‑month phase-in if systemic risks rise.
- Distribution constraints: Failure to maintain required risk-based capital (including the capital conservation buffer, GSIB surcharge, and any countercyclical buffer) or required leverage ratios triggers limits on dividends, common share repurchases, and certain executive discretionary bonus payments.
- Risk-based capital targets: The Firm targets a Basel III Standardized CET1 ratio of 13.0% for Q1 2023, increasing to 13.5% for Q1 2024, reflecting the anticipated higher GSIB surcharge and assuming no change in the Stress Capital Buffer; actual ratios may vary with market conditions.
- TLAC and eligible long-term debt: As a U.S. GSIB, the Firm must meet Federal Reserve TLAC and eligible LTD minimums.
- Leverage-based requirements: Advanced approaches banking organizations must maintain a 3.0% SLR, with certain firms (including the Firm) required to hold an additional 2.0% leverage buffer. The SLR equals Tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure, which includes average on‑balance sheet assets (net of certain deductions) plus specified off‑balance sheet exposures.
- Well-capitalized standards: The Firm and its insured depository institution subsidiaries must also meet Federal Reserve and FDICIA PCA “well‑capitalized” minimums. Additional detail is provided in the Firm’s notes and Pillar 3 disclosures.

nodes.title: Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.5 Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity
nodes.start_phrase: The Federal Reserve’s TLAC rule requires the U.S. GSIB top-tier holding companies, including the Firm, to maintain minimum levels of external TLAC and eligible long-term debt (“eligible LTD”).
nodes.summary:
- Presents the firm’s GSIB surcharge levels for 2021–2023, noting increases in 2023 to 2.5% under Method 1 and 4.0% under Method 2.
- Confirms FSB’s November 2022 affirmation of a 2.5% Method 1 surcharge effective January 1, 2023.
- Indicates Method 2 surcharge calculated from December 31, 2021 data is 4.5% (effective January 1, 2024), with the 2022 estimate also 4.5%, implying an expected rise to 4.5% on January 1, 2024.
- Describes the U.S. countercyclical capital buffer framework: 0% as of December 31, 2022; reviewed at least annually; can be raised up to 2.5% of RWA with a 12‑month implementation period.
- Explains that falling below required capital levels (risk-based minimums plus the capital conservation buffer including the GSIB surcharge, and any countercyclical buffer) or SLR minimums triggers restrictions on capital distributions and certain executive discretionary bonuses.
- Outlines risk-based capital targets: Basel III Standardized CET1 ratio target of 13.0% for Q1 2023 and 13.5% for Q1 2024, assuming no change to the Stress Capital Buffer and accounting for a potential GSIB surcharge increase; actual quarterly ratios may vary with market conditions.
- Notes TLAC requirements for U.S. GSIB top-tier holding companies, including maintaining minimum external TLAC and eligible long-term debt.
- Summarizes leverage-based capital requirements: a minimum 3.0% Supplementary Leverage Ratio plus a 2.0% leverage buffer for the firm; defines SLR and total leverage exposure components.
- Mentions additional “well-capitalized” standards under Federal Reserve and FDICIA PCA rules, with references to Note 27 and Pillar 3 disclosures for more detail.

nodes.title: Leverage-based Capital Regulatory Requirements
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.6 Leverage-based Capital Regulatory Requirements
nodes.start_phrase: Banking organizations subject to the Basel III Advanced approach are currently required to have a minimum SLR of 3.0%.
nodes.summary:
- GSIB surcharge levels and trends: For 2021–2023, Method 1 rose from 2.0% to 2.5% in 2023; Method 2 rose from 3.5% to 4.0% in 2023. The FSB’s November 21, 2022 list (based on 12/31/21 data) affirmed a 2.5% Method 1 surcharge effective 1/1/2023. Method 2, calculated using 12/31/21 data, is 4.5% effective 1/1/2024; the 12/31/22 estimate is also 4.5%, so the effective surcharge is expected to increase to 4.5% on 1/1/2024.  
- Countercyclical capital buffer: U.S. CCyB remained at 0% as of 12/31/2022. The Federal Reserve will review at least annually and can raise it up to 2.5% of RWA with a 12‑month implementation period if systemic risks are elevated.  
- Consequences of capital shortfalls: Falling below required risk‑based minimums plus the capital conservation buffer (including the GSIB surcharge) and any CCyB triggers limits on capital distributions (dividends, buybacks) and certain executive discretionary bonuses.  
- Risk‑based capital targets: Basel III Standardized CET1 target of 13.0% for Q1 2023, increasing to 13.5% for Q1 2024, reflecting potential GSIB surcharge increases and assuming no change to the Stress Capital Buffer; actual quarterly ratios may vary with market conditions.  
- TLAC and eligible LTD: The Federal Reserve’s TLAC rule requires U.S. GSIB top‑tier holding companies to maintain minimum external TLAC and eligible long‑term debt.  
- Leverage requirements (SLR): Advanced approaches firms must maintain at least a 3.0% SLR, with an additional 2.0% leverage buffer for certain firms, including the Company. SLR equals Tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure (on‑balance sheet assets minus permitted deductions plus certain off‑balance sheet exposures). Noncompliance leads to limits on distributions and certain executive bonuses.  
- Other regulatory capital standards: The Firm and its IDI subsidiaries must also meet “well‑capitalized” minimums under Federal Reserve and FDICIA PCA rules. Additional details are provided in Note 27 and the Firm’s Pillar 3 Regulatory Capital Disclosures.

nodes.title: Other regulatory capital
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.7 Other regulatory capital
nodes.start_phrase: In addition to meeting the capital ratio requirements of Basel III, the Firm and its IDI subsidiaries must also maintain minimum capital and leverage ratios in order to be “well-capitalized” under the regulations issued by the Federal Reserve and the Prompt Corrective Action (“PCA”) requirements of the FDIC Improvement Act (“FDICIA”), respectively.
nodes.summary:
- GSIB surcharge levels and trajectory: Effective surcharge increased in 2023 to 2.5% (Method 1) and 4.0% (Method 2). The FSB’s 2022 GSIB list (based on 2021 data) affirmed a 2.5% Method 1 surcharge effective Jan 1, 2023. Method 2 surcharge calculated at 4.5% using 2021 and 2022 data, with the Firm’s effective GSIB surcharge expected to rise to 4.5% on Jan 1, 2024.
- Countercyclical capital buffer: U.S. buffer remained at 0% as of Dec 31, 2022; reviewed at least annually; can be raised up to 2.5% of RWA with a 12‑month implementation period.
- Capital distribution constraints: Falling below risk-based minimums plus the capital conservation buffer (including GSIB surcharge) and any countercyclical buffer triggers limits on dividends, share repurchases, and certain executive discretionary bonuses.
- Risk-based capital targets: Basel III Standardized CET1 target of 13.0% for Q1 2023, increasing to 13.5% for Q1 2024, reflecting a potential GSIB surcharge increase and assuming no change in the Stress Capital Buffer; quarterly ratios may vary with market conditions.
- TLAC and eligible long-term debt: The Firm, as a U.S. GSIB, must meet minimum external TLAC and eligible LTD requirements under the Federal Reserve’s TLAC rule.
- Leverage-based requirements and SLR: Advanced approach firms must maintain a minimum 3.0% SLR; certain firms, including the Firm, must hold an additional 2.0% leverage buffer. SLR is Tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure (average on-balance sheet assets net of certain deductions plus specific off-balance sheet exposures). Breaches result in distribution and bonus limitations.
- Other regulatory capital standards: The Firm and its IDI subsidiaries must also meet “well-capitalized” thresholds under Federal Reserve regulations and FDICIA PCA requirements.
- Reported capital metrics: Presentation of 2022 and 2021 risk-based capital figures under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches (CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, RWA and related ratios), and leverage-based metrics (adjusted average assets, Tier 1 leverage ratio, total leverage exposure, SLR) with applicable regulatory requirements; metrics reflect CECL capital transition provisions.
- References for further detail: Note 27, and Pillar 3 Regulatory Capital Disclosures on the Firm’s website.

nodes.title: Capital components
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.8 Capital components
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents reconciliations of total stockholders’ equity to Basel III CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital and Total capital as of D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 .
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Reconciliation of stockholders’ equity to regulatory capital under Basel III and a 2022 capital rollforward, presented within Management’s Discussion and Analysis.

- Capital components (as of December 31, 2022 and 2021):
  - Starts with total stockholders’ equity and derives Basel III Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1), Tier 1, and Total capital under both Standardized and Advanced approaches.
  - Key 12/31/2022 figures:
    - CET1 capital: $218.9B (vs. $213.9B in 2021)
    - Tier 1 capital: $245.6B (vs. $246.2B)
    - Standardized Tier 2 capital: $32.1B (vs. $28.7B)
    - Standardized Total capital: $277.8B (vs. $274.9B)
    - Advanced Tier 2 capital: $19.0B (vs. $19.6B)
    - Advanced Total capital: $264.6B (vs. $265.8B)
  - Major adjustments from equity to CET1:
    - Deductions: Goodwill ($53.5B) and other intangibles ($1.2B)
    - Additions: Certain deferred tax liabilities ($2.5B) and other CET1 adjustments ($6.2B)
  - Tier 1 adjustments include preferred stock ($27.4B) and other Tier 1 deductions ($0.7B).
  - Tier 2 components include qualifying long-term debt and instruments ($13.6B), qualifying allowance for credit losses ($19.4B), and other items.
  - Advanced approach includes an adjustment reducing qualifying allowance for credit losses ($13.2B).
  - Explanatory notes:
    - Deferred tax liabilities on tax-deductible goodwill/intangibles are netted against those assets for CET1.
    - Other CET1 adjustments include AOCI impacts from cash flow hedges and DVA on structured notes, and CECL capital transition benefits.
    - 2021 Tier 1 adjustments reflect Series Z preferred stock called for redemption and redeemed in early 2022.
    - Allowance for credit losses eligible in Tier 2 is capped (1.25% of credit risk RWA; 0.6% excess allowance limit under Advanced).
    - Goodwill deductions include amounts tied to equity method investments in nonconsolidated financial institutions.

- Capital rollforward for 2022:
  - CET1 increased by $5.0B to $218.9B.
    - Drivers: Net income to common $36.1B; offsets from common dividends (-$11.9B), net treasury stock purchases (-$1.9B), AOCI changes (notably unrealized losses on investment securities of -$11.8B, FX translation -$0.6B, pension/OPEB -$1.2B), small positive fair value hedge impact (+$0.1B), and other CET1 adjustments (-$4.4B), plus APIC changes (+$0.6B).
  - Tier 1 decreased by $0.5B to $245.6B, primarily due to redemptions of noncumulative perpetual preferred stock (-$5.4B), partly offset by the CET1 increase.
  - Standardized Tier 2 increased by $3.4B to $32.1B, driven by a higher qualifying allowance for credit losses (+$4.3B), partially offset by lower qualifying long-term debt (-$0.5B) and other items (-$0.4B).
  - Advanced Tier 2 decreased by $0.7B to $19.0B, reflecting similar movements with a smaller increase in qualifying allowance and the same debt and other reductions.
  - Resulting totals: Standardized Total capital $277.8B; Advanced Total capital $264.6B.

nodes.title: Capital rollforward
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.9 Capital rollforward
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the changes in Basel III CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital and Tier 2 capital for the year ended D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Reconciles JPMorgan Chase’s total stockholders’ equity to Basel III regulatory capital measures (CET1, Tier 1, Tier 2, and Total capital) under both Standardized and Advanced approaches as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, and provides a 2022 capital rollforward explaining year-over-year changes.

- Reconciliation highlights (12/31/22 vs 12/31/21):
  - Total stockholders’ equity: $292.3B vs $294.1B.
  - Less preferred stock: $27.4B vs $34.8B → common equity $264.9B vs $259.3B.
  - Add-backs to CET1: certain deferred tax liabilities ($2.5B both years); other CET1 adjustments ($6.2B vs $3.4B), including:
    - AOCI-related net benefits from cash flow hedges and DVA on structured notes ($5.2B vs $1.4B).
    - CECL capital transition benefit ($2.2B vs $2.9B).
  - Deductions from CET1: goodwill ($53.5B vs $50.3B, including equity-method investees) and other intangibles ($1.2B vs $0.9B).
  - Resulting CET1 capital (Standardized/Advanced): $218.9B vs $213.9B.
  - Tier 1 capital: Add preferred stock and subtract other Tier 1 adjustments ($0.7B vs $2.6B; 2021 included $2.0B Series Z preferred called and redeemed Feb 1, 2022) → Tier 1 $245.6B vs $246.2B.
  - Tier 2 capital (Standardized): long-term debt and other qualifying instruments ($13.6B vs $14.1B); qualifying allowance for credit losses ($19.4B vs $15.0B; subject to 1.25% of credit risk RWA cap, with CECL transition); other adjustments → Tier 2 $32.1B vs $28.7B.
  - Total capital (Standardized): $277.8B vs $274.9B.
  - Advanced approach adjustments: reduction for qualifying allowance methodology (excess reserves over expected losses up to 0.6% of credit risk RWA, with CECL transition) → Advanced Tier 2 $19.0B vs $19.6B; Advanced Total capital $264.6B vs $265.8B.

- 2022 capital rollforward (key drivers):
  - CET1 increased by $5.0B to $218.9B, driven by net income applicable to common equity (+$36.1B), partially offset by common dividends (-$11.9B), net treasury stock purchases (-$1.9B), unfavorable AOCI movements (notably investment securities unrealized losses -$11.8B and pension/OPEB -$1.2B), and other CET1 adjustments (-$4.4B).
  - Tier 1 decreased by $0.5B to $245.6B, reflecting CET1 increase offset by preferred stock redemptions (-$5.4B).
  - Standardized Tier 2 increased by $3.4B to $32.1B, mainly from higher qualifying allowance for credit losses (+$4.3B), partially offset by lower qualifying long-term debt (-$0.5B).
  - Advanced Tier 2 decreased by $0.7B to $19.0B.

- Footnote clarifications:
  - Deferred tax liabilities related to tax-deductible goodwill/intangibles net against those items in CET1.
  - CECL capital transition provisions affect CET1 and qualifying allowance calculations.
  - Excess allowances over regulatory caps are deducted from RWA.
  - Goodwill deductions include amounts related to equity-method investees in financial institutions.

nodes.title: RWA rollforward
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.10 RWA rollforward
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents changes in the components of RWA under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches for the year ended D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2.
nodes.summary:
- RWA rollforward for 2022 under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches:
  - Standardized total RWA increased to $1,653.5B from $1,638.9B (+$14.6B), driven by portfolio movements (+$25.8B) partly offset by model/data changes (−$11.1B). Market risk RWA declined to $85.0B from $95.4B.
  - Advanced total RWA rose to $1,609.8B from $1,547.9B (+$61.9B), mainly from portfolio movements (+$64.7B) with a small offset from model/data changes (−$2.8B). Market risk RWA declined to $85.4B from $95.5B; Operational risk RWA increased to $446.3B from $405.4B.
  - Notes clarify drivers: SA-CCR adoption (Jan 1, 2022), changes in book size/composition/credit quality, market movements, rolloffs, regulatory VaR backtesting multiplier changes, and operational loss/macro model updates.
  - Off-balance sheet RWA: Standardized $210.1B (vs. $218.5B in 2021); Advanced $180.8B (vs. $188.5B).

- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR) for Q4:
  - Tier 1 capital ~$245.6B; total leverage exposure $4.367T (down from $4.572T).
  - SLR improved to 5.6% from 5.4%.
  - Off-balance sheet exposures averaged $663.2B (down from $789.8B), reflecting SA-CCR adoption effective Jan 1, 2022.
  - Footnotes detail regulatory adjustments to average assets and calculation methodology.

- Line of business (LOB) equity allocation:
  - Allocation considers Basel III Standardized and Advanced RWA, GSIB surcharge, and severe stress simulation; reviewed at least annually.
  - As of Jan 1, 2023, capital allocations updated for changes in Firm capital requirements and LOB RWA.
  - Allocated capital (in billions): CCB $52.0 (was $50.0), CIB $108.0 (was $103.0; $83.0 in 2021), Commercial Banking $28.5 (was $25.0), AWM $16.0 (was $17.0), Corporate $60.4 (was $69.9; $88.3 in 2021).
  - Total common stockholders’ equity unchanged at $264.9B.
  - References provided to Pillar 3 Regulatory Capital Disclosures for additional detail.

nodes.title: Supplementary leverage ratio
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.11 Supplementary leverage ratio
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the components of the Firm’s SLR.
nodes.summary:
- RWA rollforward: Presents year-over-year changes in Risk-Weighted Assets under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches for 2022, breaking out credit, market, and (for Advanced) operational risk. It reconciles from December 31, 2021 to December 31, 2022 by attributing changes to model and data updates and movements in portfolio levels (including the January 1, 2022 SA-CCR adoption, market movements, and regulatory multiplier effects). End-2022 totals are Standardized RWA of approximately $1.654 trillion (credit $1.569T; market $0.085T) and Advanced RWA of approximately $1.610 trillion (credit $1.078T; market $0.085T; operational $0.446T). Notes also disclose off-balance sheet RWA included in credit risk (Standardized $210.1B; Advanced $180.8B) and reference Pillar 3 disclosures for more detail.

- Supplementary leverage ratio (SLR): Details the SLR calculation for Q4 2022 and Q4 2021, including Tier 1 capital, total and adjusted average assets, off-balance sheet exposures (reflecting SA-CCR from January 1, 2022), and total leverage exposure. Reports an SLR of 5.6% at December 31, 2022 versus 5.4% a year earlier, with explanatory footnotes on regulatory adjustments and exposure measurement.

- Line of business equity (allocated capital): Explains the methodology for allocating capital to business segments, considering Basel III Standardized and Advanced RWA, the GSIB surcharge, and stressed capital simulations, with annual reassessment. Notes changes effective January 1, 2023 driven by updated capital requirements and RWA. Provides allocated capital by segment for 2023, 2022, and 2021; for January 1, 2023: Consumer & Community Banking $52.0B, Corporate & Investment Bank $108.0B, Commercial Banking $28.5B, Asset & Wealth Management $16.0B, and Corporate $60.4B, totaling $264.9B of common stockholders’ equity.

nodes.title: Line of business equity
nodes.heading: 7.8.2.12 Line of business equity
nodes.start_phrase: Each business segment is allocated capital by taking into consideration a variety of factors including capital levels of similarly rated peers and applicable regulatory capital requirements.
nodes.summary:
- RWA rollforward: Summarizes year-over-year changes in Risk-Weighted Assets under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches for 2022, separating the effects of model/data changes from portfolio movements.
  - Standardized approach: Total RWA rose to $1,653.5B from $1,638.9B, driven by portfolio movements (+$25.8B) partially offset by model/data changes (−$11.1B). Credit risk RWA increased to $1,568.5B; Market risk RWA declined to $85.0B.

- Focuses on “Other capital requirements,” specifically the Federal Reserve’s Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) rule for U.S. GSIB top-tier holding companies, requiring minimum levels of external TLAC and eligible long-term debt (LTD).
- Explains that requirements are measured against risk-weighted assets (RWA—using the greater of Standardized or Advanced approaches) and total leverage exposure; failure to meet minimums plus buffers restricts capital distributions (dividends, share repurchases) and certain executive discretionary bonuses.
- Presents JPMorgan Chase’s eligible external TLAC and LTD as of December 31, 2022 and 2021 (reflecting CECL capital transition):
  - 2022: TLAC $486.0B (29.4% of RWA; 11.1% of leverage exposure); LTD $228.5B (13.8% of RWA; 5.2% of leverage exposure).

  - Regulatory minimums: 22.5% TLAC/RWA, 9.5% LTD/RWA; 9.5% TLAC/leverage exposure, 4.5% LTD/leverage exposure.
  - Reported surpluses over both RWA- and leverage-based requirements increased in 2022 versus 2021 (e.g., 2022 TLAC surplus $114.0B RWA-based and $71.2B leverage-based; LTD surplus $71.4B RWA-based and $32.0B leverage-based).
- Notes that effective January 1, 2023, TLAC-to-RWA and LTD-to-RWA regulatory requirements rose by 50 bps to 23.0% and 10.0%, respectively, due to a higher GSIB surcharge.
- Provides cross-references to sections on GSIB surcharge details, parent company long-term debt issuance, and risk factors regarding potential outcomes for debt and equity holders in a resolution scenario.

nodes.start_phrase: Liquidity risk is the risk that the Firm will be unable to meet its contractual and contingent financial obligations as they arise or that it does not have the appropriate amount, composition and tenor of funding and liquidity to support its assets and liabilities.
