nodes.title: INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.8.10 INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Investment portfolio risk is the risk associated with the loss of principal or a reduction in expected returns on investments arising from the investment securities portfolio or from principal investments.
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced expected returns arising from investment securities and principal investments. Securities are largely held by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and asset-liability management, with a long-term holding horizon and no expectation of short-term gains.
- Investment securities risk centers on default risk of principal and interest, mitigated by a high-quality portfolio. As of December 31, 2022, the Treasury and CIO portfolio was $629.3 billion (net of allowance for credit losses) with an average AA+ credit rating (based on external or internal ratings). Related liquidity and market risks are addressed in other sections.
- Governance for investment securities: managed under the Firm’s Risk Appetite framework, reviewed by the CTC Risk Committee with updates to the Board Risk Committee. Independent control functions assess carrying values and set approved levels for risks including capital and credit.
- Principal investments comprise privately held ownership or junior capital instruments, including tax-oriented investments (alternative energy, affordable housing) and strategic investments supporting business objectives; consolidated holdings are excluded. Managed within LOBs and Corporate, aligned with strategies that include support for underserved communities and minority-owned businesses.
- Principal investment portfolio values: total carrying value of $37.0 billion at December 31, 2022 (vs. $30.5 billion in 2021), including $26.2 billion in tax-oriented investments (vs. $23.2 billion) and $10.8 billion in private equity/various debt and equity/real assets (vs. $7.3 billion). Noted stakes: 40% in C6 Bank and 49% in Viva Wallet.
- Governance for principal investments: firmwide risk policy framework with approvals by independent executives, independent reviews of carrying values, portfolio size limits by business/segment, and stress testing under scenarios of significant market moves or other risk events.

nodes.title: Investment securities risk
nodes.heading: 7.8.10.1 Investment securities risk
nodes.start_phrase: Investment securities risk includes the exposure associated with a default in the payment of principal and interest.
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced expected returns from investment securities and principal investments; notes securities are held by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and ALM purposes, while principal investments are managed by LOBs and Corporate and are intended for long-term holding with no expectation of short-term gains.
- Investment securities risk focuses on default risk (principal and interest), mitigated by a predominantly high-quality portfolio; as of December 31, 2022, Treasury and CIO held $629.3 billion (net of allowance) with an average AA+ rating, based on external or internal ratings; cross-references to Corporate segment results, Note 10, Liquidity Risk Management, and Market Risk Management.
- Governance and oversight for investment securities: governed by the Firm’s Risk Appetite framework; reviewed by the CTC Risk Committee with updates to the Board Risk Committee; independent control functions review carrying values; approved limits are set for risk categories including capital and credit risks.
- Principal investments are privately held instruments (ownership interests/junior capital), including tax-oriented investments and strategic investments; generally exclude consolidated holdings; managed by LOBs and Corporate; aligned with strategies including support for underserved communities and minority-owned businesses.
- Principal investment portfolio size and mix: total carrying value rose to $37.0 billion in 2022 from $30.5 billion in 2021; comprised of $26.2 billion in tax-oriented investments (alternative energy and affordable housing) and $10.8 billion in private equity/various debt and equity/real assets; includes 40% ownership in C6 Bank and 49% in Viva Wallet.
- Governance and oversight for principal investments: firmwide risk policy framework with approvals by independent executives; independent control functions review carrying values; approved investment levels set and monitored by business/segment; portfolios are stress tested under scenarios of significant market moves and other risk events.

nodes.title: Governance and oversight
nodes.heading: 7.8.10.2 Governance and oversight
nodes.start_phrase: Investment securities risks are governed by the Firm’s Risk Appetite framework, and reviewed at the CTC Risk Committee with regular updates provided to the Board Risk Committee.
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced expected returns from the investment securities portfolio or principal investments.
- Investment securities are predominantly held by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and asset‑liability management; principal investments are largely privately held instruments managed within LOBs and Corporate. Investments are generally long term with no expectation of short-term realized gains.
- Investment securities risk centers on default risk of principal and interest, mitigated by a high-quality portfolio: $629.3 billion net carrying value at December 31, 2022 with an average AA+ rating. Cross-references provided to Corporate segment results, Liquidity Risk Management, and Market Risk Management for related details.
- Governance for investment securities follows the Firm’s Risk Appetite framework, reviewed by the CTC Risk Committee with updates to the Board Risk Committee. Independent control functions assess carrying values and set approved levels across risk categories, including capital and credit risks.
- Principal investments comprise privately held ownership/junior capital positions, including tax-oriented investments and strategic investments (excluding consolidated entities), aligned with Firm strategy and support for underserved communities and minority-owned businesses.
- Principal investment portfolio values: total $37.0B at December 31, 2022 (vs. $30.5B in 2021), including $26.2B in tax-oriented (alternative energy and affordable housing) and $10.8B in private equity/various debt and equity/real assets; includes 40% of C6 Bank and 49% of Viva Wallet.
- Principal investment governance mirrors firmwide risk governance: a firmwide policy framework with independent executive approvals, independent valuation oversight, approved portfolio levels by business/segment, and stress testing under adverse market and risk scenarios.

nodes.title: Principal investment risk
nodes.heading: 7.8.10.3 Principal investment risk
nodes.start_phrase: Principal investments are typically privately-held financial instruments representing ownership interests or other forms of junior capital.
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced expected returns from the investment securities portfolio or principal investments; investments are generally long-term with no expectation of short-term realized gains.
- Investment securities portfolio is predominantly held by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and asset-liability management purposes; composed largely of high-quality securities.

- Governance for investment securities risk operates under the Firm’s Risk Appetite framework, reviewed by the CTC Risk Committee with regular updates to the Board Risk Committee.
- Independent control functions review the appropriateness of carrying values and enforce approved limits across risk categories, including capital and credit risks.
- Principal investments are typically privately held ownership or junior capital instruments, including tax-oriented investments and vehicles that support business strategy; managed within LOBs and Corporate and generally exclude consolidated entities.
- Commitment to evolve principal investment activities in line with strategy, including support for underserved communities and minority-owned businesses.
- Principal investments carrying values at December 31: 2022 total $37.0 billion (tax-oriented: $26.2 billion; private equity/debt/real assets: $10.8 billion, including 40% of C6 Bank and 49% of Viva Wallet); 2021 total $30.5 billion (tax-oriented: $23.2 billion; private equity/debt/real assets: $7.3 billion).
- Governance for principal investments includes a firmwide risk policy framework, approvals by independent executives, independent reviews of carrying values, approved portfolio size limits by business/segment, and stress testing under market and risk event scenarios.

nodes.title: Governance and oversight
nodes.heading: 7.8.10.4 Governance and oversight

nodes.title: MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.8.11 MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Market risk is the risk associated with the effect of changes in market factors such as interest and foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads or implied volatilities, on the value of assets and liabilities held for both the short and long term.
nodes.summary: The excerpt contains only an output-format instruction directing the responder to return just the description without any additional text; it provides no substantive topic or content beyond this directive.

nodes.title: Market Risk Management
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.1 Market Risk Management
nodes.start_phrase: Market Risk Management monitors market risks throughout the Firm and defines market risk policies and procedures.
nodes.summary:
- Defines market risk as the potential impact of changes in interest rates, FX rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities on asset and liability values over short and long horizons.
- States Market Risk Management’s mandate: oversee market risks firmwide; set and maintain policies; independently measure, monitor, and control risks across Lines of Business (LOBs), Corporate, and the Firm; define, approve, and monitor limits; perform stress testing and qualitative risk assessments; and provide transparency to senior management, the Board, and regulators.
- Objectives include managing risk, supporting efficient risk/return decisions, and reducing volatility in operating performance.
- Emphasizes a multi-metric measurement approach (no single measure captures market risk): Value-at-Risk (VaR), stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, and other sensitivity-based measures.
- Describes a tiered limit framework at Firm, LOB, Corporate, and legal-entity levels, including VaR and stress limits, supplemented by nonstatistical measures (e.g., P&L drawdowns).
- Limit-setting considers market volatility, product liquidity, client business needs, and management judgment; limits are regularly reviewed and updated, with senior management responsible for approving certain limits. Unreviewed limits are escalated.
- Governance and escalation: LOBs/Corporate must adhere to limits; breaches are reported promptly to approvers; remediation may involve reducing risk or granting temporary limit increases to accommodate client activity or volatility; significant breaches are escalated appropriately.
- Acknowledges model limitations and imprecision, particularly under sudden or severe market shifts; references broader model risk considerations and highlights periodic review and calibration of market risk measures.

nodes.title: Measures used to capture market risk
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.2 Measures used to capture market risk
nodes.start_phrase: There is no single measure to capture market risk and therefore Market Risk Management uses various metrics, both statistical and nonstatistical, to assess risk including:
nodes.summary:
- Defines market risk as the impact of changes in interest rates, FX, equity/commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatility on asset and liability values.
- Outlines Market Risk Management’s objectives: manage and control market risks firmwide, support risk/return decisions, reduce operating volatility, and provide transparency to senior management, the Board, and regulators.
- Details core responsibilities: maintain a market risk policy framework; independently measure, monitor, and control market risk across LOBs, Corporate, and Firmwide; define, approve, and monitor limits; conduct stress testing and qualitative risk assessments.
- Describes the risk measurement toolkit: Value-at-Risk (VaR), stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, and other sensitivity-based measures; notes no single metric fully captures market risk.
- Explains risk monitoring and control via a hierarchy of limits at Firm, LOB, Corporate, and legal-entity levels, using VaR, stress limits, and nonstatistical measures; limits are set considering market volatility, liquidity, client business, and judgment.
- Sets governance and escalation protocols: regular review and approval of limits by senior management; monitoring and reporting of exposures; timely reporting and escalation of breaches; remediation may include risk reduction or temporary limit increases.
- Acknowledges model limitations and uncertainty, especially under sudden or severe market shifts; commits to periodic review and calibration of market risk measures.
- Excerpt is from JPMorgan Chase & Co. 2022 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and control
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.3 Risk monitoring and control
nodes.start_phrase: Market risk exposure is managed primarily through a series of limits set in the context of the market environment and business strategy.
nodes.summary:
- Defines market risk as potential losses from changes in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities affecting assets and liabilities over short and long horizons.
- Outlines Market Risk Management’s mandate: set and maintain the market risk policy framework; independently measure, monitor and control market risk across Lines of Business (LOBs), Corporate, and Firmwide; define, approve, and monitor limits; perform stress testing and qualitative risk assessments; support risk/return decisions, reduce earnings volatility, and provide transparency to senior management, the Board, and regulators.
- Describes risk measurement approach: no single metric suffices; uses a toolkit including Value-at-Risk (VaR), stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, and other sensitivity-based measures.
- Details risk monitoring and control framework: hierarchical limits at Firm, LOB, Corporate, and legal entity levels (e.g., VaR and stress limits, plus nonstatistical measures such as P&L drawdowns); processes for limit setting, periodic review and approvals; responsibilities for adherence; timely breach reporting, escalation, and remediation (risk reduction or temporary limit increases for client activity/volatility).
- Acknowledges model limitations and uncertainty, especially under sudden market shifts; references broader model risk governance and notes periodic review and calibration of market risk measures.
- Summarizes LOB/Corporate activity-to-risk mapping and positions included in key measures:
  - Consumer & Community Banking (CCB): mortgage origination/servicing and deposits; risks include closing probability, interest rate and prepayment risk; positions include mortgage commitments and hedges (derivatives), warehouse loans (fair value option), MSRs and hedges, IO/MBS and hedges, fair value option liabilities; retained loans and deposits; DVA on certain liabilities captured via sensitivities.
  - Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB): market-making in FICC, equities, and commodities; risks include price/volatility, basis/correlation, interest rate and prepayment; positions include trading assets/liabilities and derivatives (including hedges), certain repo/securities financing, fair value option liabilities and loans, CVA and hedges, marketable equity investments; retained loans and deposits; privately held equity/real estate FVO loans; FVA and DVA sensitivities; credit component of CVA for stressed counterparties.
  - Commercial Banking (CB): lending and deposits; interest rate and prepayment risk; marketable equity investments in VaR; retained loans and deposits in earnings-at-risk.
  - Asset & Wealth Management (AWM): seed capital, co-investments, lending and deposits; general market factor risks; positions include trading debt held pre-distribution, seed capital and related hedges, deferred compensation and hedges, co-investments; retained loans and deposits.
  - Corporate: manages liquidity, funding, capital, structural interest rate, and non-USD FX risks; positions include derivatives recognized in noninterest revenue, marketable equity investments, deposits with banks, investment securities and related IR hedges, long-term debt and IR hedges, deposits; privately held equity; FX exposure from non-USD long-term debt and hedges.
- Notes that AWM and CB contributions to Firmwide average VaR were not material for 2022 and 2021.
- Cross-references related sections on investment portfolio risk and model risk for further detail.

nodes.title: Value-at-risk
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.4 Value-at-risk
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase utilizes value-at-risk (“VaR”), a statistical risk measure , to estimate the potential loss from adverse market moves in the current market environment.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and framework: JPMorgan Chase uses a single Value-at-Risk (VaR) framework across the Firm to estimate potential losses from adverse market moves, supporting both internal risk management and regulatory requirements. It employs historical simulation using the prior 12 months of data and assumes recent historical changes reflect near-term outcomes.

- Risk Management VaR: Calculated daily with a one-day holding period and an expected tail-loss approach approximating a 95% confidence level. It is used to measure risk profiles, diversification, aggregate risks, set/monitor limits, and report to senior management, the Board, and regulators.

- Model structure: Granular VaR models simulate historical returns for specific risk factors and product types, incorporating portfolio-specific sensitivities and time series. Results are aggregated to the Firm level and run daily for businesses with market risk.

- Model limitations: VaR is imperfect due to reliance on historical data, limited horizons, potential market illiquidity, and sudden regime shifts. Some products lack sufficient data; proxies are used, which may affect results. The Firm supplements VaR with non-statistical measures such as stress testing.

- Data considerations: Daily market data used in VaR can differ from independent third-party data used in the monthly VCG price testing process, and it may be impractical to use VCG data for VaR. Model calculations are periodically reviewed and enhanced as portfolios and market conditions evolve, which can affect historical comparisons.

- Regulatory VaR: Calculated separately under Basel III, with a 10-business-day holding period and expected tail loss approximating a 99% confidence level. It applies to covered positions and differs from Risk Management VaR (e.g., exclusion of certain credit derivative hedges and some diversification benefits). Additional details are provided in Pillar 3 disclosures.

- 2022 VaR results and drivers: 
  - Total average Risk Management VaR rose to $58 million in 2022 from $55 million in 2021; min and max were $34 million and $242 million, respectively (vs. $24 million and $153 million in 2021).
  - Key driver was March 2022 nickel price spikes and volatility, which elevated Credit Portfolio VaR; this was partly offset by lower Corporate and other LOB VaR due to decreased market values of a legacy publicly traded private equity position.
  - Governance changes in 1Q22 removed the credit risk component of CVA for certain counterparties (and related hedges) from Credit Portfolio VaR; exposures moved to other sensitivity-based measures.
  - Diversification benefits are material and non-additive; maximum/minimum diversification metrics may be non-meaningful due to timing differences across components.

- Trend visualization: Daily Risk Management VaR over 2022 shows a pronounced increase in March tied to nickel-related counterparty exposure in the Credit Portfolio.

nodes.title: VaR backtesting
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.5 VaR backtesting
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm performs daily VaR model backtesting, which compares the daily Risk Management VaR results with the daily gains and losses that are utilized for VaR backtesting purposes.
nodes.summary:
- VaR backtesting: Daily comparison of Risk Management VaR with backtesting gains/losses that exclude certain revenue components (e.g., intraday trading, fees, commissions, valuation adjustments, net interest), aligned to Basel III. Definition of backtesting exceptions (loss exceeds prior day’s VaR), with an expected frequency of about five per 100 trading days, and caveat that exceptions vary with volatility differences from the 12‑month historical window. For the 12 months ended December 31, 2022: 136 gain days out of 259 and 17 exceptions. A distribution chart shows losses as a percentage of VaR in 50‑point intervals, with exceptions >100%; results differ from Basel III Pillar 3 Regulatory VaR disclosures.
- Stress testing: Complement to VaR assessing losses under hypothetical, simultaneous shocks across market factors (credit spreads, equities, rates, FX, commodities) for LOBs and Corporate. Focus on tail events, cross‑factor impacts, idiosyncratic and basis risks; flexible scenario construction. Governance under Market Risk Management and the Firmwide Market Risk Stress Methodology Committee; models subject to Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy. Results reported to senior management, used in CCAR and other enterprise stress tests, and embedded in the Risk Appetite framework reported to the Board Risk Committee.
- Profit and loss drawdowns: Monitoring tool highlighting trading losses via declines from year‑to‑date peak revenue.
- Earnings‑at‑risk (interest rate risk): Overview of structural interest rate risk from both trading and traditional banking (loans, deposits, debt issuance, investment securities). Policy and limits set by the CTC Risk Committee with Board oversight; Treasury and CIO manage and review the profile; dedicated risk function under the CTC CRO provides independent oversight. Sources of risk include timing and amount mismatches in repricing/maturities, yield curve slope changes, and behavioral maturity shifts. Firmwide management via funds transfer pricing and use of the investment securities portfolio and derivatives. EaR measures sensitivity of net interest income and certain fees to rate scenarios versus a baseline using market rates and deposit pricing assumptions, with simulations across USD and non‑USD exposures.

nodes.title: Stress testing
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.6 Stress testing
nodes.start_phrase: Along with VaR, stress testing is an important tool used to assess risk.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the section: “Other risk measures” beyond VaR, specifically stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, and earnings-at-risk (EaR).

- Stress testing:
  - Complements VaR by estimating losses under hypothetical yet plausible stressed scenarios with simultaneous shocks across market factors (credit spreads, equities, interest rates, FX, commodities).
  - Covers market risk–sensitive positions across Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate; includes tail events, idiosyncratic risks, and basis risks; flexible to construct new scenarios.
  - Results are periodically reported to senior management; used to understand exposures, set/monitor limits, and inform Risk Appetite.
  - Governance: overseen by Market Risk Management; models subject to Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy; Firmwide Market Risk Stress Methodology Committee approves methodology/scenario changes; significant changes escalated to senior management.
  - Integrated into CCAR and other firmwide stress tests; results reported to the Board of Directors and Board Risk Committee.

- Profit and loss drawdowns:
  - Tool to flag trading losses that exceed risk tolerance.
  - Defined as the decline in revenue from its year-to-date peak.

- Earnings-at-risk (interest rate risk management):
  - Measures the sensitivity of net income (including certain fees) to interest rate changes versus a baseline using market rates and deposit pricing assumptions.
  - Interest rate risk arises from both trading and traditional banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance, investment securities).
  - Governance: CTC Risk Committee sets structural interest rate risk policy and limits (approved by the Board Risk Committee); Treasury and CIO, with LOBs, calculate the firm’s structural interest rate risk profile; independent oversight by a dedicated risk function reporting to the CTC CRO.
  - Management tools: investment securities portfolio and interest rate derivatives; firmwide management via funds transfer pricing that centralizes interest rate risk in Treasury/CIO.
  - Sources of structural interest rate risk: timing and amount mismatches in maturities/repricing, yield curve shifts, and changes in asset/liability maturities as rates move.
  - Simulations cover U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar exposures, primarily for rate-sensitive assets and liabilities (e.g., retained loans).

nodes.title: Profit and loss drawdowns
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.7 Profit and loss drawdowns
nodes.start_phrase: Profit and loss drawdowns are used to highlight trading losses above certain levels of risk tolerance.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of additional risk measures beyond VaR, focusing on stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, and earnings-at-risk (interest rate risk).
- Stress testing:
  - Assesses potential losses under stressed but plausible economic and market scenarios by applying simultaneous shocks to multiple market factors (credit spreads, equity prices, interest rates, currencies, commodities).
  - Covers market risk sensitive positions across Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate, including tail events, idiosyncratic risks, and basis risk; framework is flexible to construct new scenarios.
  - Results are reported periodically to senior management; used in CCAR and other firmwide stress tests; incorporated into the Firm’s Risk Appetite and reported to the Board and Board Risk Committee.
  - Governed by Market Risk Management with models subject to the Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy; the Firmwide Market Risk Stress Methodology Committee approves methodology and scenario changes; significant changes are escalated.
- Profit and loss drawdowns:
  - Used to flag trading losses beyond risk tolerances; defined as the decline in revenue from the year-to-date peak.
- Earnings-at-risk (structural interest rate risk):
  - Measures the sensitivity of net income (net interest income and certain interest-sensitive fees) to specified interest rate scenarios relative to a baseline using market rates and deposit pricing assumptions.
  - Interest rate risk arises from both trading and traditional banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance, investment securities).
  - Governance: CTC Risk Committee sets policy and limits (approved by the Board Risk Committee); Treasury and CIO, in partnership with LOBs, calculate and review the Firm’s profile; a dedicated risk function reporting to the CTC CRO provides independent oversight, governance of assumptions, and limit setting/monitoring.
  - Managed primarily through the investment securities portfolio and interest rate derivatives.
  - Key drivers of structural interest rate risk include timing and amount mismatches in repricing/maturities, changes in the yield curve slope/levels, and changes in asset/liability maturities as rates move.
  - Firmwide management via funds transfer pricing that centralizes interest rate risk in Treasury and CIO, reflecting balances, contractual rates, payment schedules, prepayments, reset dates, maturities, reference indices, and rate caps/floors.
  - Simulations are conducted for U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar exposures and primarily include retained loans.
  - References a table summarizing earnings-at-risk positions by LOB and Corporate.

nodes.title: Earnings-at-risk
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.8 Earnings-at-risk
nodes.start_phrase: The effect of interest rate exposure on the Firm’s reported net income is important as interest rate risk represents one of the Firm’s significant market risks.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of additional market risk measures beyond VaR, focusing on stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, and earnings-at-risk (EaR).
- Stress testing:
  - Complements VaR by assessing losses under hypothetical, simultaneous shocks across market factors (credit spreads, equities, rates, FX, commodities).
  - Covers market risk-sensitive positions across lines of business and Corporate; includes tail, cross-asset, geographic, idiosyncratic, and basis risk scenarios.
  - Flexible framework to design new scenarios; results measured against limits and reported to senior management.
  - Governance under Market Risk Management and the Firm’s Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy; Firmwide Market Risk Stress Methodology Committee oversees methodology and scenario changes, with escalation to senior management as needed.
  - Utilized in CCAR and incorporated into the Risk Appetite framework; results reported to the Board and Board Risk Committee.
- Profit and loss drawdowns:
  - Used to flag trading losses beyond tolerance levels; defined as the decline in revenue from the year-to-date peak.
- Earnings-at-risk (EaR) and structural interest rate risk:
  - Interest rate risk arises from both trading and core banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance, securities).
  - Governance: CTC Risk Committee sets policy/limits (approved by Board Risk Committee); Treasury and CIO assess the Firm’s structural interest rate profile; independent CTC risk function provides oversight, assumptions governance, and limit monitoring.
  - Managed via the investment securities portfolio and interest rate derivatives; interest rate risk is aggregated Firmwide with business units transferring risk to Treasury and CIO through funds transfer pricing.
  - Sources of structural interest rate risk include repricing/maturity mismatches, volume mismatches, yield curve slope changes, and changes in effective maturities as rates move.
- EaR methodology:
  - Measures sensitivity of next-12-month net interest income (and certain rate-sensitive fees) to interest rate scenarios relative to a baseline with market rates and deposit pricing assumptions.
  - Simulations cover U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar exposures (retained loans, deposits, deposits with banks, investment securities, long-term debt, hedges, and FTP of other positions).
  - Scenarios include parallel rate shifts, steepeners (long rates up, short constant), and flatteners (short up/long constant or short constant/long down).
  - Key assumptions include instantaneous rate shocks, forecasted balance sheet, modeled mortgage prepayments, reinvestment behavior, deposit forecasts (sensitive to QE reversal, Fed RRP utilization, industry loan levels, and deposit competition), and deposit betas; deposit repricing lags are under evaluation and would meaningfully affect U.S. dollar results (higher rates positive; lower rates negative).
  - EaR is a risk sensitivity, not a forecast of net interest income.
- Results and drivers:
  - Tables present U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar EaR sensitivities as of December 31, 2022 versus 2021; certain 2021 down-rate scenarios were not meaningful given rate levels.
  - 2022 U.S. dollar sensitivities reflect a higher-rate baseline, higher modeled deposit betas, and balance sheet changes; parallel and short-rate shocks are driven more by liabilities repricing than assets, while long-rate shocks are driven more by asset repricing.
  - Non-U.S. dollar steepener/flattener scenarios with only long-term rate changes were not material to EaR.

nodes.title: Non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange risk
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.9 Non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange risk
nodes.start_phrase: Non-U.S. dollar FX risk is the risk that changes in foreign exchange rates affect the value of the Firm’s assets or liabilities or future results.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s approach to non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange (FX) risk and its use of sensitivity-based measures for market risks not captured in VaR or earnings-at-risk. It defines structural non-USD FX exposures (from capital investments, projected revenues/expenses, securities, and non-USD debt) and notes that Treasury and the CIO, in partnership with lines of business, manage and may hedge these risks with derivatives. It then describes how the Firm quantifies potential impacts on net revenue, other comprehensive income (OCI), and noninterest expense from changes in market variables, with results presented net of hedges where appropriate and accompanied by caveats that sensitivities are not predictions of future outcomes.

Key sensitivity categories and examples include:
- Asset management exposures (seed capital, fund co-investments, deferred compensation) under a 10% market value decline.
- Other debt and equity holdings (real estate-related fair value option loans, privately held equity, other fair value investments) under a 10% market value decline.
- Credit and funding-related exposures:
  - Cross-currency basis risk on non-USD long-term debt (1 bp tightening).
  - FX revaluation of hedges on non-USD debt (10% currency depreciation).
  - Derivatives funding valuation adjustment spread risk (1 bp increase).
  - Counterparty credit risk (CVA) under a 10% credit spread widening, moved from Credit Portfolio VaR to sensitivity-based measures in 1Q22.
  - Fair value option liabilities’ funding spread and interest rate/own-credit-spread sensitivities (1 bp increases).
The footnotes specify where impacts are recognized (net revenue, OCI, or noninterest expense) and exclusions (e.g., certain equity securities under the measurement alternative).

nodes.title: Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.heading: 7.8.11.10 Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm quantifies the market risk of certain debt and equity and credit and funding-related exposures by assessing the potential impact on net revenue, other comprehensive income (“OCI”) and noninterest expense due to changes in relevant market variables.
nodes.summary:
- Defines non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange (FX) risk as exposure to changes in FX rates that affect assets, liabilities, and future results.
- Identifies key sources of structural non-USD FX exposure: capital investments, forecasted expenses and revenues, the investment securities portfolio, and non-USD-denominated debt issuance.
- Explains that Treasury and the Chief Investment Office (CIO), in partnership with lines of business, primarily manage these risks for the firm and may use derivatives to hedge them; references related sections for more detail.
- Introduces “other sensitivity-based measures” used to quantify market risk for certain debt, equity, and credit/funding-related positions not included in VaR or earnings-at-risk, assessing potential impacts on net revenue, other comprehensive income (OCI), and noninterest expense.
- Notes that, where appropriate, hedging instruments are shown net of hedged positions, and that disclosed sensitivities are illustrative and not predictive of future results.
- Summarizes categories covered by the sensitivity table (with illustrative 2022 and 2021 impacts):
  - Asset Management activities (seed capital, fund co-investments, deferred compensation and related hedges): 10% market value decline.
  - Other debt and equity (e.g., real estate-related fair value option loans, privately held equity, other fair value investments): 10% market value decline.
  - Non-USD long-term debt (LTD) cross-currency basis risk on derivatives hedging non-USD LTD: 1 bp parallel tightening of cross-currency basis.
  - Non-USD LTD FX hedge revaluation: 10% currency depreciation.
  - Derivatives funding valuation adjustment (FVA): 1 bp parallel increase in funding spread.
  - Credit valuation adjustment (CVA) counterparty credit risk and associated hedges: 10% credit spread widening; notes a 1Q22 governance change moving certain CVA from Credit Portfolio VaR to these measures.
  - Fair value option (FVO) elected liabilities – debit valuation adjustment (DVA) funding spread risk: 1 bp spread increase.
  - FVO liabilities – interest rate sensitivity linked to the Firm’s own credit spread and related risk management positions: 1 bp spread increase.
- Clarifies where impacts are recognized: net revenue, OCI, or noninterest expense; and that certain equity securities measured under the alternative are excluded.
- Provides cross-references to other report sections for business segment results and predominant market risk activities.

nodes.title: COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.8.12 COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm, through its LOBs and Corporate, may be exposed to country risk resulting from financial, economic, political or other significant developments which adversely affect the value of the Firm’s exposures related to a particular country or set of countries.
nodes.summary:
- Defines country risk as adverse financial, economic, political, or other developments affecting the value of the firm’s exposures to a country, and states that a dedicated group monitors portfolio impacts and diversification against strategy and risk tolerance.
- Establishes Country Risk Management as an independent function responsible for policies and standards, assigning sovereign ratings, setting country risk tolerance, measuring and stress-testing exposures, managing and approving limits, reporting trends and breaches, developing surveillance tools (signaling models, rating indicators), and conducting scenario analysis.
- Describes sources of country risk across lending, deposits, investing, and market‑making, for both government and private-sector exposures, whether cross‑border or locally funded.
- Explains attribution of exposure to a country based on where the counterparty’s assets or revenues are primarily located/derived, which may differ from legal domicile or incorporation.
- Clarifies exposure measurement as the aggregation of risk to an immediate default with zero recovery, and notes exclusions of contingent or indirect exposures (e.g., clearing services, secondary exposure to collateral on securities financing receivables).
- Notes that measurement may require assumptions (especially for non-linear or index products or complex counterparties), and that alternative approaches could change reported exposure levels.
- Details product-level measurement methods: deposits (cash at central/commercial/other banks), lending (total committed net of allowance for credit losses and eligible cash/marketable securities collateral), securities financing (receivable net of eligible collateral), debt/equity securities (fair value of long and short positions), derivatives (fair value net of eligible collateral), and credit derivatives (net notional protection bought/sold for the same reference entity inclusive of derivative fair value).
- States that internal country risk reporting differs from FFIEC regulatory reporting.

nodes.title: Organization and management
nodes.heading: 7.8.12.1 Organization and management
nodes.start_phrase: Country Risk Management is an independent risk management function that assesses, manages and monitors exposure to country risk across the Firm.
nodes.summary:
- Defines country risk as adverse financial, economic, political or other developments affecting the value of exposures tied to a country; emphasizes active monitoring and diversification relative to strategy and risk tolerance.
- Establishes Country Risk Management as an independent function overseeing policies, frameworks, sovereign ratings, risk tolerance, measurement and stress monitoring, country limits and breach reporting, surveillance tools (signaling models and indicators), and scenario analysis.
- Identifies sources of country risk across lending, deposits, investing, and market-making activities, both cross-border and locally funded, and covering government and private-sector exposures.
- Describes attribution of exposure to the country where a counterparty/issuer/obligor/guarantor has the largest share of assets or revenue (which may differ from domicile), and aggregation based on immediate default with zero recovery; excludes contingent/indirect exposures (e.g., clearing services, secondary collateral exposure in securities financing).
- Notes the use of assumptions for certain products (e.g., non-linear or index) and counterparties not suitable for single-country attribution; different methods could change reported exposure.
- Details measurement standards:
  - Deposits with banks: cash balances at central/commercial banks and other FIs.
  - Lending: total committed (funded and unfunded) net of allowance for credit losses and eligible cash/marketable securities collateral.
  - Securities financing: receivable balance net of eligible collateral.
  - Debt and equity securities: fair value of long and short positions.
  - Derivative receivables: fair value net of eligible collateral.
  - Credit derivatives: net notional protection purchased/sold for the same reference entity, inclusive of derivative fair values, aligned with management practice.
- States that internal country risk reporting differs from FFIEC regulatory reporting.

nodes.title: Sources and measurement
nodes.heading: 7.8.12.2 Sources and measurement
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm is exposed to country risk through its lending and deposits, investing, and market-making activities, whether cross-border or locally funded.
nodes.summary:
- Defines country risk as potential adverse effects from financial, economic, political, or other developments on exposures tied to a country; monitors portfolio impacts and diversification versus firm strategy and risk tolerance.
- Country Risk Management is an independent function spanning the firm.
- Core activities:
  - Maintain policies, procedures, and standards under a comprehensive country risk framework.
  - Assign sovereign ratings, assess country risks, and set country risk tolerance.
  - Measure and monitor country risk exposure and stress across the firm.
  - Manage and approve country limits; report trends and limit breaches to senior management.
  - Develop surveillance tools (signaling models, ratings indicators) for early warning.
  - Provide country risk scenario analysis.
- Sources of exposure include lending, deposits, investing, and market-making, both cross-border and locally funded, with government and private-sector counterparties.
- Country attribution is based on where the largest share of a counterparty’s assets or revenues reside, which can differ from legal domicile or incorporation.
- Exposure measure aggregates risk to an immediate default with zero recovery of attributed counterparties/issuers/obligors/guarantors; excludes contingent or indirect exposures (e.g., clearing services, secondary exposure to collateral on securities financing receivables).
- Assumptions may be required for certain products (e.g., non-linear or index instruments) or counterparties not suitable for single-country attribution; differing approaches can affect reported exposure.
- Measurement framework:
  - Deposits: cash balances placed with central, commercial, and other banks.
  - Lending: total committed amounts (funded and unfunded), net of allowance for credit losses and eligible cash/marketable securities collateral.
  - Securities financing: receivable balances, net of eligible collateral.
  - Debt and equity securities: fair value of all long and short positions.
  - Derivative receivables: fair value net of eligible collateral.
  - Credit derivatives: net notional protection purchased or sold for the same reference entity, inclusive of derivative fair values, aligned with management practices.
- Internal country risk reporting differs from FFIEC bank regulatory reporting.

nodes.title: Stress testing
nodes.heading: 7.8.12.3 Stress testing
nodes.start_phrase: Stress testing is an important component of the Firm’s country risk management framework, which aims to estimate and limit losses arising from a country crisis by measuring the impact of adverse asset price movements to a country based on market shocks combined with counterparty specific assumptions.
nodes.summary:
- Stress testing: Describes the Firm’s country risk stress testing framework, which estimates and limits losses from country crises by modeling adverse market shocks alongside counterparty-specific assumptions. Country Risk Management designs and runs tailored scenarios for specific countries or groups in response to market events, sector concerns, sovereign actions, and geopolitical risks, using results to inform risk reduction actions.

- Risk reporting: Country exposure and stress are regularly measured and reported to track trends, high usages, and limit breaches. For country risk purposes, exposures to non‑fully autonomous jurisdictions (e.g., Special Administrative Regions and dependent territories) may be reported separately from their associated sovereigns.

- Top 20 non‑U.S. country exposures (as of December 31, 2022, with 2021 comparatives): Presents the Firm’s largest total exposures by country under its internal country risk approach; figures can fluctuate with client activity and market flows. Notable drivers:
  - Germany exposure increased primarily due to higher cash placements with the German central bank tied to balance sheet and liquidity management.
  - U.K. exposure decreased mainly due to lower cash placements with the Bank of England from balance sheet and liquidity actions.
  - Australia exposure declined due to reduced cash at the Reserve Bank of Australia and lower holdings of government debt securities, reflecting client-driven market-making and lower client cash deposits amid higher interest rates.
  - Russia exposure was approximately $500 million as of December 31, 2022 (excluding certain client deposits at the Russian National Settlement Depository that were transferred to the Depository Insurance Agency of Russia on February 3, 2023).

- Table highlights and composition:
  - Largest 2022 exposures (total): Germany $93.2B; U.K. $70.1B; Japan $55.8B; Australia $25.7B; France $18.1B; Brazil $17.8B; Switzerland $15.3B; Canada $14.4B; China $13.7B; South Korea $10.0B.
  - Other notable exposures: Singapore $9.9B; Belgium $9.2B; India $9.0B; Saudi Arabia $7.9B; Netherlands $7.1B (with a small negative trading/investing component); Spain $5.8B; Mexico $5.4B; Luxembourg $5.3B; Hong Kong SAR $4.5B; Sweden $4.4B.
  - Coverage: The table reflects 87% and 88% of total firmwide non‑U.S. exposure attributed to individual countries at year‑end 2022 and 2021, respectively.
  - Category definitions:
    - Deposits with banks: Predominantly cash placed with central banks.
    - Lending: Loans and accrued interest receivable plus lending-related commitments (net of eligible collateral and allowance for credit losses); excludes intraday/operational exposures (e.g., settlement and clearing).
    - Trading and investing: Market-making inventory, investment securities, and counterparty exposure on derivatives and securities financing (net of eligible collateral and hedging), including single‑name and index positions tied to entities in listed countries.
    - Other: Physical commodities inventory and clearing house guarantee funds.
  - 2021 country rankings shown are aligned to the 2022 ranking order.

nodes.title: Risk reporting
nodes.heading: 7.8.12.4 Risk reporting
nodes.start_phrase: Country exposure and stress are measured and reported regularly, and used by Country Risk Management to identify trends and monitor high usages and breaches against limits.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines the Firm’s country risk management practices, emphasizing stress testing as a key tool to estimate and limit losses from country crises by modeling adverse market shocks with counterparty-specific assumptions. Tailored scenarios are periodically designed in response to market events, sector concerns, sovereign actions, and geopolitical risks, and results inform potential risk reduction.

- It describes risk reporting processes whereby country exposures and stress metrics are regularly measured and monitored against limits to identify trends, high usages, and breaches. For reporting, certain jurisdictions such as Special Administrative Regions and dependent territories may be shown separately from their associated sovereigns.

- A table presents the top 20 non-U.S. country exposures as of December 31, 2022, with comparatives for 2021. The selection reflects the largest exposures under the Firm’s internal approach and is not an assessment of adverse credit conditions; exposures can fluctuate with client activity and market flows.

- Notable movements:
  - Germany exposure increased to $93.2 billion, primarily due to higher cash placements with the central bank driven by balance sheet and liquidity management.
  - United Kingdom exposure decreased to $70.1 billion due to changes in central bank cash placements.
  - Australia exposure declined to $25.7 billion from reductions in central bank cash and government securities, influenced by client-driven market-making and lower client deposits amid higher interest rates.
  - As of December 31, 2022, Russia exposure was approximately $500 million, excluding certain client deposits at the Russian National Settlement Depository, which were transferred to the Depository Insurance Agency of Russia on February 3, 2023.

- Exposure categories are defined as:
  - Deposits with banks: predominantly cash with central banks.
  - Lending: loans and commitments (net of eligible collateral and allowance), excluding intra-day/operational exposures.
  - Trading and investing: market-making inventory, investment securities, and derivative/securities financing counterparty exposure net of collateral and hedging (including single-name and index exposures tied to listed countries).
  - Other: physical commodities inventory and clearing house guarantee funds.

- The table covers 87% of Firmwide non-U.S. exposure attributable to individual countries in 2022 (88% in 2021), and 2021 country rankings are presented in the order of 2022 rankings.

nodes.title: CLIMATE RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.8.13 CLIMATE RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Climate risk is the risk associated with the impacts of climate change on the Firm ’s clients, customers , operations and business strategy.
nodes.summary:
- Defines climate risk as impacts of climate change on the firm’s clients, customers, operations, and strategy, acting as a driver of existing risk types.
- Categorizes climate risk into:
  - Physical risk: acute (e.g., floods, wildfires, tropical storms) and chronic (e.g., sea-level rise, changing precipitation, higher average temperatures).
  - Transition risk: financial/economic effects of the shift to a low‑carbon economy, including policy changes, new technologies, and shifting consumer preferences, potentially influenced by physical climate changes.
- Establishes a Climate Risk Management function responsible for the firmwide framework and strategy, integrating climate risk into existing risk management.
- Key responsibilities include:
  - Setting policies, standards, procedures, and processes for identifying, escalating, monitoring, and managing climate risk.
  - Developing metrics, scenarios, and stress tests to assess potential climate-related financial and economic impacts.
  - Building a firmwide climate risk data strategy and supporting technology infrastructure.
- Assigns Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate units responsibility for identifying, assessing, and managing climate risks in their activities and complying with applicable climate-related laws and regulations.
- Governance aligns with the firm’s overall risk governance structure; LOBs and Corporate integrate climate risk into governance frameworks or create new ones as needed.
- LOBs, Corporate, and Climate Risk Management provide the Board Risk Committee with information on significant climate risks and related initiatives.

nodes.title: Organization and management
nodes.heading: 7.8.13.1 Organization and management
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm has a Climate Risk Management function that is responsible for establishing the Firmwide framework and strategy for managing climate risk.
nodes.summary:
- Defines climate risk as impacts of climate change on the firm’s clients, customers, operations, and strategy, treating it as a driver that affects existing risk types.
- Categorizes climate risk into:
  - Physical risk: acute (e.g., floods, wildfires, tropical storms) and chronic (e.g., sea-level rise, changing precipitation, higher average temperatures).
  - Transition risk: financial/economic impacts from moving to a low-carbon economy, driven by policy changes, new technologies, and shifting consumer preferences, and influenced by physical climate changes.
- Establishes a Climate Risk Management function responsible for a firmwide framework and strategy, integrating climate considerations into existing risk frameworks.
- Outlines responsibilities of Climate Risk Management: setting policies/standards/procedures; developing metrics, scenarios, and stress tests to assess potential impacts; and building a firmwide climate risk data strategy and technology infrastructure.
- Assigns LOBs and Corporate units responsibility for identifying, assessing, and managing climate risks within their activities and complying with applicable climate-related laws and regulations.
- Details governance and oversight: climate risk management aligns with the firm’s risk governance; LOBs and Corporate integrate climate risk into governance structures (or create new ones) and, along with Climate Risk Management, provide the Board Risk Committee with information on significant climate risks and initiatives.

nodes.title: Governance and oversight
nodes.heading: 7.8.13.2 Governance and oversight
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s approach to managing climate risk is consistent with the Firm’s risk governance structure.
nodes.summary:
- Defines climate risk as impacts of climate change on the firm’s clients, operations, and strategy, treating climate change as a driver of existing risk types.
- Categorizes climate risk into:
  - Physical risk: acute events (floods, wildfires, storms) and chronic changes (sea-level rise, precipitation shifts, higher average temperatures).
  - Transition risk: financial/economic effects of moving to a low‑carbon economy, driven by policy changes, new technologies, and consumer preference shifts, and influenced by physical climate changes.
- Establishes a dedicated Climate Risk Management function to set the firmwide framework and strategy, integrating climate considerations into existing risk management.
- Climate Risk Management responsibilities include:
  - Setting policies, standards, procedures, and processes for identifying, escalating, monitoring, and managing climate risk.
  - Developing metrics, scenarios, and stress-testing to assess potential climate-related financial and economic impacts.
  - Building a firmwide climate risk data strategy and supporting technology infrastructure.
- Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate are responsible for identifying, assessing, and managing climate risks in their activities and complying with applicable climate-related laws and regulations.
- Governance and oversight align with the firm’s risk governance structure; LOBs and Corporate integrate climate risk into governance or create new frameworks as needed.
- LOBs, Corporate, and Climate Risk Management provide the Board Risk Committee with information on significant climate risks and related initiatives.

nodes.title: OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 7.8.14 OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Operational risk is the risk of an adverse outcome resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes or systems; human factors; or external events impacting the Firm’s processes or systems.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed processes/systems, human factors, or external events; includes compliance, conduct, legal, estimation/model risk.
- Notes operational risk is inherent across activities and can arise from fraud, business disruptions (including extraordinary events), cyber attacks, employee misconduct, regulatory noncompliance, and third-party/vendor failures.
- States the aim of Operational Risk Management is to manage risk at appropriate levels given the firm’s financial position, businesses, markets, and regulatory environment.
- Describes the CCOR (Compliance, Conduct, and Operational Risk) Management Framework, designed to govern, identify, measure, monitor/test, manage, and report operational risk.
- Governance:
  - Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate own operational risk management.
  - Control Management Organization executes day-to-day CCOR activities within each LOB/Corporate.
  - Global Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) and Firmwide Risk Executive (FRE) for Operational Risk and Qualitative Risk Appetite define the framework and minimum standards.
  - LOB/Corporate-aligned CCOR Lead Officers report to the Global CCO/FRE and are independent of the businesses they oversee.
  - Framework is incorporated in the Risk Governance and Oversight Policy, reviewed/approved periodically by the Board Risk Committee.
- Risk identification via structured risk and control self-assessments (RCSA) by LOBs/Corporate; Operational Risk and Compliance provides oversight/challenge and may conduct independent reviews of significant events and emerging/concentrated risks.
- Measurement:
  - Independent assessments of inherent risks and control effectiveness, with reporting to senior management.
  - Quantitative assessments include operational risk capital and loss estimation under baseline and stressed conditions.
  - Loss Distribution Approach (LDA) model projects one-year aggregate losses at 99.9% confidence, incorporating internal loss data (with a one-quarter lag) that remains in estimates post-remediation.
  - Under Basel III AMA, capital methodology incorporates internal/external losses, scenario analysis for tail risk, and business environment/internal control metrics; insurance effects are excluded.
  - Stress testing framework assesses potential losses in stressed economic conditions and feeds CCAR and other firmwide stress tests; references to Capital Risk Management for RWA and CCAR details.
- Monitoring and testing: Operational Risk and Compliance uses assessment results to independently monitor/test LOBs/Corporate for compliance, identify heightened risk areas, and test control effectiveness.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Management Framework
nodes.heading: 7.8.14.1 Operational Risk Management Framework
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s Compliance, Conduct, and Operational Risk (“CCOR”) Management Framework is designed to enable the Firm to govern, identify, measure, monitor and test, manage and report on the Firm’s operational risk.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as adverse outcomes from failed processes/systems, human factors, or external events; includes compliance, conduct, legal, estimation and model risk.
- Notes operational risk is inherent and can manifest via fraud, business disruptions (including extraordinary events), cyber attacks, employee misconduct, regulatory noncompliance, and third‑party/vendor failures.
- States goal of Operational Risk Management is to manage risk at appropriate levels relative to the Firm’s financial position, business characteristics, and regulatory/market environments.
- Describes the CCOR (Compliance, Conduct, and Operational Risk) Management Framework for governing, identifying, measuring, monitoring/testing, managing, and reporting operational risk.
- Governance: Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate own operational risk; Control Management Organization executes the framework day‑to‑day.
- The Global Chief Compliance Officer and Firmwide Risk Executive for Operational Risk and Qualitative Risk Appetite define the CCOR Framework and minimum standards; CCOR Lead Officers are independent of the businesses they oversee.
- Framework governance is embedded in the Risk Governance and Oversight Policy, reviewed and approved by the Board Risk Committee periodically.
- Risk identification via structured risk and control self‑assessments by LOBs/Corporate; Operational Risk and Compliance provides oversight, challenge, and independent assessments of significant events and emerging/concentrated risks.
- Measurement includes independent assessments of inherent risks and control effectiveness, reporting to senior management, and quantitative methods for capital and loss estimation under baseline and stress.
- Primary quantitative model is the Loss Distribution Approach (LDA) estimating one‑year aggregate losses at 99.9% confidence using historical internal loss data; losses continue to influence estimates even after remediation.
- Under Basel III AMA, operational risk capital incorporates internal/external losses, scenario analysis, and business environment/internal control metrics; insurance is not recognized in the AMA capital estimate.
- Stress testing framework develops forward‑looking views of material operational losses in stressed conditions and feeds CCAR and other stress processes; references to Capital Risk Management for RWA and CCAR details.
- Monitoring and testing: Operational Risk and Compliance uses assessment results to independently monitor legal/regulatory compliance, identify heightened risk areas, and test control effectiveness across LOBs and Corporate.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Governance
nodes.heading: 7.8.14.2 Operational Risk Governance
nodes.start_phrase: The LOBs and Corporate are responsible for the management of operational risk.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed processes/systems, human factors, or external events, and states it includes compliance, conduct, legal, estimation and model risk.
- Describes how operational risk can manifest (fraud, business disruptions including extraordinary events, cyber attacks, employee misconduct, regulatory non‑compliance, and third‑party/vendor failures).
- States the objective of Operational Risk Management: manage risk at appropriate levels considering the Firm’s financial position, business profile, and regulatory/market environment.
- Introduces the CCOR (Compliance, Conduct, and Operational Risk) Management Framework to govern, identify, measure, monitor and test, manage, and report operational risk.
- Outlines governance: LOBs and Corporate own operational risk; the Control Management Organization executes the CCOR Framework daily.
- Assigns the Global Chief Compliance Officer and Functional Risk Executive for Operational Risk and Qualitative Risk Appetite responsibility for defining the framework and minimum standards; CCOR Lead Officers report to the Global CCO and are independent of the businesses they oversee.
- Notes inclusion of the CCOR Framework in the Risk Governance and Oversight Policy, reviewed and approved periodically by the Board Risk Committee.
- Details risk identification via LOB/Corporate risk and control self‑assessments (RCSA), with oversight, challenge, and independent assessments by Operational Risk and Compliance.
- Explains measurement: independent assessments of inherent risk and control effectiveness, plus quantitative methods for operational risk capital and loss estimation under baseline and stressed conditions.
- Describes the Loss Distribution Approach model used to simulate frequency/severity of losses over a one‑year horizon at 99.9% confidence, incorporating internal loss data.
- States use of the Basel III Advanced Measurement Approach, incorporating internal/external loss data, scenario analysis, and business environment/internal control metrics; insurance is not recognized in the AMA capital estimate.
- Covers stress testing of operational risk under adverse economic conditions to inform CCAR and other firmwide stress processes.
- Summarizes monitoring and testing: independent monitoring of LOB/Corporate compliance and control testing to identify heightened risks and assess control effectiveness.
- References where to find related details on operational risk RWA and CCAR in Capital Risk Management.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Identification
nodes.heading: 7.8.14.3 Operational Risk Identification
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm utilizes a structured risk and control self-
assessment process that is executed by the LOBs and Corporate.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed processes/systems, human factors, or external events, encompassing compliance, conduct, legal, and model/estimation risks; notes manifestations such as fraud, business disruptions (including extraordinary events), cyberattacks, regulatory non-compliance, and third-party failures; aims to manage risk commensurate with the Firm’s financial position, business profile, markets, and regulatory context.
- Describes the Compliance, Conduct, and Operational Risk (CCOR) Management Framework for governing, identifying, measuring, monitoring/testing, managing, and reporting operational risk.
- Outlines governance: Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate own day-to-day risk management via the Control Management Organization; the Global Chief Compliance Officer and Functional Risk Executive for Operational Risk and Qualitative Risk Appetite define the framework and minimum standards; CCOR Lead Officers are independent of the businesses they oversee; the framework sits within a Board Risk Committee–approved Risk Governance and Oversight Policy.
- Details risk identification through a structured risk and control self-assessment by LOBs/Corporate to evaluate control effectiveness, identify failures, and drive remediation; Operational Risk and Compliance provides oversight, challenge, and independent assessments of significant events and emerging/concentrated risks.
- Explains measurement: independent assessments of inherent risks and control environments with reporting to senior management; quantitative methods include operational risk capital and loss estimation under baseline and stressed conditions.
- Highlights the Loss Distribution Approach (LDA) model as the primary capital component, simulating frequency and severity of losses over a one-year horizon at the 99.9% confidence level, using internal loss data that continue to influence estimates even after remediation.
- Confirms Basel III Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) use, incorporating internal/external losses, tail-risk scenarios, and business environment/internal control metrics; insurance is not recognized in the AMA capital estimate.
- Notes stress testing of operational risk for CCAR and other firmwide stress processes, and that related RWA/CCAR details are provided elsewhere.
- Covers monitoring and testing: Operational Risk and Compliance leverages assessment results to independently monitor compliance with laws, rules, and regulations, identify heightened risk areas, and test control effectiveness across LOBs and Corporate.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Measurement
nodes.heading: 7.8.14.4 Operational Risk Measurement
nodes.start_phrase: Operational Risk and Compliance performs an independent assessment of the operational risks inherent within the LOBs and Corporate, which includes evaluating the effectiveness of the control environments and reporting the results to senior management.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed processes/systems, human factors, or external events, encompassing compliance, conduct, legal, estimation and model risk, and highlights manifestations such as fraud, business disruptions (including extraordinary events), cyber attacks, employee misconduct, regulatory noncompliance, and third‑party failures.
- States objective to manage operational risk at appropriate levels given the Firm’s financial position, business characteristics, and market/regulatory environments.
- Describes the CCOR (Compliance, Conduct, and Operational Risk) Management Framework to govern, identify, measure, monitor/test, manage, and report operational risk.
- Outlines governance: LOBs and Corporate own operational risk; Control Management Organization executes day‑to‑day CCOR activities; the Global Chief Compliance Officer and FRE for Operational Risk and Qualitative Risk Appetite define the framework and minimum standards; CCOR Lead Officers are independent of the businesses they oversee; the framework is embedded in a Board‑approved Risk Governance and Oversight Policy.
- Details risk identification via LOB/Corporate risk and control self‑assessments to evaluate control effectiveness, identify failures, and drive remediation, with Operational Risk and Compliance providing oversight, challenge, and independent assessments of significant events and emerging risks.
- Explains measurement: Operational Risk and Compliance independently assess inherent risks and control effectiveness and report to senior management; quantitative methods include operational risk capital and loss estimation under baseline and stress.
- Provides modeling specifics: primary LDA model projects one‑year aggregate losses at 99.9% confidence using historical internal losses (which continue to influence estimates post‑remediation); under Basel III AMA, capital incorporates internal/external losses, scenario analysis for tail risk, and business environment/control metrics; insurance is not recognized in AMA capital.
- Notes stress testing: considers stressed economic conditions and forward‑looking material events; operational risk stress testing feeds CCAR and other firmwide stress processes.
- Covers monitoring and testing: Operational Risk and Compliance use assessment results to independently monitor and test LOB/Corporate compliance, identify heightened risk areas, and evaluate control effectiveness.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Monitoring and testing
nodes.heading: 7.8.14.5 Operational Risk Monitoring and testing
nodes.start_phrase: The results of risk assessments performed by Operational Risk and Compliance are used in connection with their independent monitoring and testing compliance of the LOBs and Corporate with laws, rules and regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed internal processes/systems, human factors, or external events; includes compliance, conduct, legal, estimation and model risk; examples include fraud, business disruptions (incl. extraordinary events), cyber attacks, employee misconduct, regulatory noncompliance, and third‑party/vendor failures.
- Objective is to manage operational risk at appropriate levels given the Firm’s financial position, business mix, and market/regulatory environments.
- CCOR (Compliance, Conduct, and Operational Risk) Management Framework enables governance, identification, measurement, monitoring and testing, management, and reporting of operational risk.
- Governance: LOBs and Corporate own and manage operational risk; Control Management Organization executes day‑to‑day CCOR activities; Global CCO and FRE for Operational Risk and Qualitative Risk Appetite define the framework and minimum standards; CCOR Lead Officers aligned to LOBs/Corporate are independent of the businesses; the Risk Governance and Oversight Policy (including CCOR Framework) is reviewed/approved periodically by the Board Risk Committee.
- Identification: LOBs/Corporate conduct risk and control self‑assessments to evaluate control effectiveness, identify failures, and plan remediation; Operational Risk and Compliance provides oversight/challenge and conducts independent reviews of significant events and emerging/concentrated risks.
- Measurement: Operational Risk and Compliance independently assesses inherent risks and control effectiveness and reports to senior management; quantitative methods include operational risk capital and loss estimation under baseline and stress.
  - Primary model is Loss Distribution Approach (LDA), projecting one‑year aggregate losses at a 99.9% confidence level using historical data; incorporates realized internal losses with a one‑quarter lag and continues to reflect them post‑remediation.
  - Under Basel III AMA, methodology incorporates internal and external loss data, scenario analysis to capture tail risk, and business environment/internal control metrics; no recognition of insurance mitigation in AMA capital.
  - Stressed economic conditions are considered via an operational risk stress testing framework used for CCAR and other stress tests.
- Monitoring and testing: Operational Risk and Compliance uses assessment results to independently monitor and test LOB/Corporate compliance, identify heightened operational risks, and test control effectiveness.
- Cross‑reference to Capital Risk Management (pages 86–96) for details on operational risk RWA and CCAR.

nodes.title: Management of Operational Risk
nodes.heading: 7.8.14.6 Management of Operational Risk
nodes.start_phrase: The operational risk areas or issues identified through monitoring and testing are escalated to the LOBs and Corporate to be remediated through action plans, as needed, to mitigate operational risk.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on management and reporting of operational risk across the firm, with issues identified through monitoring/testing escalated to Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate for remediation via action plans, with guidance from Operational Risk and Compliance.
- Firmwide standards for consistent operational risk reporting, including evaluation of key risk and performance indicators against thresholds and risk appetite, and reinforced escalation protocols to senior management and the Board of Directors.
- Identification of operational risk subcategories (Compliance, Conduct, Legal, Estimations and Model risk) and additional examples (cybersecurity, business/technology resiliency, payment fraud, third-party outsourcing), with cross-references for more detail.
- Heightened operational risk due to the war in Ukraine and evolving global sanctions; implementation of controls to ensure compliance, prevent dealings with sanctioned parties, and block/restrict required payments.
- Extensive discussion of cybersecurity risk: definition, rising volume/complexity of attacks amid geopolitical tensions, precautionary controls (e.g., enhanced threat monitoring), and acknowledgment that defenses cannot guarantee success.
- Recognition that business expansion can introduce new cyber threats and regulatory scrutiny; continued investment in cyber defenses and collaboration with government, law enforcement, peers, and industry groups.
- Emphasis on third-party and client-related cybersecurity risks; ongoing engagement with vendors and clients to improve security, with clients responsible for losses stemming from their own security failures.
- Description of the firm’s Information Security Program to prevent, detect, and respond to cyberattacks, with periodic Board updates on program status, policies, improvements, and significant cybersecurity events, and reference to a cybersecurity incident response framework.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Reporting
nodes.heading: 7.8.14.7 Operational Risk Reporting
nodes.start_phrase: All employees of the Firm are expected to escalate risks appropriately.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the Firm’s operational risk management framework: issues identified through monitoring and testing are escalated to Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate for remediation via action plans, with Operational Risk and Compliance advising on development and implementation.
- Describes firmwide operational risk reporting standards: consistent reporting across the Firm, LOBs, and Corporate; evaluation of key risk and performance indicators against thresholds; assessment against stated risk appetite; and reinforced escalation to senior management and the Board. Emphasizes all employees’ responsibility to escalate risks.
- Lists operational risk subcategories (Compliance, Conduct, Legal, Estimations and Model risk) and highlights other examples including cybersecurity, business and technology resiliency, payment fraud, and third‑party outsourcing.
- Addresses increased operational and compliance risk from the war in Ukraine and evolving sanctions regimes, and notes controls to avoid dealings with sanctioned parties and to block/restrict payments as required.
- Provides an in‑depth view of cybersecurity risk: growing attack volume and sophistication amid geopolitical tensions; precautionary measures (e.g., enhanced threat monitoring) with no assurance of complete protection; anticipated regulatory scrutiny; continued investment in defense capabilities; collaboration with government, law enforcement, and industry; expanded employee and select client education.
- Identifies third parties and clients as significant sources of cybersecurity risk; details engagement with vendors and clients to improve security; states clients bear losses stemming from their own security failures.
- Describes governance and response: an Information Security Program to prevent, detect, and respond to cyberattacks; periodic Board updates on program status, policies, improvements, and significant events; and an established cybersecurity incident response capability.

nodes.title: Subcategories and examples of operational risks
nodes.heading: 7.8.14.8 Subcategories and examples of operational risks
nodes.start_phrase: Operational risk can manifest itself in various ways.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the firm’s operational risk management framework: issues identified through monitoring and testing are escalated to lines of business (LOBs) and Corporate for remediation via action plans, with Operational Risk and Compliance advising on development and implementation.
- Outlines operational risk reporting: all employees must escalate risks; Operational Risk and Compliance escalate to LOB and Corporate Control Committees; firmwide standards ensure consistent reporting, evaluate key risk and performance indicators against thresholds, and assess risks versus stated risk appetite; reinforced escalation to senior management and the Board.
