nodes.title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.heading: 7.9 CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase ’s accounting policies and use of estimates are integral to understanding its reported results.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates, emphasizing management judgment in determining carrying values of assets and liabilities.
- Description of robust policies, controls, independent reviews, and consistency standards for estimation methods, including controlled processes for methodology changes.
- Focus on the allowance for credit losses as a key estimate, covering:
  - Allowance for loan losses on scored and risk-rated portfolios,
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments,
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities.
- Significant judgment factors: development and weighting of macroeconomic forecasts, historical loss data, risk characteristics and ratings, collateral valuation, and determination of remaining expected life.
- Use of an eight-quarter forecast incorporating hundreds of macroeconomic variables (MEVs), with fewer than twenty key drivers varying by portfolio and geography.
  - Consumer key MEVs: regional U.S. unemployment, home price index (HPI), U.S. real GDP.
  - Wholesale key MEVs: U.S. real GDP, unemployment, equity prices, interest rates, corporate credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, and HPI.
- Sensitivity analysis comparing modeled losses under central and relative adverse scenarios:
  - Adverse scenario assumes higher U.S. unemployment (about 1.9% average increase; 2.8% peak in 4Q23),
  - Lower U.S. real GDP (about 3.1% lower at the end of the horizon; 3.9% peak difference in 4Q23),
  - Lower national HPI (peak difference ~8.4% in 3Q24).
- Key caveats: allowance at 12/31/2022 already reflects adverse scenario weighting; MEV impacts are interrelated and nonlinear; future portfolio mix and borrower behavior can materially change outcomes.
- Overall message: allowance estimates are highly sensitive to macroeconomic assumptions, are rigorously governed, and may vary significantly across periods and portfolios.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses
nodes.heading: 7.9.1 Allowance for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents management’s estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm’s financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Explains JPMorgan Chase’s framework for critical accounting estimates, emphasizing management judgment, established policies and controls, independent reviews, consistency over time, and governance of methodology changes.

- Details the allowance for credit losses:
  - Components: allowance for loan losses, lending-related commitments, and credit losses on investment securities.
  - Key judgments: development and weighting of macroeconomic forecasts, use of historical loss experience, assessment of risk characteristics and ratings, collateral valuation, and determination of remaining expected life.
  - Forecast methodology: eight-quarter forward-looking horizon using hundreds of macroeconomic variables (MEVs), with fewer than twenty main drivers varying by portfolio and geography.
  - Principal MEVs: for consumer—regional U.S. unemployment, home price index (HPI), U.S. real GDP; for wholesale—U.S. real GDP, unemployment, equity prices, interest rates, corporate credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, and HPI.
  - Sensitivity to economic assumptions: describes limitations in isolating individual factor effects due to interrelated and nonlinear impacts and differences across products and geographies.
  - Scenario analysis (as of Dec 31, 2022): compares central vs. relative adverse scenarios—adverse assumes higher unemployment (~+1.9% average; peak +2.8% in 4Q23), lower real GDP (end of horizon ~3.1% lower; peak difference ~3.9% in 4Q23), and lower national HPI (peak difference ~8.4% in 3Q24).
  - Modeled credit loss impacts under adverse vs. central (excluding other qualitative adjustments): approximately +$0.5B for residential real estate, +$2.2B for credit cards, and +$3.9B for wholesale loans and lending-related commitments.
  - Notes caveats: current allowance already reflects weighting of adverse scenarios; MEV effects are interrelated/nonlinear; portfolio mix and borrower behavior expectations matter; management overlays may adjust modeled results.
  - Concludes estimates were reasonable given uncertainty and are governed by robust processes.

- Describes fair value measurements:
  - Use of fair value on a recurring basis for derivatives, structured note products, and certain securities financing agreements; nonrecurring fair value for certain loans measured using collateral values.
  - Presents the composition of assets measured at fair value and Level 3 classification as of Dec 31, 2022:
    - Total assets at fair value: ~$1.108T; Level 3 assets: ~$25.6B.
    - Recurring fair value: ~$1.106T total; ~$23.6B Level 3. Nonrecurring fair value: ~$2.7B total; ~$2.0B Level 3.
    - Key line items: trading assets ~$454B (Level 3 ~$13.6B, including derivative receivables ~$10.7B Level 3), AFS securities ~$206B (Level 3 ~$0.2B), loans ~$42B (Level 3 ~$1.4B), MSRs ~$8.0B (all Level 3).
    - Level 3 as a percentage: ~0.7% of total firm assets ($3.666T) and ~2.3% of total assets at fair value.
    - Footnote clarifies Level 3 derivative receivables are shown before netting, unlike totals that reflect netting.

nodes.title: Fair value
nodes.heading: 7.9.2 Fair value
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase carries a portion of its assets and liabilities at fair value.
nodes.summary:
- Credit loss sensitivity: The firm compared modeled lifetime credit loss estimates under a relative adverse scenario versus its central scenario. Estimated increases (excluding offsetting/correlated effects and other qualitative adjustments) were approximately:
  - $0.5 billion for residential real estate loans and lending-related commitments
  - $2.2 billion for credit card loans
  - $3.9 billion for wholesale loans and lending-related commitments
- Modeling caveats and governance: The analysis relates only to modeled outputs and not the overall allowance, which also reflects management judgment and qualitative adjustments for uncertainty and imprecision. Despite inherent macroeconomic uncertainty, management deems its governance robust and its expected credit loss estimates reasonable as of December 31, 2022.
- Fair value framework: JPMorgan Chase measures portions of its assets and liabilities at fair value on a recurring basis (e.g., derivatives, structured notes, certain securities financing) and on a nonrecurring basis (e.g., certain mortgage, home equity, and other loans based on collateral).
- Fair value composition at December 31, 2022:
  - Total assets measured at fair value: $1,108.3 billion, of which $1,105.6 billion recurring and $2.7 billion nonrecurring
  - Total Level 3 assets: $25.6 billion
  - Key line items at fair value (Level 3 in parentheses): trading debt and equity $382.9b ($2.9b); derivative receivables $70.9b ($10.7b); AFS securities $205.9b ($0.2b); loans $42.1b ($1.4b); MSRs $8.0b ($8.0b); other $14.0b ($0.4b); federal funds sold/securities purchased under resale $311.9b ($0); securities borrowed $70.0b ($0)
  - Total firm assets: $3,665.7 billion
  - Level 3 assets as a percentage of total firm assets: 0.7%; as a percentage of total assets at fair value: 2.3%
- Derivatives netting note: Reported total derivative receivables reflect netting; the $10.7 billion Level 3 derivative receivables figure is presented without netting for valuation-input transparency and would be lower if netting (including cash collateral) were applied.

nodes.title: Assets measured at fair value
nodes.heading: 7.9.2.1 Assets measured at fair value
nodes.start_phrase: The following table includes the Firm’s assets measured at fair value and the portion of such assets that are classified within level 3 of the fair value hierarchy.
nodes.summary:
- The firm compared modeled lifetime credit loss estimates under a relative adverse scenario to its central scenario and found increases of approximately:
  - $0.5 billion for residential real estate loans and lending-related commitments
  - $2.2 billion for credit card loans
  - $3.9 billion for wholesale loans and lending-related commitments
- These figures reflect modeled credit loss estimates only; they do not represent changes to the overall allowance for credit losses and exclude potential qualitative adjustments, offsets, and correlated effects. Management judgment and macroeconomic uncertainty are emphasized, with the firm asserting its governance is appropriate and estimates reasonable as of December 31, 2022.
- Fair value overview: JPMorgan Chase measures a portion of assets and liabilities at fair value. Most are measured on a recurring basis (e.g., derivatives, structured notes, certain securities financing agreements). Some assets (e.g., certain mortgage, home equity, and other loans) are measured on a nonrecurring basis using collateral values.
- As of December 31, 2022:
  - Total assets measured at fair value: $1,108.3 billion, within total firm assets of $3,665.7 billion
  - Level 3 assets at fair value: $25.6 billion
  - Level 3 assets as a percentage of total firm assets: 0.7%
  - Level 3 assets as a percentage of total assets at fair value: 2.3%
- Key fair value categories and Level 3 composition:
  - Trading assets: $453.8 billion total, $13.6 billion Level 3 (including derivative receivables of $70.9 billion total, $10.7 billion Level 3)
  - AFS securities: $205.9 billion total, $0.2 billion Level 3
  - Loans (at fair value): $42.1 billion total, $1.4 billion Level 3

nodes.title: Valuation
nodes.heading: 7.9.2.2 Valuation
nodes.start_phrase: Details of the Firm’s processes for determining fair value are set out in Note 2.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the Firm’s fair value determination process, emphasizing the role of management judgment, especially for Level 3 instruments that rely on significant unobservable inputs and internally developed models.
- Details the selection of valuation models/techniques and key unobservable inputs used for Level 3 (e.g., yield curves, interest rates, prepayment speeds, default rates, volatilities, correlations, market prices, comparable valuations, FX rates, credit curves).
- Describes valuation adjustments for Levels 2 and 3 to reflect counterparty and own credit, funding, liquidity, unobservable parameters, and portfolio-level risk size; notes greater uncertainty and dispersion of estimates during volatile markets.
- Notes that imprecision in inputs and differing methodologies can materially affect reported gains/losses and fair values; methods may vary across businesses.
- Outlines goodwill impairment testing under U.S. GAAP by reporting unit; for the year ended December 31, 2022, no impairment was identified, with fair values exceeding carrying values by at least 10%, based on economic conditions, cost of equity, actual results, and projections benchmarked to third-party/peer data.
- Describes the credit card rewards liability: recognition of expected redemption costs for points earned, balances of $11.3 billion (2022) and $9.8 billion (2021), increase driven by higher spending and promotions, and sensitivity to key assumptions—redemption rate and cost per point—updated periodically using history, behavior, and judgment.

nodes.title: Goodwill impairment
nodes.heading: 7.9.3 Goodwill impairment
nodes.start_phrase: Under U.S. GAAP, goodwill must be allocated to reporting units and tested for impairment at least annually.
nodes.summary:
- Valuation: Describes the firm’s fair value determination process and reliance on judgment based on market observability. Explains the fair value hierarchy, emphasizing that Level 3 valuations require greater judgment due to significant unobservable inputs (e.g., transaction data, yield curves, rates, prepayments, defaults, volatilities, correlations, market prices, FX, credit curves). Outlines valuation adjustments for Levels 2 and 3 to reflect counterparty and firm credit, funding, liquidity, unobservable parameters, and portfolio-level factors, noting heightened uncertainty during volatile markets. Acknowledges that different methodologies and assumptions can yield different fair values and that estimates may vary across businesses.

- Goodwill impairment: Summarizes U.S. GAAP requirements to allocate goodwill to reporting units and test annually. Notes the 2022 assessment concluded no impairment as of December 31, 2022; each reporting unit’s fair value exceeded carrying value by at least 10%. Highlights use of current economic conditions, cost of equity, actual results, projections, and third-party/peer benchmarks in the analysis.

- Credit card rewards liability: Explains the rewards programs (no caps or expirations; redeemable for cash, gift cards, travel) and accounting for a liability representing expected redemption costs. Reports balances of $11.3 billion (2022) and $9.8 billion (2021), with the increase driven by higher earning from spend growth and promotions outpacing redemptions. Notes sensitivity to redemption rate and cost-per-point assumptions, which are periodically updated based on historical experience, cardholder behavior, and management judgment.

nodes.title: Credit card rewards liability
nodes.heading: 7.9.4 Credit card rewards liability
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase offers credit cards with various rewards programs which allow cardholders to earn rewards points based on their account activity and the terms and conditions of the rewards program.
nodes.summary:
- Valuation of financial instruments: Describes the Firm’s fair value determination process (referencing Note 2), emphasizing the increasing management judgment required from Level 1 to Level 3 of the fair value hierarchy. For Level 3, management selects appropriate models and derives significant unobservable inputs (e.g., yield curves, prepayment speeds, default rates, volatilities, correlations, prices, FX, credit curves) from empirical data. For Levels 2 and 3, valuation adjustments are applied for counterparty and own credit, funding, liquidity, unobservable parameters, and portfolio-level factors, with heightened uncertainty in volatile markets. Notes the potential impact of input imprecision on gains/losses and that differing methodologies could yield different fair values.

- Goodwill impairment: Under U.S. GAAP, goodwill is allocated to reporting units and tested annually (methodology in Note 15). Management applies significant judgment. As of December 31, 2022, goodwill was not impaired; for all reporting units, fair value exceeded carrying value by at least 10%. Projections align with current outlook and long-term assumptions, benchmarked where possible with third-party/peer data.

- Credit card rewards liability: Explains rewards programs and the accounting for the rewards liability as points are earned and redeemed. The liability was $11.3 billion at December 31, 2022 (up from $9.8 billion in 2021), driven by higher spending and promotional offers outpacing redemptions. The liability depends on redemption rate (RR) and cost per point (CPP), which are periodically reassessed based on historical data and judgment. A combined 25 bps increase in RR and 1 bp increase in CPP would raise the liability by approximately $315 million.

- Income taxes: Outlines the complexity and judgment in interpreting tax laws across jurisdictions, determining current and deferred tax provisions, and recognizing/adjusting unrecognized tax benefits. Discusses deferred tax assets (including NOLs and FTCs), realizability assessments, use of enacted tax rates, and potential valuation allowances. As of December 31, 2022, management expects to realize deferred tax assets net of existing valuation allowance. Notes that audits, legal changes, and strategy shifts can materially impact the effective tax rate and provisions (additional details in Note 25).

- Litigation reserves: Points to Note 30 for significant estimates and judgments related to establishing litigation reserves.

nodes.title: Income taxes
nodes.heading: 7.9.5 Income taxes
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase is subject to the income tax laws of the various jurisdictions in which it operates, including U.S. federal, state and local, and non-U.S. jurisdictions.
nodes.summary:
- Rewards programs: Sensitivity disclosure notes that, as of December 31, 2022, a combined increase of 25 basis points in redemption rate (RR) and 1 basis point in cost per point (CPP) would increase rewards liability by approximately $315 million.
- Income taxes overview: The Firm operates under complex, multi-jurisdictional tax laws requiring significant judgments on interpretation, timing, and application to transactions; outcomes may materially affect results.
- Tax examinations and uncertainties: Positions are subject to review by taxing authorities; unrecognized tax benefits are recorded and adjusted as matters evolve. Uncertain tax positions are recognized if more-likely-than-not and measured at the largest benefit likely to be realized upon settlement; reassessments can materially affect the effective tax rate.
- Deferred taxes and valuation: Deferred taxes arise from temporary differences and are measured using enacted tax rates. Deferred tax assets (including NOLs and foreign tax credits) are recognized when more-likely-than-not realizable, considering future taxable income and tax planning. Valuation allowances are established or reversed as estimates change. As of December 31, 2022, management expects to realize DTAs net of existing valuation allowance.
- Tax provision mechanics: The provision comprises current and deferred taxes, based on estimates that may differ from amounts in filed returns; adjustments upon filing can impact the effective tax rate.
- References: Additional details on income taxes are in Note 25; significant estimates and judgments for litigation reserves are referenced in Note 30.

nodes.title: Litigation reserves
nodes.heading: 7.9.6 Litigation reserves
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 30 for a description of the significant estimates and judgments associated with establishing litigation reserves.
nodes.summary:
- Rewards liability sensitivity: As of December 31, 2022, a combined 25 bps increase in redemption rate and 1 bp increase in cost per point would raise rewards liability by approximately $315 million.
- Income tax complexity and judgment: The Firm operates across multiple tax jurisdictions and must interpret complex laws, making significant assumptions and judgments for tax provisions and unrecognized tax benefits; outcomes are subject to audits, appeals, and litigation.
- Potential volatility: Changes in laws, interpretations, business strategies, or audit outcomes may materially affect results of operations and the effective tax rate in the period of change.
- Deferred taxes: Recognized for temporary differences using enacted rates; effects of tax rate changes are recorded when enacted. Deferred tax assets (including NOLs and foreign tax credits) are reviewed regularly, with valuation allowances established or reversed based on “more-likely-than-not” realizability and available tax planning strategies.
- Current assessment: As of December 31, 2022, management determined it is more likely than not that deferred tax assets will be realized, net of existing valuation allowances.
- Unrecognized tax benefits: Adjusted as new information arises; positions recognized if more-likely-than-not and measured at the largest amount likely to be realized. Reassessments can materially impact the effective tax rate.
- Tax provision mechanics: The provision comprises current and deferred taxes based on estimates that may differ from filed returns; true-up adjustments upon filing can affect the effective tax rate.
- Cross-references: Additional details on income taxes are in Note 25; significant estimates and judgments for litigation reserves are referenced in Note 30.

nodes.title: ACCOUNTING AND REPORTING DEVELOPMENTS
nodes.heading: 7.10 ACCOUNTING AND REPORTING DEVELOPMENTS
nodes.start_phrase: Provides optional expedients and exceptions to current accounting guidance when financial instruments, hedge accounting relationships, and other transactions are amended due to reference rate reform.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of accounting and reporting developments, focusing on FASB standards adopted since January 1, 2021 and standards issued but not yet adopted as of December 31, 2022, along with their effects on the firm’s financial statements.
- Reference Rate Reform (issued March 2020; updated January 2021 and December 2022):
  - Provides optional expedients and exceptions for contracts, financial instruments, and hedge relationships impacted by reference rate reform, including treating certain amendments as modifications rather than extinguishments, allowing hedge accounting to continue with changed critical terms, and a one-time election to transfer securities out of HTM.
  - 2021 update permits expedients for discounting, margining, or price-alignment changes; 2022 update extends the relief through December 31, 2024.
  - Firm elected certain expedients starting Q3 2020 and applied discounting transition retrospectively; no material impact on the Consolidated Financial Statements.
- Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method (issued March 2022):
  - Expands portfolio hedging to include more prepayable assets and permits inclusion of non-prepayable assets; clarifies eligible derivatives and related presentation/disclosure; allows a one-time HTM-to-AFS reclassification upon adoption.
  - Adopted prospectively on January 1, 2023; in January 2023, approximately $7.0 billion of HTM securities were transferred into a closed AFS portfolio hedged under this method.
- Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures (issued March 2022):
  - Eliminates TDR accounting and disclosure requirements, including discounted cash flow measurement; adds disclosures for certain loan modifications for borrowers in financial difficulty; requires current-period charge-offs disclosed by origination year.
  - Adopted January 1, 2023 using a modified retrospective method; resulted in a net decrease to the allowance for credit losses of about $600 million and an after-tax increase to retained earnings of about $450 million, primarily affecting residential real estate and credit card portfolios.

nodes.title: Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Standards Adopted since January 1, 2021
nodes.heading: 7.10.1 Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Standards Adopted since January 1, 2021
nodes.start_phrase: Provides optional expedients and exceptions to current accounting guidance when financial instruments, hedge accounting relationships, and other transactions are amended due to reference rate reform.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt summarizes JPMorgan Chase’s recent accounting and reporting developments, focusing on FASB standards:

- FASB standards adopted since January 1, 2021: Reference Rate Reform guidance providing optional expedients for contract and hedge accounting changes due to benchmark transitions, an election to treat qualifying amendments as modifications, allowance to adjust hedge terms without de-designation, and a one-time option to transfer securities out of HTM. Updates permitted discounting-transition modifications and extended relief through December 31, 2024. The Firm applied certain expedients (beginning Q3 2020, with discounting transition applied retrospectively), with no material impact on the Consolidated Financial Statements.

- FASB standards issued but not adopted as of December 31, 2022, and subsequently adopted in 2023:
  - Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method expands portfolio hedging to include prepayable and non-prepayable assets, clarifies eligible derivatives and presentation/disclosures, and allows a one-time HTM-to-AFS reclassification. Adopted prospectively on January 1, 2023; approximately $7.0 billion of HTM securities were transferred to a closed AFS portfolio hedged under this method.
  - Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures eliminates TDR accounting/disclosure requirements (including DCF for allowance), requires disclosures for certain borrower modification types and charge-offs by vintage, and was adopted January 1, 2023 via a modified retrospective method. Adoption reduced the allowance for credit losses by about $600 million and increased retained earnings by about $450 million after tax, largely in residential real estate and credit card portfolios.

nodes.title: FASB Standards Issued but Not Adopted as of December 31, 2022
nodes.heading: 7.10.2 FASB Standards Issued but Not Adopted as of December 31, 2022
nodes.start_phrase: Expands the current ability to hedge a portfolio of prepayable assets to allow more of the portfolio to be hedged.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Accounting and Reporting Developments focusing on FASB standards recently adopted and those issued but not yet adopted as of December 31, 2022.
- Reference Rate Reform (issued March 2020; updated January 2021 and December 2022):
  - Provides optional expedients and exceptions for contract modifications, hedge accounting, and other transactions affected by reference rate reform.
  - Elections allow treating certain contract changes as modifications (not extinguishments), adjusting hedge terms without terminating hedge relationships, and a one-time transfer from held-to-maturity (HTM) to available-for-sale (AFS).
  - Adds an election to treat discounting transition changes in derivatives as modifications; extends expedients through December 31, 2024.
  - Firm adopted certain expedients beginning Q3 2020; discounting transition applied retrospectively; no material impact on consolidated financial statements.
- Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method (issued March 2022):
  - Expands portfolio hedging to include more prepayable assets and allows inclusion of non-prepayable assets; clarifies eligible derivatives and related presentation/disclosure.
  - Permits a one-time HTM-to-AFS reclassification upon adoption.
  - Adopted prospectively on January 1, 2023; approximately $7.0 billion of HTM securities transferred to a closed AFS portfolio hedged under the portfolio layer method.
- Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings (TDRs) and Vintage Disclosures (issued March 2022):
  - Eliminates TDR accounting and related discounted cash flow measurement requirement.
  - Requires disclosures for certain loan modifications to borrowers in financial difficulty and charge-off information by origination year.
  - Adopted January 1, 2023 using a modified retrospective method; resulted in a net decrease to the allowance for credit losses of about $600 million and an after-tax increase to retained earnings of about $450 million, primarily in residential real estate and credit card portfolios.

nodes.title: FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS
nodes.heading: 7.11 FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS
nodes.start_phrase: From time to time, the Firm has made and will make forward-looking statements.
nodes.summary:
- Cautionary note on forward-looking statements: defines what they are, how to identify them, and where JPMorgan Chase may make them (2022 Form 10-K, other SEC filings, and oral remarks by senior management).
- Emphasis that such statements are subject to significant risks and uncertainties beyond the Firm’s control, and actual results may differ materially.
- Summary of principal risk factors that could cause deviations, including:
  - Macroeconomic, political, and geopolitical conditions (e.g., war in Ukraine).
  - Regulatory, capital, liquidity, trade, monetary and fiscal policy changes; taxation changes; heightened oversight.
  - Market dynamics: liquidity, volatility, investor sentiment, consumer behavior.
  - Firm-specific factors: capital/liquidity management, credit ratings, reputation, ESG considerations, ability to innovate, product/service lifecycle risks, expense control, competitive pressures, talent attraction/retention.
  - Client/counterparty credit quality; adequacy of risk management, disclosure controls, and ICFR.
  - Legal/regulatory proceedings; accounting policy changes and valuation challenges.
  - Operational and external events: disasters, pandemics, climate effects, geopolitical instability; systems security, third-party failures, and cybersecurity threats.
  - Reference to additional risks in Item 1A: Risk Factors.
- Statement that forward-looking statements speak only as of their date; no obligation to update, with future disclosures to be consulted in subsequent SEC filings.
- Management’s report on internal control over financial reporting (ICFR): outlines responsibility of management (under Board oversight) to maintain ICFR to ensure reliable U.S. GAAP financial reporting, proper authorization of transactions, and prevention/detection of unauthorized asset use.
- Notes inherent limitations of ICFR and risks related to future changes or compliance deterioration.
- Management’s assessment as of December 31, 2022, using the COSO 2013 framework concluded ICFR was effective with no material weaknesses.
- Independent auditor (PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP) audited the effectiveness of ICFR; report included; signed by Chairman & CEO James Dimon and CFO Jeremy Barnum on February 21, 2023.

nodes.title: Management’s report on internal control over financial reporting
nodes.heading: 8.1 Management’s report on internal control over financial reporting
nodes.start_phrase: Management of JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“ JPMorgan Chase ” or the “Firm”) is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting.
nodes.summary:
- Management asserts responsibility for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) at JPMorgan Chase & Co., designed to ensure reliable financial reporting and U.S. GAAP compliance.
- ICFR components outlined: accurate recordkeeping, proper authorization and recording of transactions, and prevention/detection of unauthorized asset use that could materially affect the financial statements.
- Acknowledgement of inherent ICFR limitations and risks over time.
- Management assessed ICFR effectiveness as of December 31, 2022, using the COSO 2013 Internal Control—Integrated Framework, concluding controls were effective with no material weaknesses.
- Report signed by Chairman & CEO James Dimon and EVP & CFO Jeremy Barnum, dated February 21, 2023.
- Independent auditor PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP audited both the consolidated financial statements (balance sheets as of December 31, 2022 and 2021; results and cash flows for the three years ended December 31, 2022) and ICFR as of December 31, 2022.
- PwC issued unqualified opinions: the financial statements present fairly in conformity with U.S. GAAP, and ICFR was effective as of December 31, 2022.
- Noted change in accounting principle: adoption in 2020 of a new method for credit losses on certain financial instruments (referenced in Note 1).
- Audit conducted under PCAOB standards; description of auditor and management responsibilities, independence, scope and nature of procedures, and reiteration of ICFR definition and inherent limitations.

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
nodes.heading: 8.2 Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
nodes.start_phrase: We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheets of JPMorgan Chase & Co. and its subsidiaries (the “Firm”) as of D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 , and the related consolidated statements of income, comprehensive income, changes in stockholders’ equity and cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2, including the related notes (collectively referred to as the “consolidated financial statements”).
nodes.summary:
- Independent auditor’s report from PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP to JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Board and shareholders.
- Audited consolidated financial statements: balance sheets as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, and statements of income, comprehensive income, changes in stockholders’ equity, and cash flows for each of the three years ended December 31, 2022, including notes.
- Unqualified opinion that the financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the Firm’s financial position and results in conformity with U.S. GAAP.
- Unqualified opinion that the Firm maintained effective internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022, based on the COSO 2013 framework.
- Disclosure of a change in accounting principle in 2020 related to the method of accounting for credit losses on certain financial instruments.
- Basis for opinions: management is responsible for the financial statements and internal control; auditors are independent (per SEC and PCAOB rules) and conducted audits in accordance with PCAOB standards to obtain reasonable assurance regarding material misstatements (due to error or fraud) and effectiveness of internal control.
- Audit procedures summarized: risk assessment, test-based examination of evidence, evaluation of accounting principles and significant estimates, overall presentation review, and testing design and operating effectiveness of internal controls.
- Definition and inherent limitations of internal control over financial reporting, including that it may not prevent or detect misstatements and controls may change over time.
- Report identifies PwC as the independent registered public accounting firm (New York office) and appears in JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s 2022 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Critical Audit Matters
nodes.heading: 8.2.1 Critical Audit Matters
nodes.start_phrase: The critical audit matters communicated below are matters arising from the current period audit of the consolidated financial statements that were communicated or required to be communicated to the audit committee and that (i) relate to accounts or disclosures that are material to the consolidated financial statements and (ii) involved our especially challenging, subjective, or complex judgments.
nodes.summary:
- Excerpt from the Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm in JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s 2022 Form 10-K (dated February 21, 2023; auditor since 1965), communicating Critical Audit Matters (CAMs) without altering the overall unqualified opinion or providing separate opinions on the CAMs.
- CAM 1: Allowance for loan losses — portfolio-based component of wholesale and credit card loans.
  - Balance at 12/31/22: $17.0B allowance on $785.9B portfolio-based retained loans.
  - Methodology: Quantitative expected credit loss models using a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios; key drivers include U.S. unemployment and U.S. real GDP; qualitative adjustments for model imprecision, emerging risks, trends, and other subjective factors.
  - Why a CAM: Significant management judgment in macro forecasts and model/adjustment choices; high auditor judgment and effort; involvement of specialists.
  - Audit response: Tested controls (model validation, macro scenario generation); evaluated models/methodologies; assessed reasonableness of unemployment and GDP forecasts; tested data completeness/accuracy; evaluated qualitative adjustments; used professionals with specialized skill and knowledge.
- CAM 2: Fair value of certain Level 3 financial instruments.
  - Context: Firm measures $1.1T of assets and $453.7B of liabilities at fair value on a recurring basis; includes $13.6B trading assets and $37.8B liabilities classified as Level 3.
  - Valuation approach: Internally developed models with unobservable inputs (e.g., interest rate volatility and correlation, equity prices, credit and FX factors, Bermudan switch values).
  - Why a CAM: Significant judgment in unobservable inputs; high auditor judgment and effort; use of specialists.
  - Audit response: Tested controls over models, inputs, and data; with specialists, developed independent fair value estimates for a sample and compared to management; tested data completeness/accuracy; developed independent inputs and evaluated management’s unobservable inputs.
- Consolidated statements of income (2022, 2021, 2020) highlights:
  - Total net revenue: $128.7B (2022), $121.6B (2021), $120.0B (2020); net interest income rose to $66.7B in 2022; noninterest revenue $62.0B.
  - Provision for credit losses: $6.4B expense (2022) vs $(9.3)B benefit (2021) vs $17.5B expense (2020).
  - Total noninterest expense: $76.1B (2022), including compensation, occupancy, technology, professional services, marketing, and other costs.
  - Net income: $37.7B (2022), $48.3B (2021), $29.1B (2020); diluted EPS: $12.09 (2022), $15.36 (2021), $8.88 (2020).

nodes.title: Consolidated statements of income
nodes.heading: 8.3 Consolidated statements of income
nodes.start_phrase: The Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements are an integral part of these statements.
nodes.summary:
- Presents JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Consolidated Statements of Income and Comprehensive Income for the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020 (in millions, except per share data), from the 2022 Form 10-K.
- Income statement highlights:
  - Detailed breakdown of noninterest revenue: investment banking fees (notably lower in 2022 vs. 2021), principal transactions, lending- and deposit-related fees, asset management/administration/commissions, investment securities gains/losses (loss in 2022), mortgage fees (declined), card income (declined), and other income.
  - Interest income and interest expense, with net interest income rising in 2022; total net revenue increased to $128.7B in 2022 (from $121.6B in 2021).
  - Provision for credit losses: expense of $6.4B in 2022 vs. a $9.3B release in 2021 and a $17.5B build in 2020.
  - Noninterest expense categories and totals: compensation, occupancy, technology/communications/equipment, professional/outsourced services, marketing, and other; total noninterest expense increased to $76.1B in 2022.
  - Income before tax, income tax expense, and net income: net income of $37.7B in 2022 (down from $48.3B in 2021; $29.1B in 2020).
  - Net income applicable to common stockholders, and EPS: basic $12.10 and diluted $12.09 in 2022; weighted-average basic and diluted shares declined year over year.
- Comprehensive income statement highlights:
  - Other comprehensive income (OCI) components after tax: unrealized gains/losses on investment securities (large losses in 2022), translation adjustments (losses), fair value hedges, cash flow hedges (losses), defined benefit pension/OPEB plan adjustments, and DVA on fair value option liabilities (gain).

nodes.title: Note 1 – Basis of presentation
nodes.heading: 8.8 Note 1 – Basis of presentation
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“ JPMorgan Chase ” or the “Firm”), a financial holding company incorporated under Delaware law in 1968, is a leading financial services firm based in the U.S., with operations worldwide.
nodes.summary:
- Describes JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s basis of presentation, noting it follows U.S. GAAP and applicable regulatory guidelines, with certain prior-period amounts revised to conform to current presentation.
- Outlines consolidation policies:
  - Consolidates entities where the Firm has a controlling financial interest; eliminates intercompany balances/transactions.
  - Assets held in agency/fiduciary capacity are excluded from the balance sheet.
  - Voting interest entities: consolidation based on majority voting rights or contractual control; significant influence investments accounted for via equity method or fair value option; many Firm-sponsored funds not consolidated due to substantive kick-out/participating rights; if such rights are not substantive, evaluated as VIEs and consolidated when the Firm has power and a potentially significant interest.
  - Investment companies/asset management funds measured at fair value under specialized guidance, regardless of ownership percentage.
- Details variable interest entities (VIEs):
  - Defines VIEs and common use in securitizations via SPEs.
  - Consolidation required for the primary beneficiary—party with both power over significant activities and exposure to potentially significant benefits/losses.
  - Explains assessment of power and economic exposure, and ongoing reassessments that can change consolidation conclusions.
- Summarizes revenue recognition:
  - Interest income recognized on a level-yield basis.
  - Noninterest revenue from contracts with customers recognized upon satisfaction of performance obligations (e.g., investment banking, deposit-related, asset management, certain card fees).
  - Principal transactions revenue reflects changes in fair value of certain assets and liabilities.
- Notes use of estimates affecting reported amounts and disclosures.
- Explains foreign currency translation:
  - Functional currency translation gains/losses in OCI; nonfunctional currency transaction gains/losses in income.
- Describes offsetting/netting:
  - Net presentation of derivatives and certain securities financing transactions when legally enforceable master netting agreements exist; outlines collateral/margin mechanics and rights upon default.
- Defines “cash” for the statement of cash flows as cash and due from banks plus deposits with banks.
- Highlights recently adopted accounting standards:
  - 2023 TDR guidance: eliminates TDR accounting/disclosure requirements; permits non-DCF portfolio-based allowance for modified loans; Firm elected non-DCF approach except for modified nonaccrual risk-rated loans (DCF retained). Adoption reduced the allowance by ~$600 million and increased retained earnings by ~$450 million after tax, mainly in residential real estate and credit card.
  - 2020 CECL adoption: established life-of-instrument expected credit loss model incorporating macroeconomic expectations, replacing the prior incurred-loss framework.
- Provides a roadmap to other significant accounting policies with references to related notes (e.g., fair value, derivatives, noninterest revenue/expense, loans, allowance for credit losses, VIEs, leases, debt, EPS, taxes, off-balance sheet commitments, and litigation).

nodes.title: Note 2 – Fair value measurement
nodes.heading: 8.9 Note 2 – Fair value measurement
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase carries a portion of its assets and liabilities at fair value.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Explains JPMorgan Chase’s use of fair value for a portion of assets, liabilities, and certain unfunded lending-related commitments—both on a recurring basis (reported each period) and on a nonrecurring basis (only when specific events like impairment occur).
- Definition: Fair value is the exit price in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date.
- Valuation approaches: Uses quoted market prices when available; otherwise applies valuation models and techniques that incorporate transaction characteristics and market inputs (observable and unobservable), such as yield curves, interest rates, volatilities, prices, correlations, FX rates, and credit curves.
- Valuation adjustments: May be applied to ensure instruments are recorded at fair value; precision of unobservable inputs can affect reported gains/losses. Different methodologies or assumptions could yield different fair values across firms.
- Governance and responsibilities: Risk-taking functions produce fair value estimates; the independent Valuation Control Group (VCG) verifies estimates and determines needed adjustments; the Valuation Governance Forum (VGF), comprising senior finance and risk leaders and chaired by the head of VCG, oversees valuation risk across business lines (CIB, CCB, CB, AWM, Treasury, CIO).
- Price verification by VCG: Relies on independently derived prices, inputs, and market data. When unavailable, performs additional procedures (e.g., analyzing limited market activity, benchmarking inputs, decomposing structured products, comparing expected vs. actual cash flows, reviewing P&L and collateral trends). Significant/complex positions receive heightened management review.
- Adjustment policy: No adjustments to quoted prices for Level 1 instruments. For other positions, judgment is applied to reflect liquidity, unobservable parameters, and—in qualifying portfolios managed on a net open risk basis—the size of the position relative to normal market size.
- Liquidity valuation adjustments: Consider current market conditions, estimated bid-ask spreads, alternative pricing for similar actively traded instruments, and the range of reasonable values for prices/parameters.
- Net open risk/market-size adjustments: For portfolios valued as a transfer of the entire net risk (as permitted under U.S. GAAP), adjustments reflect the expected cost to exit a larger-than-normal position, considering the probable adverse market move over the time needed to reduce to normal market size.

nodes.title: Valuation process
nodes.heading: 8.9.1 Valuation process
nodes.start_phrase: Risk-taking functions are responsible for providing fair value estimates for assets and liabilities carried on the Consolidated balance sheets at fair value.
nodes.summary:
The note explains JPMorgan Chase’s approach to fair value measurement for certain assets, liabilities, and some unfunded lending-related commitments, distinguishing between recurring (reported each period) and nonrecurring (only upon certain events, such as impairment) measurements. Fair value is defined as the exit price in an orderly transaction at the measurement date, determined using quoted market prices when available, or valuation models incorporating observable and unobservable inputs (e.g., yield curves, rates, volatilities, prices, correlations, FX, credit curves), with valuation adjustments made as needed. The Firm highlights the role of management judgment, the potential variability across businesses, and that different market participant assumptions could yield different fair values.

Governance and controls include: risk-taking units providing initial estimates; the independent Valuation Control Group (VCG) verifying prices, inputs, and market data, and setting necessary adjustments; and the Valuation Governance Forum (VGF) overseeing valuation risk across business lines and certain corporate functions.

Price verification involves independent data where possible; otherwise, additional reviews (e.g., benchmarking, component analysis, cash flow comparisons, P&L and collateral trends) and heightened management review for complex positions. No adjustments are made to Level 1 quoted prices; for others, the VCG may apply adjustments for liquidity, unobservable parameters, and portfolio-level net open risk exposure (consistent with U.S. GAAP), reflecting costs and potential adverse market moves required to reduce positions to normal market size.

nodes.title: Price verification process
nodes.heading: 8.9.2 Price verification process
nodes.start_phrase: The VCG verifies fair value estimates provided by the risk-taking functions by leveraging independently derived prices, valuation inputs and other market data, where available.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and basis: JPMorgan Chase measures portions of its assets, liabilities, and certain unfunded lending commitments at fair value, primarily on a recurring basis; some are measured on a nonrecurring basis when certain events (e.g., impairment) occur.
- Fair value definition and methods: Fair value is the exit price in an orderly transaction at the measurement date. When quotes are unavailable, valuation models and techniques are used with observable and/or unobservable inputs (e.g., yield curves, interest rates, volatilities, prices, correlations, FX rates, credit curves). Valuation adjustments may be applied.
- Judgment and uncertainty: Estimation precision for unobservable inputs can affect gains/losses; methods reflect management judgment and may differ across businesses, and different market participant assumptions could yield different fair values.
- Governance and responsibilities: Risk-taking functions propose fair values; the independent Valuation Control Group (VCG) verifies estimates and sets needed adjustments; the Valuation Governance Forum (VGF), comprising senior finance and risk leaders with firmwide and line-of-business sub-forums, oversees valuation risk management.
- Price verification: VCG validates prices/inputs using independent data where available; when not, it performs additional analyses (e.g., review limited market activity and client unwinds, benchmark inputs, decompose structured trades, compare expected vs. actual cash flows, review P&L and collateral trends), with heightened management review for complex or significant positions.
- Valuation adjustments framework:
  - No adjustments to quoted Level 1 prices.
  - Liquidity adjustments based on market conditions (e.g., bid-ask spreads, alternative pricing points, reasonable value ranges).
  - Adjustments for the cost to exit larger-than-normal net open risk positions when portfolios are managed and valued on a net exposure basis.
  - Uncertainty adjustments for unobservable inputs due to limited market activity.
  - Credit and funding adjustments: CVA (counterparty credit), DVA (own credit), and FVA (funding), applied consistently across the firm.
- Model usage and control: When market prices/quotes are unavailable, models are used with independently sourced inputs and subject to the same verification. Model Risk Governance & Review (MRGR) reviews/approves new and materially changed models under policy; exceptions may allow interim use with mitigants (e.g., trading limits).
- Fair value hierarchy: Disclosures follow a three-level hierarchy:
  - Level 1: unadjusted quoted prices for identical items in active markets.
  - Level 2: observable inputs, including quotes for similar items, for substantially the full instrument term.
  - Level 3: significant unobservable inputs.
  Classification is based on the lowest-level significant input.

nodes.title: Valuation model review and approval
nodes.heading: 8.9.3 Valuation model review and approval
nodes.start_phrase: If prices or quotes are not available for an instrument or a similar instrument, fair value is generally determined using valuation models that consider relevant transaction terms such as maturity and use as inputs market-based or independently sourced parameters.
nodes.summary:
- Explains uncertainty adjustments applied when valuing positions using unobservable prices or inputs due to limited market activity, emphasizing management judgment and the need to reflect valuation uncertainty.
- Describes firmwide application of credit and funding valuation adjustments—CVA (counterparty credit), DVA (own credit), and FVA (funding)—within a consistent framework, with a cross-reference for more detail.
- Outlines use of valuation models when market prices or quotes are unavailable, including independent price verification of model inputs.
- Details model risk governance under the Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy: MRGR reviews and approves new models and material changes before use, may grant exceptions, and can require interim risk mitigations (e.g., trading limits).
- Defines the U.S. GAAP fair value hierarchy:
  - Level 1: unadjusted quoted prices for identical items in active markets.
  - Level 2: observable inputs, including quotes for similar items and other market-based inputs.
  - Level 3: significant unobservable inputs.
- States that instruments are classified based on the lowest-level significant input to the valuation.

nodes.title: Fair value hierarchy
nodes.heading: 8.9.4 Fair value hierarchy
nodes.start_phrase: A three-level fair value hierarchy has been established under U.S. GAAP for disclosure of fair value measurements.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the need for valuation uncertainty adjustments when fair values rely on unobservable inputs due to illiquid markets or lack of inferable market data; highlights management judgment and explicit add-ons to reflect estimation risk.
- Describes firmwide application of credit and funding valuation adjustments—CVA (counterparty), DVA (own credit), and FVA (funding)—within a consistent framework, with a cross‑reference for further detail.
- Outlines the approach when quoted prices are unavailable: use of valuation models incorporating relevant terms and independently sourced or market‑based inputs, with price verification applied to model inputs.
- Summarizes model governance under the Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy: MRGR review/approval of new models and material changes before production, allowance for limited exceptions, and required interim risk mitigants (e.g., trading limits) when models are used prior to full approval.
- Defines the U.S. GAAP fair value hierarchy:
  - Level 1: unadjusted quoted prices for identical instruments in active markets.
  - Level 2: observable inputs (including quotes for similar items) for most of the instrument’s term.
  - Level 3: significant unobservable inputs.
  - Classification is based on the lowest level input significant to the valuation.
- Provides product‑specific valuation methodologies and typical hierarchy classifications, including:
  - Securities financing agreements: discounted cash flows (DCF); predominantly Level 2.
  - Wholesale loans and related commitments: observable prices/quotes where available; otherwise DCF using CDS‑derived or benchmark credit curves, prepayments, collateral; Level 2 or 3.
  - Consumer loans: based on prices of similar MBS with adjustments; predominantly Level 2.
  - Investment and trading securities: Level 1 when quoted; otherwise Level 2/3 using comparable prices, broker quotes, or DCF with product‑specific inputs (e.g., collateral, prepayment/default/loss assumptions, spreads, ratings).
  - Physical commodities: observable market data; Level 1 or 2.
  - Derivatives: exchange‑traded at Level 1; OTC valued via option/simulation models with observable and/or unobservable inputs (e.g., prices, volatilities, correlations, credit and recovery, prepayments); Level 2 or 3; includes CVA/FVA.
  - Mortgage servicing rights: Level 3.
  - Private equity direct investments: based on transaction prices, comparables/multiples, operating performance, and liquidity/other adjustments; Level 2 or 3.
  - Fund investments: measured at NAV; Level 1 if freely redeemable at NAV; Level 2/3 with redemption restrictions or limited observable activity; some NAV‑practical‑expedient positions excluded from hierarchy tables.
  - Beneficial interests in consolidated VIEs: Level 2 or 3, tied to observable data or underlying asset fair values.
  - Structured notes (in deposits/borrowings/debt): DCF incorporating embedded derivative models and DVA; Level 2 or 3.
- Presents detailed tables of assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, disaggregated by major product category and hierarchy level, including derivative netting adjustments.
- Notes key disclosures/footnotes: treatment of GSE obligations, physical commodities inventories measured effectively at (or approximating) fair value via net realizable value and hedge accounting, NAV‑practical‑expedient investments excluded from hierarchy classification, composition details for loans at fair value, and effects of legally enforceable netting and cash collateral on reported derivative balances (including implications for Level 3).

nodes.title: Level 3 valuations
nodes.heading: 8.9.5 Level 3 valuations
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm has established well-structured processes for determining fair value, including for instruments where fair value is estimated using significant unobservable inputs (level 3).
nodes.summary:
- Describes the firm’s structured fair value determination processes, with emphasis on Level 3 instruments that rely on significant unobservable inputs; references additional detail elsewhere in the note.
- Explains that estimating fair value involves management judgment that increases as market observability decreases; Level 3 requires more judgment than Levels 1 and 2.
- Outlines the two-step approach for Level 3: select an appropriate valuation model/technique, then derive inputs from empirical data (e.g., transaction details, yield curves, interest rates, prepayment speeds, default rates, volatilities, correlations, commodity/equity/debt prices, comparable valuations, FX rates, credit curves).
- Presents a table (as of December 31, 2022) of primary Level 3 instruments, their valuation techniques (discounted cash flows, market comparables, option pricing), significant unobservable inputs, and input ranges/averages.
- Notes that Level 3 instruments often include observable components; Level 1/2 inputs are excluded from the table; observable components are risk-managed using Level 1 or 2 securities/derivatives.
- Clarifies that input ranges show highest/lowest values used across instrument groups and averages are fair value-weighted (arithmetic for derivatives); these do not indicate uncertainty or reasonableness, and vary over time with the mix and characteristics of positions (illustrated with option-implied volatility differences).
- Highlights major Level 3 balances and key inputs/techniques:
  - MSRs: $7.97B, discounted cash flows (see Note 15).
  - Long-term debt, short-term borrowings, and deposits (incl. structured notes): $26.58B via option pricing (rate/FX/equity volatilities and correlations, Bermudan features) and $1.07B via discounted cash flows (credit correlation).
  - RMBS and loans: $1.65B, discounted cash flows with yield, prepayment speed, conditional default rate, loss severity.
  - CMBS and loans: $423M, market comparables (price).
  - Corporate debt: $702M, market comparables (price).
  - Loans: $876M, market comparables (price).
  - Non-U.S. government debt: $155M, market comparables (price).
  - Net interest rate derivatives: $735M (option pricing; rate and spread volatilities, Bermudan switch, rate and IR-FX correlations) and -$34M (DCF; prepayment speed).
  - Net credit derivatives: -$9M (DCF; credit correlation, credit spread, recovery rate) and $22M (market comparables; price).
  - Net foreign exchange derivatives: $577M (option pricing; IR-FX correlation) and -$88M (DCF; prepayment speed, interest rate curve).
  - Net equity derivatives: -$384M (option pricing; forward equity price, equity volatility, equity/FX/IR correlations).
  - Net commodity derivatives: -$146M (option pricing; oil and natural gas forwards, commodity volatility and correlation).
  - Other Level 3 assets/liabilities, net: $1.03B.
- Provides footnote context: product categories are aggregated; not all inputs apply to every instrument; RMBS/CMBS/loans split between trading and non-trading and agency/nonagency; structured notes include embedded derivatives and share inputs with derivative receivables; “other Level 3” includes $880M of equity securities valued using internal techniques (e.g., EBITDA multiples, comparables); price inputs assume $100 par; forward equity price stated as a percent of current; averages are fair value-weighted except derivative inputs use arithmetic averages.

nodes.title: Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.heading: 8.9.6 Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.start_phrase: The following discussion provides a description of the impact on a fair value measurement of a change in each unobservable input in isolation, and the interrelationship between unobservable inputs, where relevant and significant.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Explains how changes in key unobservable inputs affect fair value measurements, including interrelationships among inputs and factors driving the range of inputs used.
- Interdependencies: Notes that inputs can be interrelated (and that inverse relationships generally apply); observable–unobservable relationships exist but are not detailed here.
- Drivers of input ranges: Attributes of underlying instruments and external market conditions shape input ranges. For MBS, key drivers include tranche subordination, borrower FICO, LTV, property/tenant characteristics; for corporate/municipal debt, credit quality of the obligor and tenor.
- Yield: Discount rate for DCF; higher yield decreases fair value. Yield reflects both risk and coupon level.
- Credit spread: Incremental return for credit risk; higher spread decreases fair value; reflects obligor credit quality and tenor.
- Prepayment speed: Unscheduled principal repayments; typically decline as delinquencies rise. Higher speeds decrease fair value for premium assets and increase it for discount assets. Varies by borrower type/location, tenor, and rate type; higher-quality borrowers typically prepay more.
- Conditional default rate (CDR): Rate of collateral defaults; often inversely related to high prepayment pools; increases in CDR usually coincide with higher loss severity and credit spreads, and decrease fair value. Firm’s market-making portfolios typically exhibit lower CDRs.
- Loss severity (inverse of recovery rate): Expected loss upon liquidation; higher severity decreases fair value. Influenced by LTV, lien position, and instrument specifics.
- Correlation: Relationship between risk factors; effect on fair value depends on position and asset class. For a short correlation position, higher correlation decreases fair value. Levels depend on risk type, tenor, and market conditions, and can vary widely.
- Volatility: Variability of returns; key for options. For long options, higher volatility increases fair value. Depends on underlying risk, tenor, and strike.
- Bermudan switch value: Incremental value of multiple exercise dates versus the richest European swaption; higher switch value increases fair value. Sensitive to market conditions, swap tenor, and strike.
- Interest rate curve: Relationship of rates across tenors; used to set and discount derivative cash flows.
- Forward price: Contracted future price with zero initial value; depends on interest rates, spot price, income/carry costs. An increase can raise or lower fair value depending on position.
- Level 3 rollforward: Describes rollforward of Level 3 fair value measurements for 2020–2022. Classification is based on the significance of unobservable inputs, though Level 3 instruments also include observable components.
- Gains/losses context: Reported changes in Level 3 fair values include effects from observable inputs. Risk management hedges using Level 1/2 instruments are excluded, so reported gains/losses do not reflect those hedging effects.

nodes.title: Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.heading: 8.9.7 Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables include a rollforward of the Consolidated balance sheets amounts (including changes in fair value) for financial instruments classified by the Firm within level 3 of the fair value hierarchy for the years ended D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2022 , 2021 and 2020 .
nodes.summary:
- Explains key valuation inputs used in fair value measurements of derivatives and other instruments:
  - Correlation: definition; positive vs. negative relationships; dependence on risk type, tenor, and market conditions; effect on fair value varies by position (e.g., short correlation generally declines when correlation rises).
  - Volatility: definition as variability of returns; central to option pricing across asset classes; dependence on underlying, tenor, and strike; higher volatility generally increases option values for long positions.
  - Bermudan switch value: incremental value of multiple exercise dates versus the richest European swaption; driven by market conditions, tenor, and strike; increases generally raise fair value.
  - Interest rate curve: relationship of rates across tenors; used to set and discount derivative cash flows.
  - Forward price: contract price setting zero value at inception; driven by interest rates, spot price, expected income/carry costs; increases can raise or lower fair value depending on position.

- Provides comprehensive Level 3 fair value disclosures (significant unobservable inputs):
  - Rollforwards for 2022, 2021, and 2020 covering assets and liabilities: beginning balances, realized/unrealized gains/losses, purchases, sales, issuances, settlements, and transfers between levels.
  - Asset categories include trading assets (various MBS, government/non-U.S. debt, corporate debt, loans, ABS, equities, physical commodities, other), net derivative receivables by asset class (interest rate, credit, FX, equity, commodity), AFS securities, loans, mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), and other assets.
  - Liability categories include deposits, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities, accounts payable and other liabilities, and long-term debt.
  - Clarifies Level 3 classification is based on significance of unobservable inputs, though instruments may also contain observable components; gains/losses may reflect both observable and unobservable factors.
  - Notes that hedging/risk-management positions in Level 1/2 are excluded from the Level 3 tables, so reported gains/losses do not show hedge effects.
  - Indicates where changes are reported in the income statement or OCI (e.g., principal transactions revenue, mortgage fees and related income, DVA in OCI for fair value option liabilities, AFS in OCI).

- Summarizes Level 3 proportions of total fair value: Level 3 assets were about 2% (2022 and 2021) and 1% (2020) of total assets at fair value; Level 3 liabilities were about 8% (2022), 10% (2021), and 9% (2020).

- Provides 2022 Level 3 analysis:

  - Details significant transfers between Level 2 and Level 3 driven primarily by changes in market observability and the significance of unobservable inputs:

nodes.title: Credit and funding adjustments – derivatives
nodes.heading: 8.9.11 Credit and funding adjustments – derivatives
nodes.start_phrase: Derivatives are generally valued using models that use as their basis observable market parameters.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt explains how the firm adjusts derivative fair values for credit and funding effects that are not captured by base market parameters. It details:
- Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA): an adjustment for counterparty nonperformance risk, estimated via scenario analysis of expected positive exposure by counterparty, using inputs such as counterparty default probabilities (from observed/estimated CDS spreads), recovery rates (implied by CDS and adjusted for derivative creditor status), and contractual mitigants (collateral, netting).
- Funding Valuation Adjustment (FVA): an adjustment for funding impacts that market participants would include in the principal market. For uncollateralized or partially collateralized OTC derivatives, FVA reflects expected funding needs given positions and collateral terms, and market funding costs, including own-credit effects for derivative liabilities (DVA). For collateralized derivatives discounted at the relevant OIS rate per the collateral agreement, no separate FVA is needed.
- Reported impacts on principal transactions revenue (excluding hedges): a table shows derivatives CVA and FVA effects for 2022, 2021, and 2020; FVA includes both inception effects of the firm’s own credit quality on liabilities and subsequent changes. (2022: CVA $22mm, FVA $42mm; 2021: CVA $362mm, FVA $47mm; 2020: CVA $(337)mm, FVA $(64)mm.)
- Valuation of liabilities with the fair value option: Debit Valuation Adjustment (DVA) reflects changes after issuance in the firm’s probability of default and loss given default, derived from bond market credit spreads. Realized DVA gains/losses are recorded in principal transactions revenue; unrealized DVA gains/losses are recorded in OCI. References to related disclosures are provided.

nodes.title: Valuation adjustments on fair value option elected liabilities
nodes.heading: 8.9.12 Valuation adjustments on fair value option elected liabilities
nodes.start_phrase: The valuation of the Firm’s liabilities for which the fair value option has been elected requires consideration of the Firm’s own credit risk.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Explains why and how JPMorgan Chase adjusts model-based fair values of derivatives and certain liabilities to reflect counterparty credit risk, the Firm’s own credit risk, and funding costs that base market parameters do not capture.
- CVA (Credit Valuation Adjustment): Adjustment to reflect counterparty nonperformance risk. Estimated via scenario analysis of expected positive exposure by counterparty, incorporating collateral and netting; losses derived from counterparty default probabilities (from observed/estimated CDS spreads) and recovery rates adjusted for derivative creditor status.
- FVA (Funding Valuation Adjustment): Adjustment to reflect the cost/benefit of funding uncollateralized (including partially collateralized) OTC derivatives where a market participant would include it. Key inputs are expected funding needs by counterparty/collateral terms and market funding costs; for derivative liabilities, incorporates the Firm’s own credit risk (DVA). For collateralized derivatives, discounting at OIS per collateral terms generally eliminates the need for a separate FVA.
- Revenue impacts: Provides the impact of CVA and FVA on principal transactions revenue for 2020–2022, excluding hedging. FVA includes the effect of the Firm’s own credit quality both at inception of liabilities and from subsequent changes.
- Fair value option liabilities (DVA): For liabilities with the fair value option, valuation includes the Firm’s own credit risk. DVA reflects changes after issuance in the Firm’s default probability and loss given default based on bond-market credit spreads. Realized DVA gains/losses are recognized in principal transactions revenue; unrealized amounts are recorded in OCI.

- Describes the Firm’s accounting for equity securities without readily determinable fair values under the ASC 321 measurement alternative: carried at cost minus impairment plus/minus observable price changes in identical or similar securities of the same issuer, with gains/losses recognized in other income.

- Presents carrying values and changes:

- Details Visa Class B common shares:

  - November 2022 sale of ~3 million Visa B shares produced a net pretax gain of $914 million (other income).

  - Visa reported a conversion rate decrease from 1.6059 to 1.5991 effective Dec 29, 2022; further adjustments may occur depending on litigation; significant uncertainty remains regarding timing of transfer restriction termination and final conversion rate, so Visa B shares continue at nominal value.
- Summarizes U.S. GAAP requirements to disclose estimated fair values for certain financial instruments not carried at fair value, noting exclusions (e.g., nonfinancial and certain intangible items).
- Identifies instruments whose carrying amounts approximate fair value due to short-term nature and low credit risk, including: cash and due from banks; deposits with banks; federal funds sold; securities purchased under resale agreements and securities borrowed; short-term receivables and accrued interest receivable; short-term borrowings; federal funds purchased; securities loaned and sold under repurchase agreements; and accounts payable.
