- Lending- and deposit-related fees:
  - Defines lending-related fees (loan commitments, standby letters of credit, financial guarantees, servicing) and deposit-related fees (overdraft, deposit account services, cash management).

- Asset management, administration and commissions:

  - Outlines components: production revenue from loans intended for sale (including gains/losses on sale, lower of cost or fair value adjustments, fair value option impacts, and pipeline/warehouse risk management), and net mortgage servicing revenue (servicing income recognized over service period, changes in MSR fair value, and associated risk management).
  - Section is partially shown and concludes mid-discussion of risk management activities.

nodes.title: Asset management, administration and commissions
nodes.heading: 8.13.1.4 Asset management, administration and commissions
nodes.start_phrase:
This revenue category includes fees from investment 
management and related services, custody, brokerage 
services and other products.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Revenue disclosures for JPMorgan Chase covering principal transactions and major fee-based revenues, with 2022, 2021, and 2020 comparative figures, related accounting/recognition policies, and segment attribution.

- Principal transactions and trading revenue:
  - Detailed trading revenue by instrument type: interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, and commodity.
  - 2022 totals: total trading revenue $19,957 million; private equity losses $(45) million; principal transactions revenue $19,912 million (vs. $16,304 million in 2021 and $18,021 million in 2020).
  - Footnotes explain impacts from funding valuation adjustments (FVA) on derivatives, credit valuation adjustments (CVA) net of hedges, and 2021 net markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (primarily unfunded commitments).
  - Principal transactions revenue is earned primarily by CIB; Note 32 provides segment results.

- Lending- and deposit-related fees:
  - Definitions: lending-related fees from loan commitments, standby letters of credit, financial guarantees, and servicing; deposit-related fees from overdraft and deposit account services and cash management.
  - Revenue is recognized over the period services are provided.
  - 2022 totals: lending-related fees $1,468 million; deposit-related fees $5,630 million; combined $7,098 million (vs. $7,032 million in 2021 and $6,511 million in 2020).
  - Earned by CCB, CIB, CB, and AWM; Note 32 for segment results.

- Asset management, administration and commissions:
  - Includes investment management and related services, custody, brokerage, and other products.
  - Management fees are typically AUM-based and recognized over the service period; performance fees recognized when the probability of reversal is remote (typically at period end).
  - The Firm uses third parties for distribution/other services; related amounts are recorded in professional and outside services expense.
  - 2022 totals: asset management fees $14,096 million (investment management $13,765; other asset management fees $331); administration fees $2,348 million; commissions and other fees $4,233 million (brokerage commissions $2,831; all other $1,402); combined $20,677 million (vs. $21,029 million in 2021 and $18,177 million in 2020).
  - Footnotes clarify timing and nature of revenues: ancillary distribution fees (point-in-time or over time), custody/securities lending/fund services (over time), brokerage commissions (at trade execution, net of certain third-party costs), and other service fees (when rendered).
  - Earned primarily by AWM, CIB, and CCB; Note 32 for segment results.

- Mortgage fees and related income (CCB):
  - Covers Home Lending production and net mortgage servicing revenue.
  - Production revenue includes fees on loans originated for sale, results of risk management on the mortgage pipeline and warehouse, gains/losses on loan sales, lower-of-cost-or-fair-value adjustments on held-for-sale loans (with noted exclusions), and changes in fair value for instruments under the fair value option.
  - Net mortgage servicing revenue includes servicing fees on third-party loans (recognized over the service period), changes in the fair value of MSRs, and related risk management impacts.
  - Section is truncated after introducing risk management related to MSRs.

nodes.title: Mortgage fees and related income
nodes.heading: 8.13.1.5 Mortgage fees and related income
nodes.start_phrase:
This revenue category reflects CCB’s Home Lending 
production and net mortgage servicing revenue.
nodes.summary:
- Presents JPMorgan Chase’s revenue composition and related accounting policies for 2022, 2021, and 2020, with segment references.
- Principal transactions (primarily CIB): Trading revenue by instrument type—interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, and commodity—totaling $19.96B in 2022 ($16.33B in 2021; $17.84B in 2020); includes notes on funding and credit valuation adjustments (FVA/CVA) and 2021 bridge financing markdowns; private equity gains/losses included; total principal transactions revenue $19.91B in 2022.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees (earned by CCB, CIB, CB, AWM): Definitions and over-time recognition; 2022 totals $7.10B (lending $1.47B; deposit $5.63B).
- Asset management, administration and commissions (primarily AWM, CIB, CCB): Fee types and recognition (AUM-based, performance fees, custody, brokerage); treatment of third-party distribution costs; 2022 totals $20.68B (asset management fees $14.10B, administration $2.35B, commissions $4.23B) with explanatory footnotes on what each line represents.
- Mortgage fees and related income (CCB Home Lending): Components and recognition for production and net mortgage servicing revenue, including MSR fair value changes and related risk management; references to relevant notes.
- Card income (primarily CCB, CIB, CB): Interchange and merchant processing, deferral of origination/annual fees, rewards program liability and costs; co-brand partner arrangements (terms, payment types, and accounting: marketing expense, reductions of card income, and deferrals); 2022 net card income $4.42B (interchange/processing $28.09B; rewards/partner payments $(22.16)B; other card income $(1.50)B).
- Other income: Operating lease income, losses on tax-oriented investments (offset by tax credits), and gain on sale of Visa B shares; 2022 includes $3.65B operating lease income, $(1.49)B losses on tax-oriented investments, and $914M Visa B share gain; references to notes.
- Noninterest expense—Other expense: Legal expense disclosed ($266M in 2022; $426M in 2021; $1.12B in 2020).

nodes.title: Card income
nodes.heading: 8.13.1.6 Card income
nodes.start_phrase:
This revenue category includes interchange and other 
income from credit and debit card transactions; and fees 
earned from processing card transactions for merchants, 
both of which are recognized when purchases are made by 
a cardholder and presented net of certain transaction-
related costs.
nodes.summary:
- Mortgage servicing: Describes components of net mortgage servicing revenue, including servicing fees, changes in fair value of MSRs and related risk management results, gains/losses on securitizations of excess servicing, and gains/losses or lower of cost or fair value adjustments on certain repurchased U.S. government–insured loans. Notes that net interest income from mortgage loans is recorded in interest income. References Note 15 for MSRs and risk management.

- Card income: Defines revenue sources (interchange and merchant processing income; deferred account origination costs and annual fees recognized over 12 months). Explains proprietary rewards programs, related liability, and recognition of reward costs as a reduction of card income. Details co-brand revenue-sharing agreements (exclusive issuing/marketing rights, typical 5–10 year terms) and accounting for partner payments:
  - Partner marketing costs expensed as marketing.
  - Partner loyalty rewards reduce card income when incurred.
  - New account origination payments deferred and amortized as a reduction of card income over 12 months.
  - Sales volume–based payments reduce card income when related interchange is earned.
  Presents card income components (in millions): Interchange and merchant processing income $28,085/$23,592/$18,563; Reward costs and partner payments $(22,162)/$(17,868)/$(13,637); Other card income $(1,503)/$(622)/$(491); Total card income $4,420/$5,102/$4,435 for 2022/2021/2020. Notes “other card income” is predominantly amortization of origination costs and annual fees. Indicates card income is earned primarily by CCB, CIB, and CB; references Note 32.

- Other income: Includes operating lease income and losses on tax-oriented investments (mainly alternative energy equity-method investments in CIB), with tax losses more than offset by related tax credits. Reports (in millions) for 2022/2021/2020: Operating lease income $3,654/$4,914/$5,539; Losses on tax-oriented investments $(1,491)/$(1,570)/$(1,280); Gain on sale of Visa B shares $914/$0/$0. References Notes 2 (Visa B shares) and 18 (operating leases).

- Noninterest expense – Other expense: Presents legal expense (in millions) $266/$426/$1,115 for 2022/2021/2020, as part of the Consolidated statements of income.

The Firm has contractual agreements with numerous co-
brand partners that grant the Firm exclusive rights to issue

nodes.summary:

  - Notes “other card income” mainly reflects amortization of deferred account origination costs and annual fees.
  - Card income earned primarily by CCB, CIB, and CB; references Note 32 for segment results.
- Summarizes other income: operating lease income; losses on tax-oriented (predominantly alternative energy, equity-method) investments that are more than offset by tax credits; and gain on sale of Visa B shares. Selected amounts (in millions):
  - 2022: Operating lease income $3,654; losses on tax-oriented investments $(1,491); gain on sale of Visa B shares $914.
  - 2021: $4,914; $(1,570); —.
  - 2020: $5,539; $(1,280); —.
  - References Notes 2 (Visa B shares) and 18 (operating leases).
- Notes noninterest expense—other expense includes legal expense: $266 million (2022), $426 million (2021), $1,115 million (2020).
- Extract is from JPMorgan Chase & Co. 2022 Form 10-K, Notes to consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Other income

nodes.title: Note 8 – Pension and other postretirement employee benefit plans

nodes.title: Gains and losses

nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s employee benefit plans: multiple defined benefit pension and OPEB plans in the U.S. and certain non-U.S. locations, with substantially all defined benefit plans closed to new participants; the principal U.S. plan is frozen for existing participants (effective Jan 1, 2020) with ongoing interest credits on accumulated balances.
- Postretirement medical and life insurance (funded and unfunded) for eligible employees/retirees and dependents; these OPEB plans are not material to the Firm’s Consolidated Financial Statements.
- Defined contribution arrangements, chiefly the JPMorgan Chase 401(k) Savings Plan covering most U.S. employees, allowing pretax and Roth contributions; the Firm provides annual matching and profit-sharing contributions.
- Key balances (Dec 31): projected benefit obligations, fair value of plan assets, net funded status, and AOCI for significant pension and OPEB plans; 2022 vs 2021 show lower PBO ($13.5B vs $18.0B), lower plan assets ($19.9B vs $25.7B), positive net funded status ($6.3B vs $7.6B), and higher AOCI loss; discount rate increased to 5.14% in 2022 from 2.54% in 2021.
- Accounting for gains/losses: changes in obligations and assets recorded in OCI; amortization applies when net gains/losses exceed the 10% corridor, generally over the average remaining lifetime of participants due to frozen plan status.
- 2022 remeasurement due to a U.S. pension settlement: decreased plan assets by $4.0B and PBO by $2.6B, resulting in a $1.4B pre-tax decrease in AOCI; 2021 gains primarily reflected market-driven asset increases and discount rate effects.
- Expense and OCI impacts: net periodic defined benefit cost/(credit) was a credit in 2020–2022; defined contribution expense was roughly $1.3–$1.4B annually; total pension/OPEB cost in noninterest expense rose modestly; OCI recognized a significant loss in 2022 and gains in 2021; pension settlement losses were $92M (2022) and $33M (2021).
- Actuarial assumptions: discount rate and expected long-term return on assets disclosed for 2020–2022; expected returns derived using forward-looking, asset-mix-weighted estimates; discount rates set with reference to bond yield curves matched to plan cash flows.
- Investment strategy: diversified portfolios across debt, equity, real estate, and alternatives; target ranges for the principal plan are 42–100% debt, 0–40% equity, 0–3% real estate, 0–12% alternatives, with ongoing review and rebalancing.
- Investment holdings: no direct JPMorgan-issued securities held (only indirect via third-party funds); affiliate-sponsored/managed investments totaled $1.7B (2022) and $2.5B (2021).
- Fair value measurement: plan assets categorized by levels (1–3) and NAV practical expedient, with 2022/2021 totals provided; composition notes include equities and government debt (Level 1), corporate and government debt (Level 2), and COLI/participating annuities (Level 3).

nodes.title: Note 9 – Employee share-based incentives
nodes.heading: 8.16 Note 9 – Employee share-based incentives
nodes.start_phrase:
In 2022 , 2021 and 2020 , JPMorgan Chase granted long-
term share-based awards to certain employees unde r its 
LTIP, as amended and restated effective May 15, 2018, and 
subsequently amended effective May 18, 2021.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 9 covers JPMorgan Chase’s employee share‑based incentive programs under its Long‑Term Incentive Plan (LTIP), the only active plan, as amended May 15, 2018 and May 18, 2021.
- Share pool: As of December 31, 2022, 69 million common shares remained available for issuance under the LTIP through May 2025.
- RSUs: Granted at no cost; typically vest 50% after two years and 50% after three years; subject to forfeiture and clawbacks; include full‑career eligibility provisions allowing continued vesting upon qualifying voluntary termination; provide cash dividend equivalents while outstanding; convert to common stock at vesting.
- PSUs: Granted annually to Operating Committee members, subject to three‑year performance criteria; payout can range from 0% to 150% of grant; accrued dividends are reinvested as dividend equivalent share units; convert to common stock after vesting; delivered shares must be held for an additional period, resulting in a total vesting/holding timeline of approximately five to eight years depending on jurisdiction.
- SARs and stock options: Generally granted at fair market value; 10‑year term. In 2021, 1.5 million SARs were granted to the Chairman & CEO and 750,000 to the President & COO; no SAR or option grants in 2022; 2020 grants were not material.
- Expense recognition: Compensation cost is recognized separately for each tranche, net of estimated forfeitures. Straight‑line recognition from grant to vesting, with specific treatment for awards with full‑career eligibility or no substantive future service (accrued at grant based on expected awards). For tranches where employees attain full‑career eligibility during vesting, expense is recognized from grant to the earlier of eligibility or vesting date.
- Settlement: The firm issues new or treasury shares; in 2020–2022, all settlements used treasury shares.
- EPS: Note 23 provides additional information on classification of share‑based awards for earnings per share calculations.

nodes.title: Employee share-based awards
nodes.heading: 8.16.1 Employee share-based awards
nodes.start_phrase:
In 2022 , 2021 and 2020 , JPMorgan Chase granted long-
term share-based awards to certain employees unde r its 
LTIP, as amended and restated effective May 15, 2018, and 
subsequently amended effective May 18, 2021.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s employee share-based incentive programs under the Long-Term Incentive Plan (LTIP), as amended in 2018 and 2021; as of December 31, 2022, 69 million shares remained available for issuance through May 2025. LTIP is the only active plan; “LTI Plans” include the LTIP plus legacy and assumed plans.
- Restricted stock units (RSUs): awarded at no cost, generally granted annually; vest 50% after two years and 50% after three years; convert to common shares at vesting. Include full-career eligibility provisions allowing continued vesting upon certain voluntary terminations, subject to restrictions; subject to forfeiture and clawback; most RSUs provide cash dividend equivalents while outstanding.
- Performance share units (PSUs): granted annually to Operating Committee members under the variable compensation program and approved by the Board; vest based on Firm performance over three years with outcomes from 0% to 150% of grant. Dividends accrue and are reinvested in dividend equivalent share units; upon vesting, PSUs and equivalents convert to common shares. Vested shares must be held for an additional period, resulting in a combined vesting and holding period of approximately five to eight years from grant, depending on jurisdiction.
- Stock appreciation rights (SARs) and stock options: generally granted at fair value (at-the-money) with 10-year terms. In 2021, 1.5 million SARs were awarded to the Chairman and CEO and 750,000 to the President and COO; no SAR or option grants in 2022; 2020 grants were not material.
- Compensation expense recognition: each award tranche treated as a separate award; expense recognized on a straight-line basis from grant to vest, net of estimated forfeitures. For awards with full-career eligibility provisions or no substantive future service requirement, the Firm accrues the estimated grant-date value without considering post-employment restrictions. For tranches where employees will become full-career eligible during vesting, expense is recognized to the earlier of the eligibility date or vesting date.
- Settlement of awards: the Firm may issue new or treasury shares; all awards in 2020–2022 were settled using treasury shares.
- Reference to Note 23 for earnings per share classification of share-based awards.

- Notes unrecognized compensation cost of approximately $1.0 billion (pretax) at December 31, 2022, to be amortized over a weighted-average 1.8 years; the firm does not capitalize share-based compensation.
- Provides income tax benefits from share-based incentive arrangements: $901 million (2022), $957 million (2021), $837 million (2020).

nodes.title: Note 10 – Investment securities
nodes.heading: 8.17 Note 10 – Investment securities
nodes.start_phrase:
Investment securities consist of debt securities that are 
classified as AFS or HTM.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and classification: Note 10 covers investment securities classified as available-for-sale (AFS) and held-to-maturity (HTM), predominantly held by Treasury and the CIO for asset-liability management. Trading securities are addressed elsewhere (Note 2).
- Accounting policies:
  - AFS: carried at fair value; unrealized gains/losses (after hedge accounting adjustments and any allowance for credit losses) recorded in AOCI; realized gains/losses recognized in earnings using specific identification.
  - HTM: carried at amortized cost net of allowance for credit losses; the Firm asserts intent and ability to hold to maturity.
  - Premiums/discounts amortized to interest income on a level-yield basis; premiums on certain callable debt amortized to earliest call date.
- Transfers between categories: In 2022 and 2021, $78.3 billion and $104.5 billion, respectively, were transferred from AFS to HTM for capital management. Related unrealized amounts remained in AOCI (pretax $(4.8) billion loss in 2022; $425 million gain in 2021) and are amortized into interest income over remaining lives, offsetting premium/discount effects. Transfers are non-cash and recorded at fair value.
- Portfolio composition and values (December 31, 2022 vs. 2021): Detailed by category (MBS, U.S. Treasury/government, states/municipalities, non-U.S. government, corporates, ABS including CLOs). Totals:
  - AFS: amortized cost $216.2B; fair value $205.9B; gross unrealized gains $0.9B; losses $11.2B (2022). Prior year: amortized cost $308.3B; fair value $308.5B.
  - HTM: amortized cost $425.3B; fair value $388.6B; gross unrealized gains $0.1B; losses $36.8B (2022). Prior year: amortized cost $363.7B; fair value $362.6B.
  - Total investment securities, net of allowance for credit losses: fair value $594.5B (2022) vs. $671.2B (2021).
- Activity and allowances:
  - HTM purchases: $33.7B (2022), $111.8B (2021), $12.4B (2020).
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities: $96M (2022) and $42M (2021) included in amortized cost.
  - Accrued interest receivable excluded from amortized cost: $2.5B (2022) and $1.9B (2021); no ACL recognized on accrued interest receivable; policy to write off by 90 days past due; no reversals through interest income in 2022 or 2021.
- Credit quality and risk management: As of December 31, 2022, average portfolio credit rating AA+. Internal risk ratings (aligned to external agencies qualitatively) are assigned at acquisition, reviewed regularly by Credit Risk Management, and updated as needed; quantitative PD/LGD may differ due to internal experience and assumptions.

nodes.title: AFS securities impairment
nodes.heading: 8.17.1 AFS securities impairment
nodes.start_phrase:
The following tables present the fair value and gross unrealized losses by aging category for AFS securities at D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 
2022 and 2021 .
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Disclosure on available-for-sale (AFS) securities impairment, including detailed aging of gross unrealized losses and fair values at December 31, 2022 and 2021, plus policies for recognizing impairment and credit loss evaluation. Also covers held-to-maturity (HTM) securities credit risk, allowance methodology, credit quality, and income statement impacts.

- AFS unrealized loss tables:
  - Excludes U.S. Treasury/government agency securities and U.S. GSE/government agency MBS with unrealized losses of $9.6 billion (2022) and $2.2 billion (2021), noting these are largely interest-rate driven.
  - 2022 totals: Fair value $29.4 billion with $1.59 billion gross unrealized losses (less than 12 months: $20.9b FV/$846m losses; 12 months or more: $8.5b FV/$746m losses). Key categories include mortgage-backed securities (residential and commercial), obligations of U.S. states/municipalities, non-U.S. government debt, corporate debt, and asset-backed securities (notably CLOs).
  - 2021 totals: Fair value $17.9 billion with $107 million gross unrealized losses (less than 12 months: $16.5b FV/$65m losses; 12 months or more: $1.3b FV/$42m losses).

- AFS impairment accounting:
  - AFS is impaired when fair value is below amortized cost.
  - If there is intent to sell or it is more likely than not the security will be required to be sold before recovery, the full difference between amortized cost (net of allowance) and fair value is recognized in earnings (investment securities gains/losses).
  - If the firm intends and is able to hold, it evaluates for credit loss; any credit loss is recorded as an allowance through provision for credit losses (limited to the impairment amount). Non-credit impairment is recorded in OCI.
  - Credit loss evaluation factors include issuer/collateral financial condition, industry/geographic conditions, and security payment structure.
  - For securitizations, expected cash flows, collateral performance, and structural credit enhancement (e.g., subordination, excess spread, overcollateralization) are assessed; credit losses are recognized if enhancements are insufficient to absorb projected pool losses.
  - Beneficial interests rated below AA at acquisition or with settlement features that could prevent recovery are evaluated for credit impairment upon adverse changes in expected cash flows.

- HTM securities credit risk and allowance:
  - Allowance reflects expected credit losses over remaining life.
  - For HTM obligations of U.S. states/municipalities and CMBS: allowance based on PD/LGD factors derived from a weighted average of five internally developed eight-quarter macroeconomic scenarios, followed by a one-year straight-line reversion to long-run history.
  - For HTM CLOs and U.S. RMBS: allowance equals amortized cost minus the present value of expected cash flows (discounted at the effective rate), using the same macro forecast and considering structural features.
  - Significant management judgment applies; different inputs/assumptions could change the allowance estimate.
  - Credit quality: All HTM securities were investment grade, current and accruing at year-end 2022 and 2021; approximately 98% rated at least AA+.

- Allowance for credit losses on investment securities (AFS and HTM combined): $96 million (2022), $42 million (2021), $78 million (2020).

- Income statement impacts:
  - Realized gains/(losses) on investment securities: 2022: $198m gains, $(2,578)m losses, net $(2,380)m; 2021: $595m gains, $(940)m losses, net $(345)m; 2020: $3,080m gains, $(2,278)m losses, net $802m.
  - Provision for credit losses on investment securities: $54m (2022), $(36)m (2021), $68m (2020).

nodes.title: HTM securities – credit risk
nodes.heading: 8.17.2 HTM securities – credit risk
nodes.start_phrase:
The allowance for credit losses represents expected credit 
losses over the remaining expected life of HTM securities.
nodes.summary:
- Impairment of AFS debt securities: recognized in earnings at the full difference between amortized cost (net of allowance) and fair value when the firm intends to sell or will likely be required to sell before cost recovery. If the firm intends and is able to hold, it evaluates for credit loss; any credit loss is recorded as an allowance through the provision for credit losses (limited to the fair value shortfall), while non‑credit impairment is recorded in OCI.
- Credit loss evaluation factors: issuer/collateral financial condition, industry and geographic conditions, and security payment structure.
- Securitization assessments: estimate cash flows using market/economic data, loan-level performance, and structural credit enhancements (e.g., subordination, excess spread, overcollateralization); compare projected pool losses to available credit enhancement to determine credit loss. For certain below‑AA beneficial interests or those subject to potentially non‑recoverable settlements, evaluate for impairment upon adverse changes in expected cash flows.
- HTM securities allowance: represents expected lifetime credit losses.
  - For HTM U.S. states/municipal obligations and CMBS: apply PD/LGD statistical factors to amortized cost using a weighted average of five internally developed eight‑quarter macroeconomic scenarios, followed by a one‑year straight‑line reversion to long‑run history.
  - For HTM CLOs and U.S. RMBS: measure as the difference between amortized cost and the present value of expected cash flows (discounted at the effective interest rate), with cash flows informed by the eight‑quarter forecast, reversion, and structural features.
  - Estimates involve significant management judgment; different assumptions can materially affect the allowance.
- Credit quality of HTM: primary indicator is risk rating; as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, all HTM were investment grade, current and accruing, with ~98% rated at least AA+.
- Allowance for credit losses on investment securities: $96 million (2022), $42 million (2021), $78 million (2020).
- Income statement impacts (investment securities): realized gains of $198m (2022), $595m (2021), $3,080m (2020); realized losses of $(2,578)m (2022), $(940)m (2021), $(2,278)m (2020); net investment securities gains/(losses) of $(2,380)m (2022), $(345)m (2021), $802m (2020). Provision for credit losses: $54m (2022), $(36)m (2021), $68m (2020).

nodes.title: Credit quality indicator
nodes.heading: 8.17.2.1 Credit quality indicator
nodes.start_phrase:
The primary credit quality indicator for HTM securities is the 
risk rating assigned to each security.
nodes.summary:
- Criteria for recognizing impairment on available-for-sale (AFS) debt securities, including full loss recognition in earnings when the firm intends or is likely required to sell before cost recovery.
- Treatment of AFS impairments when the firm intends and is able to hold: separation of credit losses (recognized via an allowance through provision for credit losses) versus non-credit losses (recorded in other comprehensive income).
- Key factors used to assess credit losses on AFS securities, such as issuer/industry/geographic conditions, collateral, payment structures, and securitization features (subordination, excess spread, overcollateralization, credit enhancement).
- Approach to evaluating securitized assets for credit loss by projecting collateral pool losses against available credit enhancement and testing for adverse changes in expected cash flows for certain lower-rated or prepayable beneficial interests.
- Held-to-maturity (HTM) securities credit risk framework and lifetime expected credit loss allowance methodology.
- HTM allowance calculations: PD/LGD-based model for U.S. states and municipalities and CMBS using a weighted average of five internally developed eight‑quarter macroeconomic scenarios with reversion; cash flow discounting method for CLOs and U.S. RMBS using expected collateral performance and structural features.
- Emphasis on management judgment and sensitivity of allowance estimates to inputs and assumptions.
- Credit quality indicators for HTM: reliance on risk ratings; all HTM rated investment grade and current/accruing, with about 98% rated at least AA+ at December 31, 2022 and 2021.
- Reported allowance for credit losses on investment securities: $96 million (2022), $42 million (2021), $78 million (2020).

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses on investment securities
nodes.heading: 8.17.2.2 Allowance for credit losses on investment securities

The allowance for credit losses on investment securities was 
$ 9 6 m i l l i o n, $ 4 2 m i l l i o n and $ 7 8 m i l l i o n as of 
D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2, 2021 and 2020 , respectively.
nodes.summary:
- AFS securities impairment policy:
  - Impaired when fair value is below amortized cost.
  - If the firm intends to sell or is more likely than not required to sell before cost recovery, recognize the full impairment in earnings (investment securities gains/losses) equal to amortized cost (net of allowance) minus fair value.
  - If the firm intends and is able to hold, evaluate for credit loss; recognize credit losses via an allowance through the provision for credit losses (limited to the impairment amount). Non-credit impairment is recorded in OCI.
  - Credit loss evaluation considers issuer/industry/geographic conditions, collateral, and payment structure.
  - For securitization exposures, estimate cash flows using market/economic data, loan-level data, and structural credit enhancement (subordination, excess spread, overcollateralization) and compare projected pool losses to credit enhancement to determine credit loss.
  - Beneficial interests rated below AA at acquisition or with settlement features that may prevent recovery are evaluated for credit losses upon adverse changes in expected cash flows.

- HTM securities – allowance for credit losses:

  - For CLOs and U.S. RMBS: measure as amortized cost minus PV of expected cash flows discounted at the effective interest rate, using macro forecasts and considering structural features.

nodes.title: Note 11 – Securities financing activities
nodes.heading: 8.18 Note 11 – Securities financing activities
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase enters into resale, repurchase, securities borrowed and securities loaned agreements (collectively, “securities financing agreements”) primarily to finance the Firm’s inventory positions, acquire securities to cover short sales, accommodate customers’ financing needs,
nodes.summary:
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s use of securities financing agreements—resale, repurchase, securities borrowed, and securities loaned—to finance inventory, cover short sales, meet client financing needs, settle securities obligations, and deploy excess cash.
- Explains accounting treatment as collateralized financings on the Consolidated balance sheets, with net presentation when permitted under accounting guidance (see Note 1), and fee recognition in interest income/expense over the life of the agreements.
- Details election of the fair value option (see Note 3) for certain agreements, reported within securities purchased under resale agreements, securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements, and securities borrowed. For FVO items, interest accruals go to interest income/expense, and fair value changes go to principal transactions revenue; for hybrid instruments with embedded derivatives, all fair value changes, including interest elements, go to principal transactions revenue.
- Notes that agreements not under the fair value option are measured at amortized cost, and no allowance for credit losses was held for resale and securities borrowed as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, due to credit risk mitigation practices.
- Outlines credit and liquidity risk management: monitoring collateral values versus cash and exchanged collateral; setting and maintaining margin levels based on counterparty, collateral type, and eligibility; predominant use of high-quality collateral (government debt, U.S. GSEs and agency MBS).
- Clarifies credit risk exposures: in resale/securities borrowed when collateral value is below cash advanced; in repurchase/securities loaned when securities delivered exceed cash received. Mitigants include master netting agreements with rights to liquidate collateral on default and a policy to take possession of collateral securities where possible.
- References Note 29 for additional information on assets pledged and collateral received.

nodes.title: Credit risk mitigation practices
nodes.heading: 8.18.1 Credit risk mitigation practices
nodes.start_phrase: Securities financing agreements expose the Firm primarily to credit and liquidity risk.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Describes JPMorgan Chase’s securities financing activities—resale and repurchase (reverse repos/repos), and securities borrowed/loaned—used to finance inventory, cover short sales, meet client financing and settlement needs, and deploy excess cash.

- Accounting treatment: These agreements are recorded as collateralized financings on the Consolidated balance sheets and netted when U.S. GAAP criteria and legal opinions support offsetting. Related fees are recognized in interest income/expense over the life of the agreements.

- Fair value vs. amortized cost: The Firm elects the fair value option for certain agreements (reported within resale, repo, and securities borrowed/loaned line items). For fair value-elected positions, interest accruals go to interest income/expense and changes in fair value to principal transactions revenue; for instruments with embedded derivatives, all fair value changes (including interest) go to principal transactions revenue. Other agreements are measured at amortized cost.

- Credit risk and mitigation: Primary risks are credit and liquidity. The Firm manages these by monitoring collateral values (predominantly high-quality government and agency securities and MBS), setting and maintaining margins by counterparty and collateral type, using master netting agreements with appropriate legal opinions, and taking possession of collateral where possible. Given these practices, no allowance for credit losses was held on resale and securities borrowed as of December 31, 2022 and 2021.

- Netting disclosures: Provides tables reconciling gross, netted, and balance-sheet-presented amounts for 2022 and 2021, plus “amounts not nettable” (e.g., collateral exchanged and positions without qualifying legal opinions). When acting as lender in securities-for-securities transactions and receiving pledgeable securities, the Firm recognizes the received securities at fair value in other assets with a corresponding obligation in accounts payable and other liabilities.

- Collateral composition and maturities: Details the types of assets pledged in repos and securities loaned (notably U.S. Treasuries/GSEs/agency MBS, non-U.S. government debt, corporates, and equities) and provides remaining contractual maturity profiles showing significant activity in overnight/short-term buckets.

- Transfers not qualifying as sales: Notes certain transfers of financial assets that did not meet sale accounting, recognized instead as collateralized financings (with related assets in trading assets/loans and liabilities mainly in short-term borrowings).

- Cross-references: Points to other notes for offsetting (Note 1), fair value option (Note 3), and assets pledged/collateral received (Note 29).

nodes.title: Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting
nodes.heading: 8.18.2 Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting

- Scope: Discloses, as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, the types of financial assets pledged in securities financing agreements and the remaining contractual maturity profiles of those agreements.
- Gross liability balances: Breaks down balances for securities sold under repurchase agreements and for securities loaned and other by asset class (U.S. GSE/government agency MBS, residential and commercial nonagency MBS, U.S. Treasury/GSE/government, U.S. states and municipalities, non-U.S. government debt, corporate debt, asset-backed securities, and equities). Totals:
