The assets remain in trading assets and loans; corresponding liabilities are recorded predominantly in short-term borrowings.
- Context: Extract from the Notes to consolidated financial statements in JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s 2022 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Note 12 – Loans
nodes.heading: 8.19 Note 12 – Loans
nodes.start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note outlines the Firm’s loan accounting framework and details policies for loans held-for-investment; other categories (held-for-sale, at fair value) are noted but not elaborated here.
- Loan categories: (1) Originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (including PCD), (2) Loans held-for-sale, (3) Loans at fair value.
- Measurement for held-for-investment: Recorded at amortized cost (principal outstanding net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, and FX). Credit card loans include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income (performing loans): Accrued at contractual rate; purchase discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs amortized into interest income over the contractual life as a yield adjustment.
- Accrued interest presentation and treatment:
  - Classified in accrued interest and accounts receivable.
  - Credit cards: once billed, accrued interest moves into loan balances with an associated allowance; allowance changes flow through provision for credit losses; charge-offs reverse interest income.
  - Other loans: generally no allowance on accrued interest; written off no later than 90 days past due by reversing interest income.
- Nonaccrual policy:
  - Loans (excluding credit cards and certain government-insured consumer loans) go on nonaccrual when full collectibility is not expected or when 90+ days past due unless well-secured and in collection; collateral-dependent loans typically nonaccrual.
  - Past due generally when minimum payment not received by due date; for certain loans (e.g., residential real estate), when 30+ days past due.
  - Upon nonaccrual: reverse accrued but unpaid interest; suspend amortization of deferred amounts.
  - Recognition on nonaccrual: cash-basis if fully collectible; otherwise apply cash to reduce carrying value (cost recovery). Consumer nonaccrual interest typically recognized on a cash basis.
  - Return to accrual when repayment is reasonably assured with demonstrated performance or per restructured terms.
  - Credit cards are generally exempt from nonaccrual; interest/fees continue accruing until charge-off or payoff.
- Allowance for loan losses: Contra-asset for expected credit losses on held-for-investment loans, reducing amortized cost to net carrying value; changes recognized in provision for credit losses (with further policy detail referenced in another note).
- Charge-off policy (consumer loans):
  - Generally charged off or written down to net realizable collateral value at specified delinquency thresholds per FFIEC.
  - Timing: residential real estate, unmodified credit card, and scored business banking—no later than 180 days past due; scored auto and modified credit card—no later than 120 days past due.
  - Earlier charge-offs when: (a) TDRs that are collateral-dependent, or (b) borrower-specific events indicate losses are known or highly certain (accelerated standards).

nodes.title: Loan accounting framework
nodes.heading: 8.19.1 Loan accounting framework
nodes.start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 12 outlines the Firm’s loan accounting framework and policies by category: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (including PCD), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value; this excerpt details held-for-investment loans.
- Measurement for held-for-investment: Recorded at amortized cost (principal net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, FX). Credit card loans include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income recognition: Accrual at contractual rates on performing loans; premiums/discounts and net deferred fees/costs amortized into interest income over the loan’s life as a yield adjustment.
- Accrued interest handling:
  - Presented in accrued interest and accounts receivable.
  - Credit cards: once billed, accrued interest moves into loan balances; related allowance recognized within the allowance for credit losses (ACL). Changes in ACL for accrued card interest run through provision; charge-offs reverse interest income.
  - Other loans: generally no ACL on accrued interest receivables; written off by 90 days past due by reversing interest income.
- Nonaccrual policy:
  - Loans (excluding credit cards and certain government-insured consumer loans) placed on nonaccrual when full payment isn’t expected or when 90+ days past due unless well-secured and in collection; “past due” generally means missed minimum payment by due date or 30+ days for certain loans (e.g., residential real estate).
  - Collateral-dependent loans typically remain on nonaccrual.
  - Upon nonaccrual designation: reverse unpaid accrued interest; suspend amortization of deferred amounts.
  - Interest on nonaccrual: recognized on a cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise apply cash to principal (cost recovery). Consumer nonaccrual interest typically recognized on a cash basis.
  - Return to accrual when repayment is reasonably assured and performance is demonstrated (including for restructured loans).
  - Credit cards are generally exempt from nonaccrual; interest and fees continue accruing until charge-off or payoff.
- Allowance for loan losses: Contra-asset reflecting expected credit losses on held-for-investment loans at the balance sheet date; changes recorded in provision for credit losses (see Note 13 for policy detail).
- Charge-offs:
  - Consumer loans charged off or written down to net realizable collateral value (fair value less costs to sell) per FFIEC delinquency standards, with offset to ACL.
  - Timing: residential real estate, unmodified credit cards, and scored business banking—no later than 180 days past due; scored auto and modified credit cards—no later than 120 days past due.
  - Earlier charge-offs in certain cases, including collateral-dependent TDRs and when events make losses known or highly certain (excerpt truncated).

nodes.title: Loans held-for-investment
nodes.heading: 8.19.1.1 Loans held-for-investment
nodes.start_phrase: Originated or purchased loans held-for-investment, including PCD, are recorded at amortized cost, reflecting the principal amount outstanding, net of the following: unamortized deferred loan fees, costs, premiums or discounts; charge-offs; collection of cash; and foreign exchange.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the Firm’s loan accounting framework and categories: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (including PCD), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value; this excerpt focuses on held-for-investment loans.
- Measurement for held-for-investment loans: recorded at amortized cost (principal net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts), charge-offs, cash collections, and foreign exchange; credit card loans also include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income recognition: accrued at contractual rates on performing loans; purchase discounts/premiums and deferred fees/costs are amortized into interest income over the loan’s life.
- Accrued interest handling: presented in accrued interest and accounts receivable; for credit cards, once billed, accrued interest is included in loan balances with a related allowance; allowance changes flow through provision for credit losses, and charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, no allowance is generally recorded on accrued interest receivables, which are written off by 90 days past due by reversing interest income.
- Nonaccrual policy: loans (excluding credit cards and certain government-insured consumer loans) placed on nonaccrual when full payment is not expected or when 90+ days past due unless well-secured and in collection; collateral-dependent loans typically on nonaccrual. Upon nonaccrual, previously accrued interest is reversed and amortization of deferred amounts is suspended.
- Interest on nonaccrual loans: recognized on a cash basis if the loan’s recorded balance is fully collectible; otherwise, cash receipts reduce principal (cost recovery method). Consumer nonaccrual loans generally follow cash-basis recognition. Loans may return to accrual when repayment is reasonably assured with demonstrated performance. Credit card loans are generally exempt from nonaccrual and continue to accrue until charge-off or payoff.
- Allowance for loan losses: represents expected credit losses on held-for-investment loans; recorded as a contra-asset; changes recognized in provision for credit losses (with further policy details referenced in another note).
- Charge-off policies: consumer loans charged off or written down to net realizable collateral value upon specified delinquency stages per FFIEC standards. Timing includes: residential real estate, unmodified credit cards, and scored business banking no later than 180 days past due; scored auto and modified credit cards no later than 120 days past due.
- Early/accelerated charge-offs: applied in certain situations, such as collateral-dependent TDRs and when events indicate losses are known or highly certain (details continue beyond the excerpt).

nodes.title: Interest income
nodes.heading: 8.19.1.1.1 Interest income
nodes.start_phrase: Interest income on performing loans held-for-investment is accrued and recognized as interest income at the contractual rate of interest.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the Firm’s loan accounting framework and categories: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value; this section details loans held-for-investment.
- Measurement for loans held-for-investment: recorded at amortized cost (principal net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, and FX). Credit card loans include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income recognition: accrue contractual interest on performing loans; amortize purchase discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs over the loan’s contractual life as yield adjustments.
- Accrued interest handling: recorded in accrued interest and accounts receivable. For credit cards, accrued interest once billed is included in loan balances with a related allowance; changes in that allowance flow through provision for credit losses and charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, generally no allowance is recorded on accrued interest receivables; these are written off no later than 90 days past due by reversing interest income.
- Nonaccrual policy: loans (excluding credit cards and certain U.S. government–insured consumer loans) are placed on nonaccrual when full collection is not expected or when 90+ days past due unless well-secured and in collection; collateral-dependent loans are typically nonaccrual. Upon nonaccrual, reverse accrued but unpaid interest and suspend amortization of deferred amounts. Interest may be recognized on a cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise, cash receipts reduce principal (cost recovery). Return to accrual requires reasonable assurance of repayment and demonstrated performance. Credit card loans are generally exempt from nonaccrual.
- Allowance for loan losses: a contra-asset reflecting expected credit losses on held-for-investment loans at the balance sheet date; changes recognized in provision for credit losses.
- Charge-off policies: consumer loans charged off or written down to net realizable collateral value based on FFIEC delinquency standards—generally no later than 180 days past due for residential real estate, unmodified credit cards, and scored business banking; and no later than 120 days for scored auto and modified credit cards. Earlier charge-offs occur for collateral-dependent TDRs and when borrower-specific events make losses known or highly certain.

nodes.title: Nonaccrual loans
nodes.heading: 8.19.1.1.2 Nonaccrual loans
nodes.start_phrase: Nonaccrual loans are those on which the accrual of interest has been suspended.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the Firm’s loan accounting framework by management’s strategy, with three categories: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value; provides detailed policies primarily for loans held-for-investment (HFI).
- Measurement for HFI (including PCD): recorded at amortized cost net of unamortized fees/costs, premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, and foreign exchange; credit card loans include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income recognition: accrual at contractual rates for performing HFI; amortization of purchase discounts/premiums and deferred fees/costs into interest income over the loan’s life. Accrued interest is recorded in accrued interest and receivables; for credit cards, once billed it is included in loan balances with related allowance and changes booked to provision, and charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, generally no allowance on accrued interest; write-off by 90 days past due via reversal of interest income.
- Nonaccrual policy: loans (excluding credit cards and certain U.S. government–insured consumer loans) placed on nonaccrual when full collection isn’t expected or when 90+ days past due unless well-secured and in collection; collateral-dependent loans typically nonaccrual. Upon nonaccrual, reverse accrued but uncollected interest and suspend amortization of deferred amounts. Interest on nonaccrual recognized on a cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise apply cost recovery method. Return to accrual requires reasonable assurance of repayment and demonstrated performance. Credit card loans are generally exempt from nonaccrual and continue accruing until paid or charged off.
- Allowance for loan losses: contra-asset reflecting expected credit losses on HFI at the balance sheet date; changes recognized in provision for credit losses (with further detail referenced in a separate note).
- Charge-off policies: consumer loans charged off or written down to net realizable collateral value based on FFIEC delinquency criteria—generally by 180 days past due for residential real estate, unmodified credit cards, and scored business banking; and by 120 days for scored auto and modified credit cards. Earlier charge-offs occur for collateral-dependent TDRs and when loss is known or highly certain, with charge-offs recorded against the allowance.

nodes.title: Allowance for loan losses
nodes.heading: 8.19.1.1.3 Allowance for loan losses
nodes.start_phrase: The allowance for loan losses represents the estimated expected credit losses in the held-for-investment loan portfolio at the balance sheet date and is recognized on the balance sheet as a contra asset, which brings the amortized cost to the net carrying value.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 12 outlines the Firm’s loan accounting framework and policies.
- Loan categories: (1) originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (including PCD), (2) loans held-for-sale, and (3) loans at fair value.
- Held-for-investment measurement: recorded at amortized cost (principal net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, and FX). Credit card loans include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income recognition: accrued at contractual rates on performing HFI loans; purchase discounts/premiums and deferred fees/costs amortized into interest income as yield adjustments.
- Accrued interest policy: accrued interest (including unbilled credit card interest) is recorded in accrued interest and accounts receivable. For credit cards, once billed it is included in loan balances with an associated allowance; changes flow through provision for credit losses and charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, generally no allowance on accrued interest; written off no later than 90 days past due by reversing interest income.
- Nonaccrual loans: placed on nonaccrual when full payment is not expected or 90+ days past due (unless well-secured and in collection); collateral-dependent loans typically nonaccrual. Upon nonaccrual, accrued but unpaid interest is reversed and amortization of deferred amounts suspended. Interest may be recognized on a cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise cash receipts reduce principal (cost-recovery). Loans may return to accrual when repayment is reasonably assured and performance is demonstrated. Credit card loans are generally exempt from nonaccrual.
- Allowance for loan losses: contra-asset reflecting expected credit losses on HFI loans; changes recognized in provision for credit losses; additional policy details referenced to Note 13.
- Charge-offs: consumer loans charged off or written down to net realizable value per FFIEC delinquency standards—generally by 180 days past due for residential real estate, unmodified credit cards, and scored business banking; by 120 days for scored auto and modified credit cards. Earlier charge-offs occur for collateral-dependent TDRs and when events indicate losses are known or highly certain.
- Note: Loans held-for-sale and loans at fair value are identified categories, with detailed accounting discussion implied outside this excerpt.

nodes.title: Charge-offs
nodes.heading: 8.19.1.1.4 Charge-offs
nodes.start_phrase: Consumer loans are generally charged off or charged down to the lower of the amortized cost or the net realizable value of the underlying collateral (i.e., fair value less estimated costs to sell), with an offset to the allowance for loan losses,
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 12 outlines the Firm’s loan accounting framework by management strategy and measurement category: loans held-for-investment (including PCD), loans held-for-sale, and loans carried at fair value (fair value option), with cross-references to Notes 2, 3, and 13.

- Loans held-for-investment:
  - Measurement: Amortized cost (principal net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, FX). Credit card loans include billed finance charges/fees.
  - Interest income: Accrued at contractual rate; premiums/discounts and deferred fees/costs amortized into interest yield.
  - Accrued interest: Recorded in accrued interest and accounts receivable. For credit cards, accrued interest moves to loan balance once billed with related allowance; changes flow through provision; charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, generally no allowance on accrued interest; written off by 90 days past due via reversing interest income.
  - Nonaccrual policy: Loans (excluding credit cards and certain government-insured consumer loans) placed on nonaccrual when full payment isn’t expected or 90+ days past due (unless well-secured and in collection); collateral-dependent loans typically nonaccrual. Accrued interest reversed and amortization suspended at designation. Interest recognized on cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise cash reduces principal (cost recovery). Return to accrual upon demonstrated performance and assured repayment. Credit card loans generally exempt from nonaccrual; interest accrues until charge-off or payoff.
  - Allowance for loan losses: Contra-asset for expected credit losses on held-for-investment loans; changes recorded in provision for credit losses (see Note 13).
  - Charge-offs:
    - Consumer: Generally per FFIEC—residential real estate, unmodified credit card, and scored business banking by 180 days past due; scored auto and modified credit card by 120 days. Earlier for collateral-dependent TDRs, bankruptcy (e.g., residential real estate and auto within 60 days of notification), and auto upon repossession. Government-guaranteed portions typically not charged off.
    - Wholesale: Charged off when loss is highly certain, considering bankruptcy priority, expected workout/restructuring, and collateral/equity valuation.
  - Collateral valuation: Liquid securities via quotes; illiquid assets via DCF. Residential real estate uses broker price opinions/appraisals/AVMs (exterior) updated at least annually; interior appraisals upon taking possession; values discounted for liquidation experience and state factors. Commercial real estate appraisals internal/external, typically updated every 6–12 months; frequency may increase based on borrower/market conditions.

- Loans held-for-sale:
  - Measurement: Lower of cost or fair value; valuation changes in noninterest revenue (consumer on a portfolio basis; wholesale individually).
  - Interest income: Accrued at contractual rate.
  - Fees/costs/premiums/discounts: Deferred in a contra account until sale; included in LCM adjustments and gain/loss on sale.
  - No allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies apply; nonaccrual policies do apply.

- Loans at fair value (fair value option):
  - Measurement: Fair value with changes in noninterest revenue.
  - Interest income: Accrued at contractual rate.
  - Fees/costs: Origination fees recognized upfront in noninterest revenue; origination costs expensed as incurred.
  - No allowance or charge-off policies apply; nonaccrual policies do apply.
  - References: Note 3 for fair value option elections; Notes 2 and 3 for loans at fair value classified as trading assets.

nodes.title: Loans held-for-sale
nodes.heading: 8.19.1.2 Loans held-for-sale
nodes.start_phrase: Loans held-for-sale are measured at the lower of cost or fair value, with valuation changes recorded in noninterest revenue.
nodes.summary:
- Charge-off policies:
  - Consumer loans: residential real estate and auto loans are charged off/charged down within 60 days of bankruptcy notification; auto loans are charged off upon repossession. Government‑guaranteed portions are generally not charged off except in limited cases.
  - Wholesale loans: charged off when a loss is highly certain, considering bankruptcy claim priority, expected workout/restructuring, and borrower equity/collateral valuation.
  - Charge-downs to the lower of amortized cost or estimated net realizable collateral value; collateral fair value determined by asset type.

- Collateral valuation methods:
  - Liquid securities: quoted market prices or broker quotes.
  - Illiquid securities/financial assets: discounted cash flow models.
  - Residential real estate: external valuation sources; use exterior-only opinions/AVMs when repayment concern arises (updated at least every 12 months or more often); obtain interior appraisals after taking possession; apply discounts based on realized liquidation experience and state factors.
  - Commercial real estate: internal/external appraisals with updates every 6–12 months; borrower and market factors may prompt more frequent updates or broker price opinions.

- Loans held-for-sale (HFS):
  - Measured at lower of cost or fair value; valuation changes recorded in noninterest revenue.
  - Consumer HFS valued on a portfolio basis; wholesale HFS individually.
  - Interest accrued at contractual rate.
  - Origination fees/costs and purchase discounts/premiums deferred in a contra account until sale and included in lower-of-cost-or-FV adjustments and gain/loss on sale.
  - Not subject to the Firm’s allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies; subject to nonaccrual policies.

- Loans at fair value (fair value option):
  - Measured at fair value with changes in noninterest revenue.
  - Interest accrued at contractual rate; fair value changes recognized in noninterest revenue.
  - Origination fees recognized upfront in noninterest revenue; origination costs expensed as incurred.
  - Not subject to the Firm’s allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies; subject to nonaccrual policies.
  - Cross-references to Notes 2 and 3 for additional details and trading asset classifications.

nodes.title: Loans at fair value
nodes.heading: 8.19.1.3 Loans at fair value
nodes.start_phrase: Loans for which the fair value option has been elected are measured at fair value, with changes in fair value recorded in noninterest revenue.
nodes.summary:
- Charge-off policies:
  - Consumer loans: Residential real estate and auto loans are charged off or down within 60 days of bankruptcy notification; auto loans are also charged off upon repossession.
  - Government-guaranteed loans: Generally no charge-offs on the guaranteed portion, except in limited circumstances.
  - Wholesale loans: Charged off when loss realization is highly certain, considering bankruptcy claim priority, workout/restructuring expectations, and borrower equity/collateral valuation.

- Collateral valuation and charge-downs:
  - Loans charged down to the lower of amortized cost or estimated net realizable collateral value.
  - Liquid securities collateral valued using quoted prices or broker quotes; illiquid assets via discounted cash flow models.
  - Residential real estate: Uses external valuation sources; when default likely, relies on exterior opinions (broker price opinions, appraisals, AVMs) updated at least every 12 months; interior appraisals obtained upon taking possession; values discounted based on liquidation experience and state-specific factors.
  - Commercial real estate: Appraisals from internal/external sources; values updated every 6–12 months via new appraisals or internal analyses, with more frequent updates possible based on borrower/market conditions.

- Loans held-for-sale:
  - Measured at lower of cost or fair value; valuation changes recorded in noninterest revenue.
  - Consumer portfolios valued on a portfolio basis; wholesale on an individual loan basis.
  - Interest income accrued at contractual rates.
  - Origination fees/costs and purchase discounts/premiums deferred and included in lower-of-cost-or-fair-value adjustments and sale gains/losses.
  - Not subject to allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies; subject to nonaccrual policies.

- Loans at fair value (fair value option):
  - Measured at fair value; changes recognized in noninterest revenue.
  - Interest income accrued at contractual rates.
  - Origination fees recognized upfront in noninterest revenue; origination costs expensed as incurred.
  - Not subject to allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies; subject to nonaccrual policies.
  - Cross-references to Notes 2 and 3 for further details and trading asset classifications.

nodes.title: Loan classification changes
nodes.heading: 8.19.2 Loan classification changes
nodes.start_phrase: Loans in the held-for-investment portfolio that management decides to sell are transferred to the held-for-sale portfolio at the lower of cost or fair value on the date of transfer.
nodes.summary:
- Loan classification changes: Criteria and accounting for transferring loans between held‑for‑investment (HFI) and held‑for‑sale (HFS). Transfers to HFS are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value; credit-related losses reduce the allowance for loan losses, while non‑credit losses (e.g., interest rate or FX changes) are recognized in noninterest revenue. Loans retained in HFS and moved back to HFI are recorded at amortized cost and then assessed for impairment under the Firm’s allowance methodology (see Note 13).

- Loan modifications and TDRs: The Firm modifies loans as part of loss mitigation by granting concessions (e.g., rate reductions, term extensions, payment delays, principal forgiveness, or accepting equity/other assets) to borrowers in financial difficulty, which are accounted for as troubled debt restructurings (TDRs). Short‑term or insignificant changes that are not concessions are not TDRs.

- Nonaccrual and return to accrual: Non‑credit card loans modified in a TDR are generally placed on nonaccrual (often already nonaccrual pre‑modification). They may return to accrual after at least six months/six payments of performance and if repayment is reasonably assured based on borrower capacity, collateral values, LTVs, and market factors. In limited cases where the loan is current at modification, nonaccrual may be avoided.

- Impairment measurement for TDRs: TDRs are measured using the Firm’s asset‑specific allowance methodology, incorporating expected re‑default rates, and generally remain subject to asset‑specific allowance for their remaining life, even if performing and back on accrual (see Note 13).

- Foreclosed property: Recognition of assets obtained via restructurings, workouts, or foreclosures (real and personal/commercial property). Foreclosed assets are recorded in other assets at fair value less estimated costs to sell upon receipt (e.g., foreclosure sale or deed‑in‑lieu). Values are reviewed quarterly and adjusted to the lower of cost or fair value, with changes recorded in noninterest revenue; operating costs (e.g., taxes, maintenance) are recorded in other expense.

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.heading: 8.19.3 Loan modifications
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm seeks to modify certain loans in conjunction with its loss mitigation activities.
nodes.summary:
- Loan classification changes: Loans moved from held-for-investment to held-for-sale are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value at transfer; credit-related losses reduce the allowance for loan losses, while non-credit losses (e.g., interest rate or FX changes) flow through noninterest revenue. Loans retained in held-for-sale and moved back to held-for-investment are transferred at amortized cost and subsequently evaluated for impairment under the Firm’s allowance methodology (see Note 13).

- Loan modifications (TDRs): As part of loss mitigation, the Firm may grant concessions (e.g., interest rate reductions, term extensions, payment deferrals, principal forgiveness, or acceptance of other assets) to borrowers in financial difficulty. Short-term or insignificant changes that are not concessions are not TDRs. With the exception of credit card loans, TDR-modified loans are generally placed on nonaccrual and may return to accrual after at least six months/six payments of performance and if repayment is reasonably assured based on borrower capacity, collateral, LTV, and market factors; certain current loans at modification may avoid nonaccrual. TDRs are measured for impairment using an asset-specific allowance that incorporates expected re-default rates and remains applicable for the life of the loan, even if returned to accrual (see Note 13).

- Foreclosed property: Assets obtained via restructurings, workouts, or foreclosure (including real and personal property) are recognized when received in satisfaction of a loan—typically at foreclosure sale or deed-in-lieu for real estate—and recorded in other assets at fair value less costs to sell. Values are reviewed quarterly and adjusted to the lower of cost or fair value, with subsequent valuation changes recognized in noninterest revenue; related operating costs (e.g., taxes, maintenance) are recorded in other expense.

nodes.title: Foreclosed property
nodes.heading: 8.19.4 Foreclosed property
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm acquires property from borrowers through loan restructurings, workouts, and foreclosures.
nodes.summary:
- Loan classification changes: Loans moved from held-for-investment (HFI) to held-for-sale (HFS) are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value at transfer; credit-related losses reduce the allowance for loan losses, while non-credit losses (e.g., interest rate or FX changes) go to noninterest revenue. Loans retained in HFS and moved back to HFI are recorded at amortized cost and then evaluated for impairment under the Firm’s allowance methodology (see Note 13).
- Loan modifications: The Firm modifies loans as part of loss mitigation, granting concessions to borrowers in financial difficulty (e.g., rate reductions, term extensions, payment delays, principal forgiveness, or accepting equity/other assets) to minimize losses and avoid foreclosure; such concessions are treated as Troubled Debt Restructurings (TDRs). Short-term or insignificant changes that are not concessions are not TDRs.
- Nonaccrual and return to accrual: With the exception of credit card loans, TDR-modified loans are generally placed on nonaccrual (often already nonaccrual pre-modification). They may return to accrual after at least six months/six payments of performance and when repayment is reasonably assured based on borrower capacity, collateral/LTV, and market factors. In limited cases where loans are current at modification, they may remain on accrual.
- Impairment measurement of TDRs: TDRs are evaluated using an asset-specific allowance methodology that incorporates expected re-default rates and typically remain subject to this asset-specific allowance for their remaining life, even if returned to accrual (see Note 13).
- Foreclosed property: The Firm recognizes assets obtained via restructurings, workouts, or foreclosures (real and personal property) when it receives title or possession, including at foreclosure sale or deed-in-lieu for real estate. These assets are recorded in other assets at fair value less estimated costs to sell, reviewed quarterly and carried at the lower of cost or fair value; subsequent fair value changes affect noninterest revenue, and operating costs (e.g., taxes, maintenance) are expensed to other expense.

nodes.title: Loan portfolio
nodes.heading: 8.19.5 Loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s loan portfolio is divided into three portfolio segments, which are the same segments used by the Firm to determine the allowance for loan losses: Consumer, excluding credit card; Credit card; and Wholesale.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and structure: Describes the Firm’s loan portfolio segmentation used for the allowance for loan losses—Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale—and the loan classes monitored within each segment.
- Loan classes:
  - Consumer, excluding credit card: Residential real estate; Auto and other.
  - Credit card: Credit card loans.
  - Wholesale: Secured by real estate; Commercial and industrial; Other.
- Methodology and definitions:
  - Includes loans held across CCB, AWM, CIB, Corporate; certain risk‑rated business (e.g., BWM and auto dealer loans) in CCB use wholesale methodology.
  - Wholesale classes align with bank regulatory classifications by collateral, purpose, and borrower type.
  - “Other” wholesale includes loans to financial institutions, states/political subdivisions, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies/trusts, and individuals (notably Global Private Bank and J.P. Morgan Wealth Management). References Note 14 for SPEs.
- Portfolio balances (in millions):
  - December 31, 2022: Retained $1,089,598; Held‑for‑sale $3,970; At fair value $42,079; Total $1,135,647 (Consumer ex‑card $311,375; Credit card $185,175; Wholesale $639,097).
  - December 31, 2021: Retained $1,010,206; Held‑for‑sale $8,688; At fair value $58,820; Total $1,077,714 (Consumer ex‑card $323,306; Credit card $154,296; Wholesale $600,112).
  - Excludes accrued interest receivable of $5.2B (2022) and $2.7B (2021); accrued interest write‑offs were $39M (2022) and $56M (2021). Balances (other than FVO) are net of unamortized discounts/premiums and deferred fees/costs (not material).
- Loan activity—retained loans purchased, sold, and reclassified to held‑for‑sale (in millions; reclassifications are non‑cash):
  - 2022: Purchases $2,713 (Consumer ex‑card $1,625; Wholesale $1,088); Sales $44,818 (Wholesale‑driven); Reclassified to HFS $1,284.
  - 2021: Purchases $1,637; Sales $31,821; Reclassified to HFS $3,403.
  - 2020: Purchases $4,633; Sales $18,268; Reclassified to HFS $4,451 (including $787 in Credit card).
  - Purchases predominantly include voluntary repurchases of certain delinquent Ginnie Mae loans serviced by the Firm (consistent with FHA/RHS/VA/Ginnie Mae guidelines). Separately, purchases of retained loans sourced via the correspondent channel and underwritten to Firm standards were $12.4B (2022), $25.8B (2021), and $16.3B (2020) and are excluded from the purchases line.
- Gains and losses:
  - 2022: Net losses on sales of loans and lending‑related commitments of $(186)M, of which $(48)M related to loans.
  - 2021: Net gains $261M, of which $253M related to loans.
  - 2020: Net losses on sales of loans $(36)M.
  - Sales may also drive write‑downs, recoveries, or allowance changes recorded in the provision for credit losses.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
nodes.heading: 8.19.6 Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: Consumer loans, excluding credit card loans, consist primarily of scored residential mortgages, home equity loans and lines of credit, auto and business banking loans, with a focus on serving the prime consumer credit market.
nodes.summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s consumer loan portfolio excluding credit cards, focused on prime borrowers and comprising scored residential mortgages, home equity loans/lines (including junior liens), auto loans, and business banking loans, with some interest-only and payment-option mortgages that can negatively amortize. Presents retained loan balances by class as of December 31, 2022 vs. 2021: Residential real estate $237.6B vs. $224.8B; Auto and other $63.2B vs. $70.8B; Total $300.8B vs. $295.6B, noting PPP loans within Business Banking of $350M (2022) and $5.4B (2021). Describes credit quality monitoring: delinquency rates as the primary indicator (30+ days past due as early warning; 150+ days in residential as a strong predictor of foreclosure), with additional metrics by loan class—residential real estate uses current/combined LTV, refreshed FICO (with <660 viewed as higher risk), and geographic distribution; scored auto and business banking loans use geographic distribution to assess performance given regional economic conditions and events.

nodes.title: Residential real estate
nodes.heading: 8.19.6.1 Residential real estate
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables provide information on delinquency, which is the primary credit quality indicator for retained residential real estate loans .
nodes.summary:
This excerpt from JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K summarizes credit quality for the firm’s retained residential real estate loans, focusing on delinquency as the primary indicator. It presents detailed tables as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, splitting the portfolio into:
- Term loans by origination year (recent vintages through older cohorts).
- Revolving loans (within the revolving period) and revolving loans converted to term.

Key figures and trends:
- Portfolio size grew: total retained loans were $237.6B in 2022 vs. $224.8B in 2021; current (not past due) balances were $236.0B in 2022 vs. $222.5B in 2021.
- Overall delinquency improved: 30+ days past due fell to 0.66% of total in 2022 from 1.02% in 2021, driven by a sharp decline in 150+ day delinquencies ($684M in 2022 vs. $1,449M in 2021); 30–149 day delinquencies were $914M in 2022 vs. $883M in 2021.
- Vintage performance: newer term-loan vintages show very low delinquency (e.g., 2022: 0.08%; 2021: 0.02%), with higher rates in older vintages (2019: 0.42%; 2018: 0.42; prior to 2018: 2.07% in 2022).
- Product-type differences: revolving loans converted to term have much higher delinquency (3.80% in both 2022 and 2021) than those still in the revolving period (0.34% in 2022; 0.27% in 2021), reflecting higher fully amortizing payments after conversion.

Disclosures and methodology:
- Government-insured mortgage loans were not material and are excluded from 30+ day delinquency ratios due to the guarantee.
- Loans in COVID-19 deferral programs that are performing under modified terms are generally not treated as delinquent.
- Purchased loans are grouped by their original year of origination.
- About 37% of revolving loans are senior liens and the rest junior; lien position is considered in the allowance for credit losses.

nodes.title: Nonaccrual loans and other credit quality indicators
nodes.heading: 8.19.6.1.1 Nonaccrual loans and other credit quality indicators
nodes.start_phrase: The following table provides information on nonaccrual and other credit quality indicators for retained residential real estate loans.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Nonaccrual loans and credit quality indicators for retained residential real estate loans, as part of the notes to consolidated financial statements.
- Nonaccrual loans: Declined to $3.745 billion at December 31, 2022 from $4.759 billion at December 31, 2021.
- Portfolio size: Total retained residential real estate loans increased to $237.561 billion in 2022 from $224.795 billion in 2021.
- Credit quality mix by current estimated LTV and refreshed FICO:
  - Breakouts provided for LTV bands (>125%, 101–125%, 80–100%, <80%) split by FICO ≥660 and <660.
  - Additional categories: “No FICO/LTV available” and “U.S. government‑guaranteed.”
- Weighted averages: LTV 51% in 2022 (50% in 2021); FICO 769 in 2022 (765 in 2021), excluding loans without FICO/LTV.
- Geographic distribution: State-level balances listed, led by California ($73.1B), New York ($34.5B), Florida ($18.9B), Texas ($15.0B), Illinois ($11.3B), with totals reconciling to portfolio totals; regions ordered by 2022 balances.
- Key footnotes and definitions:
  - Collateral-dependent nonaccrual loans are charged down to collateral fair value less costs to sell; some may show negative allowance if collateral values subsequently improve.
  - Chapter 7 bankruptcy residential loans not reaffirmed are reported as collateral-dependent nonaccrual TDRs regardless of delinquency; about 5% were 30+ days past due at 12/31/22.
  - Nonaccrual totals exclude mortgage loans insured by U.S. government agencies (not material).
  - Interest income on nonaccrual loans recognized on a cash basis: $175 million (2022) and $172 million (2021).
  - Generally excludes loans under COVID-19 payment deferral programs.
  - LTV is based on unpaid principal over estimated current property value, updated at least quarterly using home price index models; combined LTV for junior liens considers all liens and unused lines.
  - Refreshed FICO scores are obtained at least quarterly; certain loans without refreshed FICO (primarily in AWM LLCs) are classified by management-estimated credit quality.

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.heading: 8.19.6.1.2 Loan modifications
nodes.start_phrase: Modifications of residential real estate loans, where the Firm grants concessions to borrowers who are experiencing financial difficulty are generally accounted for and reported as TDRs.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and accounting: Describes how JPMorgan Chase accounts for residential real estate loan modifications as troubled debt restructurings (TDRs) when concessions are granted to borrowers in financial difficulty; short‑term or insignificant changes that are not concessions are excluded from TDRs.
- Volume and balances: New TDR carrying values were $362 million (2022), $866 million (2021), and $819 million (2020). No additional lending commitments existed to borrowers with loans modified as TDRs.
- Modification programs and concessions: Through proprietary and government (including U.S. GSE) programs, the Firm offers interest rate reductions, term/payment extensions, deferrals of principal and/or interest, principal forgiveness, and other actions (e.g., converting variable to fixed rates and certain payment delays).
- Activity metrics:
  - Trial modifications approved: 3,902 (2022), 6,246 (2021), 5,522 (2020).
  - Permanent modifications completed: 4,182 (2022), 4,588 (2021), 6,850 (2020).
  - Concessions on permanently modified loans (percent of loans; multiple concessions per loan common): interest rate reduction 54%/74%/50%; term or payment extension 67%/53%/49%; principal and/or interest deferred 10%/23%/14%; principal forgiveness 1%/2%/2%; other 37%/36%/66% for 2022/2021/2020, respectively.
- Financial effects:
  - Weighted‑average interest rates on loans with rate reductions changed from 4.75%→3.35% (2022), 4.54%→2.92% (2021), and 5.09%→3.28% (2020).
  - Weighted‑average remaining contractual terms on loans with extensions increased from 22/23/22 years before to 38/38/39 years after (2022/2021/2020).
  - Charge‑offs at modification: $1m (2022), $0 (2021), $5m (2020).
  - Principal deferred: $16m (2022), $28m (2021), $16m (2020); principal forgiven: $2m (2022), $1m (2021), $5m (2020).
- Redefault experience: Balances of loans that redefaulted within one year of permanent modification were $147m (2022), $160m (2021), and $199m (2020). Redefaults defined as becoming two contractual payments past due; such loans are generally liquidated via foreclosure or similar, and recent redefault rates may not indicate ultimate outcomes.
- Portfolio life: As of December 31, 2022, the weighted‑average estimated remaining life of permanently modified TDR loans was six years, reflecting expected voluntary and involuntary prepayments.

nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s proprietary modification programs as well as government programs, including U.S. GSE programs, generally provide various concessions to financially troubled borrowers including, but not limited to, interest rate reductions, term or payment extensions and delays of principal and/or interest payments that would otherwise have been required under the terms of the original agreement.

nodes.title: Credit card loan portfolio
nodes.heading: 8.19.7 Credit card loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: The credit card portfolio segment includes credit card loans originated and purchased by the Firm.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Credit card loan portfolio of the Firm (JPMorgan Chase), including originated and purchased credit card loans; excerpt from Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements (2022 Form 10-K).
- Primary credit quality indicator: Delinquency rates, with focus on 30+ days past due as early warning and 90+ days past due as further deterioration. Geographic distribution is also used to assess credit quality.
- Role of credit scores: FICO scores are considered a lagging indicator and not the Firm’s primary credit quality measure. They are refreshed at least quarterly for a statistically significant random sample and used to gauge trends. The Firm generally originates to prime borrowers, though cardholders’ scores can decline over time.
- Delinquency data (still accruing) is presented for loans within the revolving period versus loans converted to term (classified as TDRs), highlighting:
  - December 31, 2022 totals: $185.2B retained loans; 30–89 DPD $1.42B; 90+ DPD $1.27B; 30+ DPD ratio 1.45%; 90+ DPD ratio 0.68%.
  - December 31, 2021 totals: $154.3B retained loans; 30–89 DPD $0.83B; 90+ DPD $0.77B; 30+ DPD ratio 1.04%; 90+ DPD ratio 0.50%.
  - Converted-to-term loans (TDRs) carry much higher delinquency ratios than revolving loans (e.g., 12.56% vs. 1.40% for 30+ DPD in 2022; 4.52% vs. 0.67% for 90+ DPD in 2022).
- Trends: Year-over-year growth in total retained credit card loans and an increase in both 30+ and 90+ days past due ratios from 2021 to 2022.

nodes.title: Wholesale loan portfolio
nodes.heading: 8.19.8 Wholesale loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: Wholesale loans include loans made to a variety of clients, ranging from large corporate and institutional clients to high-net-worth individuals.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Describes the Firm’s wholesale loan portfolio, which serves large corporate and institutional clients as well as high-net-worth individuals.
- Primary credit quality indicator: Internal risk ratings that differentiate risk within the portfolio based on probability of default (PD) and loss given default (LGD), with LGD reflecting collateral and structural support.
- Rating methodology: Management assesses obligor debt capacity, earnings and repayment sources, contingencies, management strength, and industry/geographic factors. Qualitative characteristics generally align with S&P/Moody’s; quantitative measures (PD/LGD) differ due to internal experience.
- Grading framework: Investment-grade corresponds to ratings qualitatively equivalent to BBB-/Baa3 or higher (lower PD/LGD). Noninvestment-grade is split into noncriticized and criticized; criticized is further divided into performing and nonaccrual and aligns with U.S. regulatory categories (special mention, substandard, doubtful). Criticized loans carry higher PD.
- Governance and concentration management: Credit Risk Management reviews ratings regularly and adjusts for new information. The Firm monitors and diversifies industry and client exposures, focusing on sectors with emerging or actual credit concerns.
- Portfolio composition and trends (Dec 31):
  - Total retained wholesale loans rose to $603.7B in 2022 from $560.4B in 2021.
  - Investment-grade totaled $425.4B (70.47% of total) in 2022 vs $410.0B (73.17%) in 2021.
  - Noninvestment-grade increased to $178.3B from $150.3B, including:
    - Noncriticized: $162.6B (vs $137.0B)
    - Criticized performing: $13.7B (vs $11.3B)
    - Criticized nonaccrual: $2.0B (vs $2.1B)
  - Criticized loans as a percent of total: 2.60% in 2022 (vs 2.39% in 2021); criticized nonaccrual: 0.33% (vs 0.37%).
- Category breakouts (2022):
  - Secured by real estate: $126.7B total; $99.6B IG (78.55% IG); criticized 3.08%; nonaccrual 0.19%.
  - Commercial & industrial: $167.7B total; $76.3B IG (45.49% IG); criticized 5.96%; nonaccrual 0.61%; notable rise in noncriticized noninvestment-grade ($81.4B vs $62.0B in 2021).
  - Other: $309.3B total; $249.6B IG (80.70% IG); criticized 0.58%; nonaccrual 0.23%. “Other” includes loans to financial institutions, states/political subdivisions, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies/trusts, and individuals (Global Private Bank and J.P. Morgan Wealth Management).
- Vintage detail: Tables present secured-by-real-estate term loans by origination year and revolving loans (within revolving period or converted to term) for 2022 and 2021, showing IG vs non-IG composition across vintages.
- Footnotes and references: 2021 nonaccruals exclude $127MM of SBA-guaranteed PPP loans 90+ days past due (not material in 2022). References provided for industry concentrations (Note 4) and SPE information (Note 14).

nodes.title: Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses
nodes.heading: 8.20 Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm's financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the Firm’s allowance for credit losses as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
- Describes the three components: (1) allowance for loan losses (retained scored and risk-rated loan portfolios), (2) allowance for lending-related commitments (recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities), and (3) allowance for credit losses on investment securities (recorded within investment securities).
- Notes that all changes in the allowance flow through the provision for credit losses on the income statement.
- Highlights the judgmental and complex nature of estimating the allowance, with at least quarterly reviews by the CRO, CFO, and Controller; acknowledges potential for significant changes due to macroeconomic conditions and forecasts.
- Explains methodology for loans and lending-related commitments: expected credit losses are measured over the remaining expected life of loans and non-cancellable commitments; no allowance for future draws on unconditionally cancellable commitments (e.g., credit cards).
- States treatment of accrued interest: expected losses on credit card accrued interest are included in the loan loss allowance; other accrued interest receivables are not reserved because they are written off by 90 days past due via reversal of interest income.
- Outlines expected life determination using contractual term, prepayments, cancellation features, and options; for credit cards, expected repayments are allocated per CARD Act rules (highest-rate balances paid first).
- Includes expected recoveries of prior or future charge-offs in the estimate, even if this results in a negative allowance.
- Distinguishes collective (portfolio-based) versus individual (asset-specific) assessments based on shared risk characteristics.
- Lists key risk characteristics: for consumer (product type, delinquency, FICO, geography, LTV) and for wholesale (risk rating, delinquency, tenor, collateral, line of business, geography, industry, credit enhancement, product type, facility purpose, payment terms).
- Notes most exposures are collectively assessed (consumer loans, performing risk-rated loans, certain commitments); individual assessments apply to modified PCD loans, TDR or expected TDR modifications, collateral-dependent loans, and nonaccrual risk-rated loans.
- Describes the portfolio-based component: quantitative modeling of delinquency/risk rating migration over expected life, applying credit loss factors (probability of default and loss given default) to estimated exposure at default.

nodes.title: Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lending-related commitments
nodes.heading: 8.20.1 Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lending-related commitments
nodes.start_phrase: The allowance for loan losses and allowance for lending-related commitments represents expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of retained loans and lending-related commitments that are not unconditionally cancellable.
nodes.summary:
This section explains the Firm’s framework for estimating and recording expected credit losses across its financial assets and certain commitments.

- Scope and components: The allowance for credit losses covers (1) allowance for loan losses on retained loan portfolios, (2) allowance for lending-related commitments presented in accounts payable and other liabilities, and (3) allowance on investment securities (see Note 10). All changes flow through the provision for credit losses on the income statement.
- Governance and judgment: The allowance involves significant management judgment, reflecting macroeconomic conditions and forecasts, and is reviewed at least quarterly by the Firm’s CRO, CFO, and Controller. Allowances may change materially with evolving conditions.
- Methodology for loans and lending-related commitments:
  - Measures expected credit losses over the instruments’ remaining expected life for loans and non–unconditionally cancellable commitments.
  - No allowance is recorded for unconditionally cancellable commitments (e.g., credit cards future draws).
  - Accrued interest: Expected losses on credit card loan interest are included in the loan loss allowance; no allowance on other accrued interest receivables because they are written off by 90 days past due via reversal of interest income.
  - Expected life considers contractual term, prepayments, cancellation features, and extension/call options. For funded credit card loans, expected life and payment allocation reflect CARD Act rules (payments applied first to higher-rate balances).
  - Expected credit loss estimates include anticipated recoveries of amounts previously charged off (which can result in a negative allowance).
- Collective vs. individual assessment:
  - Exposures with similar risk characteristics are assessed collectively (portfolio-based component); those without are assessed individually (asset-specific component).
  - Consumer portfolio risk characteristics: product type, delinquency, FICO, geography, and current LTV for collateralized loans.
  - Wholesale portfolio risk characteristics: internal risk rating, delinquency, tenor, collateral level/type, line of business, geography, industry, credit enhancement, product, facility purpose, and payment terms.
  - Portfolio-based component typically covers consumer loans, performing risk-rated loans, and certain lending-related commitments.
  - Asset-specific component applies to modified PCD loans, loans modified or expected to be modified in a TDR, collateral-dependent loans, and risk-rated loans on nonaccrual.
- Portfolio-based quantitative approach: Starts with modeling transitions in delinquency or risk ratings over the expected life, applying credit loss factors to exposure at default. These factors incorporate probability of default and loss given default (loss severity).

nodes.title: Collective and Individual Assessments
nodes.heading: 8.20.2 Collective and Individual Assessments
nodes.start_phrase: When calculating the allowance for loan losses and the allowance for lending-related commitments, the Firm assesses whether exposures share similar risk characteristics.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the Firm’s allowance for credit losses as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining expected life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
- Identifies three components and their balance sheet presentation: (1) allowance for loan losses (separate line), (2) allowance for lending-related commitments (accounts payable and other liabilities), and (3) allowance for credit losses on investment securities (within investment securities).
- States that all changes in the allowance flow through the provision for credit losses in the income statement.
- Emphasizes the judgmental and complex nature of estimating the allowance; governance includes at least quarterly reviews by the Firm’s CRO, CFO, and Controller, with allowances sensitive to macroeconomic conditions and forecasts.
- Notes that policies for loan losses and lending-related commitments are detailed here, while policies for investment securities are in Note 10.
- Methodology for loans and lending-related commitments:
  - Covers expected credit losses over the remaining expected life for retained loans and commitments that are not unconditionally cancellable.
  - No allowance is recorded for future draws on unconditionally cancellable commitments (e.g., credit cards).
  - Expected losses on accrued interest for credit card loans are included in the allowance; other accrued interest receivables are written off no later than 90 days past due by reversing interest income, so no allowance is recorded on them.
  - Expected life reflects contractual term, expected prepayments, cancellation features, and extension/call options; for funded credit card loans, expected life is estimated using payment allocation rules under the CARD Act (highest interest rate balances paid first).
  - Expected recoveries of amounts previously charged off are included and can result in a negative allowance.
- Collective vs. individual assessment:
  - Exposures sharing similar risk characteristics are assessed collectively; significant judgment is applied in defining risk pools.
  - Key consumer risk characteristics: product type, delinquency, current FICO, geography, and current LTV for collateralized loans.
  - Key wholesale risk characteristics: internal risk rating, delinquency, tenor, collateral type/level, line of business, geography, industry, credit enhancement, product type, facility purpose, and payment terms.
  - Most exposures are collectively assessed (portfolio-based component), covering consumer loans, performing risk-rated loans, and certain lending-related commitments.
  - Individual (asset-specific) assessments apply to modified PCD loans, loans modified or expected to be modified in a TDR, collateral-dependent loans, and risk-rated loans on nonaccrual.
- Portfolio-based component mechanics (quantitative framework):
  - Starts with estimating transitions in delinquency status or risk ratings over the instrument’s expected life.
  - Applies credit loss factors to estimated exposure at default; factors reflect probability of default and loss given default.

nodes.title: Portfolio-based component
nodes.heading: 8.20.3 Portfolio-based component
nodes.start_phrase: The portfolio-based component begins with a quantitative calculation that considers the likelihood of the borrower changing delinquency status or moving from one risk rating to another.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and scope: Describes the Firm’s allowance for credit losses (ACL) as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining expected life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
- Components and presentation: 
  - Allowance for loan losses (retained, scored and risk-rated loan portfolios) presented separately on the Consolidated balance sheets.
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments presented in accounts payable and other liabilities.
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities reflected within investment securities (methodology referenced to Note 10).
  - All changes flow through the provision for credit losses in the income statement.
- Governance and judgment: ACL is complex, uncertain, and reviewed at least quarterly by the CRO, CFO, and Controller; subsequent macroeconomic changes may materially impact future ACL levels.
- Methodology for loans and lending-related commitments:
  - Covers expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of loans and non–unconditionally cancellable commitments.
  - No allowance for future draws on unconditionally cancellable commitments (e.g., credit cards).
  - Credit card accrued interest losses included in loan loss allowance; other accrued interest receivables written off by 90 days past due, so no allowance recorded.
  - Expected life determined using contractual term, prepayments, cancellation features, and certain extension/call options; credit card life estimated via payment allocation consistent with the CARD Act (higher-rate balances paid first).
  - Expected losses include anticipated recoveries of prior or future charge-offs, potentially resulting in negative allowance.
- Collective vs. individual assessments:
  - Exposures with similar risk characteristics are collectively assessed; otherwise, assessed individually.
  - Consumer risk characteristics: product type, delinquency, current FICO, geography, and LTV for collateralized loans.
  - Wholesale risk characteristics: risk rating, delinquency, tenor, collateral level/type, line of business, geography, industry, credit enhancement, product type, purpose, and payment terms.
  - Most exposures are collectively assessed (portfolio-based component); individual assessments apply to modified PCD loans, TDRs (or expected TDRs), collateral-dependent loans, and nonaccrual risk-rated loans.
- Portfolio-based component:
  - Quantitative expected loss over instrument life via credit loss factors (probability of default and loss severity) applied to exposure at default.
  - Factors derived from five internal macroeconomic scenarios (central, relative adverse, extreme adverse, relative upside, extreme upside) over an eight-quarter forecast, then a one-year straight-line reversion to long-run historical information.
  - Scenarios are produced through a governed process incorporating Firm outlook, SME input, and market consensus.
  - Qualitative adjustments address model imprecision, emerging risks, trends, and uncertainties (economic/political conditions, underwriting quality, borrower behavior, concentrations, industry/product/portfolio factors).
  - Significant management judgment; results are sensitive to inputs and assumptions.
- Asset-specific component:
  - Individual evaluation for collateral-dependent loans and larger nonaccrual wholesale loans; smaller loans may be aggregated with relevant factors.
  - Measurement generally equals amortized cost minus present value of expected cash flows discounted at original EIR; changes flow through the allowance.
  - For collateral-dependent loans, fair value of collateral less costs to sell determines charge-offs or negative allowance for recoveries.
  - TDRs: incorporates concessions, forgone interest/principal, and redefault risk.
    - Residential real estate: product-specific PDs using credit characteristics with housing price and unemployment assumptions, plus Firm’s redefault experience.
    - Credit cards: projected delinquencies and charge-offs by modification program based on Firm history.
    - Wholesale: management’s expectation of repayment under modified terms.
  - Estimation is highly judgmental given uncertainties in severities, valuations, default/redefault rates, payment timing/prepayments, economic duration, borrower/industry/portfolio dynamics, and insolvency outcomes.

nodes.title: Asset-specific component
nodes.heading: 8.20.4 Asset-specific component
nodes.start_phrase: To determine the asset-specific component of the allowance, collateral-dependent loans (including those loans for which foreclosure is probable) and larger, nonaccrual risk-rated loans in the wholesale portfolio segment are generally evaluated individually, while smaller loans (both scored and risk-rated) are aggregated for evaluation using factors relevant for the respective class of assets.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Firm’s methodology for estimating the allowance for loan losses and lending-related commitments, anchored in a quantitative framework that averages five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios (central, relative adverse, extreme adverse, relative upside, extreme upside) over an eight-quarter forecast, followed by a one-year straight-line reversion to long-run historical conditions. Scenarios are governed and updated by a central forecasting team with inputs from subject matter experts, market consensus, and senior management across businesses and risk functions.
- Explains qualitative adjustments layered onto the quantitative estimate to capture model imprecision, emerging risks, trends, and factors not yet reflected in models. These rely on historical loss experience (including stressed periods) and management judgment about economic/political conditions, underwriting quality, borrower behavior, credit concentrations, and industry/product/portfolio dynamics, acknowledging compounding uncertainties among these factors.
- Emphasizes sensitivity of the allowance to management’s assumptions and inputs; different weightings or alternative assumptions can materially change estimated reserves.
- Details the asset-specific component: collateral-dependent loans and larger nonaccrual risk-rated wholesale loans are evaluated individually; smaller loans are pooled. Measurement generally uses the present value of expected cash flows discounted at the original effective rate; for collateral-dependent loans, fair value of collateral less costs to sell determines charge-offs or negative allowances for recoveries.
- Outlines treatment of loans modified or expected to be modified in TDRs: incorporates modification effects (forgone interest, principal forgiveness, other concessions) and redefault risk. Residential real estate uses product-specific PDs tied to borrower credit characteristics and assumptions on home prices and unemployment, informed by industry data and the Firm’s redefault experience; credit cards use projected delinquencies and charge-offs by modification type; wholesale relies on management’s view of repayment capacity under modified terms.
- Highlights that estimating future cash flows is highly judgmental, depending on loss severities, asset valuations, default/redefault rates, payment timing and prepayments, macroeconomic duration, borrower/industry/portfolio conditions, insolvency outcomes, and other economic factors; many assumptions are subjective and require significant management judgment.

nodes.title: Note 14 – Variable interest entities
nodes.heading: 8.21 Note 14 – Variable interest entities
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 1 on page 164 for a further description of JPMorgan Chase’s accounting policies regarding consolidation of VIEs.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 14 focuses on JPMorgan Chase’s involvement with variable interest entities (VIEs), referencing Note 1 for consolidation accounting policies. It defines “Firm-sponsored” VIEs as those where the Firm is the primary beneficiary, uses the VIE to securitize Firm assets, the VIE issues instruments with the JPMorgan Chase name, or it is a Firm-administered ABCP conduit.

- Business segment overview and activities:
  - Consumer & Community Banking (CCB): 
    - Credit card securitization trusts (securitization of originated credit card receivables).
    - Mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated and purchased residential mortgages).
  - Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB):
    - Mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential, commercial mortgages, other consumer loans).
    - Multi-seller conduits (client funding access and investor-focused structures).
    - Municipal bond vehicles (financing municipal bond investments).
  - Page references provided in the 2022 Form 10-K for each activity.

- Other segments’ involvement:
  - Asset & Wealth Management (AWM): Sponsors/manages funds that may be VIEs; earns asset-based fees; consolidates certain funds when its interests are significant variable interests.
  - Commercial Banking (CB): Provides financing/lending services to entities that may be VIEs but does not control or consolidate them; maximum loss exposure generally limited to loans and commitments.
  - Corporate (including Treasury and CIO): Involved with entities often subject to specialized investment company accounting (generally no consolidation); invests in third-party-issued securities that may be VIEs (e.g., ABS) without power to direct significant activities; Note 10 referenced for investment securities.
  - CIB also invests in and provides financing/services to third-party-sponsored VIEs; pages 251–252 referenced for consolidated VIE assets/liabilities and third-party VIEs.

- Significant Firm-sponsored VIEs—Credit card securitizations:
  - Platform: Chase Issuance Trust.
  - Continuing involvement: Servicing receivables, retaining undivided seller’s interest, retaining certain senior/subordinated securities, maintaining escrow accounts.
  - Consolidation: Firm consolidates the trusts as primary beneficiary due to power to direct significant activities (via servicing and asset transfer/modification decisions) and exposure to potentially significant benefits/losses.
  - Creditor recourse: Securitized receivables and other trust assets are only available to pay trust beneficial interests, not the Firm’s other obligations.
  - Risk retention: Required minimum undivided interest (generally 5%); undivided interests held were $6.1 billion at December 31, 2022, and $7.1 billion at December 31, 2021; an average undivided interest in principal was maintained (amount truncated in excerpt).

nodes.title: Credit card securitizations
nodes.heading: 8.21.1 Credit card securitizations
nodes.start_phrase: CCB’s Card Services business may securitize originated credit card loans, primarily through the Chase Issuance Trust (the “Trust”).
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s disclosures on variable interest entities (VIEs) in Note 14 of its 2022 Form 10-K. It:
- Defines “Firm-sponsored” VIEs as entities where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary, uses the VIE to securitize Firm assets, the VIE issues instruments bearing the Firm’s name, or it is a Firm-administered asset-backed commercial paper conduit.
- Summarizes key Firm-sponsored VIEs by segment:
  - Consumer & Community Banking (CCB): credit card securitization trusts; mortgage securitization trusts.
  - Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB): residential and commercial mortgage and other securitization trusts; multi-seller conduits; municipal bond vehicles.
  - Notes other segments’ involvement: AWM sponsors/manages certain fund VIEs (sometimes consolidated); Commercial Banking provides financing to third-party VIEs (not consolidated; exposure limited to loans/commitments); Corporate/Treasury/CIO invest in third-party VIE securities and generally do not consolidate under specialized investment company accounting. References Note 10 for investment securities and pages 251–252 for consolidated VIEs and third-party-sponsored VIEs.
- Details significant Firm-sponsored credit card securitizations (Chase Issuance Trust):

  - The Firm consolidates these trusts as primary beneficiary due to power over significant activities (servicing, receivable transfers, modifications) and exposure to potentially significant benefits/losses.
  - Trust assets are restricted to trust investors and are not available to Firm creditors.
  - Minimum undivided interest ~5%; undivided interests held were $6.1 billion (2022) and $7.1 billion (2021); average undivided interest in principal receivables was ~62% (2022) and 57% (2021). No senior securities retained; $1.5 billion of subordinated securities retained at both year-ends; amounts eliminated in consolidation.
- Covers Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts:

  - Presents unpaid principal in Firm-sponsored private-label securitization VIEs (both consolidated and with continuing involvement) and JPMorgan Chase’s interests in nonconsolidated VIEs. Continuing involvement includes servicing, retained senior/subordinated interests (including risk retention), recourse/guarantees, and derivatives. Maximum loss on retained/purchased interests is limited to carrying value.
  - 12/31/2022: total securitization VIE assets $230.0B; consolidated $0.8B; nonconsolidated with continuing involvement $165.8B. JPMorgan Chase interests in nonconsolidated VIEs totaled $9.6B (trading $1.6B; investment securities $7.3B; other financial assets $0.7B). By collateral: Prime/Alt-A/option ARM $2.7B of interests; Subprime ~$0.01B; Commercial and other $6.9B.
  - 12/31/2021: total securitization VIE assets $216.7B; consolidated $1.0B; nonconsolidated with continuing involvement $146.3B. JPMorgan Chase interests totaled $6.2B (trading $1.6B; investment securities $4.0B; other $0.6B).
  - Credit quality: 84% (2022) and 79% (2021) of retained securitization interests rated A or better. Prime RMBS retained interests: $2.6B investment-grade (2022) vs. $1.6B investment-grade and $131MM non-investment grade (2021). Commercial/other retained interests: $5.8B investment-grade and $1.1B non-investment grade (2022); $3.5B investment-grade and $929MM non-investment grade (2021).
  - Notes key exclusions (e.g., GSE/government securitizations) and that certain market-making positions are excluded from presented totals.
