Due to opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive case continues with partial class certification granted in 2021. Some opting-out merchants filed individual suits; many have been settled, covering over half of combined Visa/Mastercard sales volume.
- Jeffrey Epstein litigation: Two SDNY lawsuits allege JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. facilitated Epstein’s unlawful conduct by providing banking services until 2013—one a putative class action by a victim (filed November 2022), and one by the U.S. Virgin Islands (filed December 2022). The bank has moved to dismiss both.
- LIBOR and benchmark rate matters: The Firm has responded to global inquiries regarding LIBOR and EURIBOR. A Swiss Competition Commission investigation related to EURIBOR continues. The European Commission issued a 2016 decision finding an antitrust infringement related to EURIBOR; the Firm has appealed.

nodes.title: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation
nodes.heading: 8.37.8 LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase has responded to inquiries from various governmental agencies and entities around the world relating primarily to the British Bankers Association’s (“BBA”) London Interbank Offered Rate (“LIBOR”) for various currencies and the European Banking Federation’s Euro Interbank Offered Rate (“EURIBOR”).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of significant legal and regulatory matters disclosed in JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s 2022 Form 10-K, including case outcomes, settlements, ongoing investigations, and class action statuses.
- FRN litigation: Trial concluded with full dismissal in favor of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; appeal denied and matter closed in 2022.
- Foreign exchange (FX) matters: Prior regulatory settlements, including a 2015 antitrust guilty plea; DOL exemptions granted to maintain ERISA QPAM status during the 10-year disqualification period; remaining governmental inquiry in South Africa pending before the Competition Tribunal.
- FX civil litigation: U.S. class settlement approved (2018); additional resolutions with opt-outs reached in Dec 2022; ongoing putative consumer class action; international actions in the U.K., Israel, the Netherlands, Brazil, and Australia, with partial resolutions/appeals and a settlement in principle in Israel subject to court approval.
- Interchange fee litigation: Merchant suits against Visa, Mastercard, and banks; amended monetary class settlement (2018) adding $900 million to the prior $5.3 billion escrow, approved in 2019; appeals pending; $700 million returned to defendants based on opt-outs; injunctive case continues with partial class certification (2021); many individual opt-out merchant cases settled.
- Jeffrey Epstein litigation: Two SDNY suits alleging JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. facilitated Epstein’s conduct—one putative class by a victim (Nov 2022) and one by the U.S. Virgin Islands (Dec 2022); motions to dismiss filed.
- LIBOR and benchmark rates: Ongoing inquiries regarding LIBOR/EURIBOR; Swiss competition probe continues; 2016 European Commission decision appealed and pending; multiple civil actions with mixed outcomes—some dismissals, class certification granted for certain antitrust claims related to bonds and swaps; ICE-era USD LIBOR class action dismissed; new antitrust suit dismissed in Sept 2022 with amended complaint challenged; settlements relating to SIBOR/SOR and BBSW approved (Nov 2022); Swiss franc LIBOR settlement pending approval.
- Securities lending antitrust litigation: Putative class action alleging a conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading; motion to dismiss denied; plaintiffs seek class certification, which defendants oppose.
- Shareholder litigation: Putative class and derivative actions tied to historical trading practices (precious metals/U.S. Treasuries) and fiduciary/recordkeeping oversight; one NY derivative suit dismissed (Dec 2022); additional EDNY derivative and class actions pending with motions to dismiss filed or pending.
- General litigation posture: Firm asserts meritorious defenses and intends vigorous defense; numerous additional proceedings may arise.
- Legal reserves and expenses: Reserves established consistent with U.S. GAAP when loss is probable and estimable; quarterly reassessment; legal expenses were $266 million (2022), $426 million (2021), and $1.1 billion (2020); reserves may be adjusted in the future.

nodes.title: Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation
nodes.heading: 8.37.9 Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, J.P. Morgan Prime, Inc., and J.P. Morgan Strategic Securities Lending Corp. are named as defendants in a putative class action filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York.
nodes.summary:
- Ongoing benchmark-rate litigation: JPMorgan is involved in multiple individual and putative class actions tied to benchmark rates (including U.S. dollar LIBOR). For the BBA-administered period, some suits were dismissed or resolved; others continue. The court certified antitrust classes for bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants. A consolidated class action for the ICE-administered LIBOR period was dismissed. An individual antitrust case alleging LIBOR manipulation and market monopolization was dismissed in September 2022; plaintiffs filed an amended complaint that defendants moved to dismiss. Settlements related to SIBOR/SOR and BBSW received final approval in November 2022; a Swiss franc LIBOR settlement awaits approval. An appeal related to a European General Court decision is pending.
- Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation: Several JPMorgan entities are defendants in an SDNY putative class action alleging a conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading in securities lending. The motion to dismiss was denied; plaintiffs have moved for class certification, which defendants oppose.
- Shareholder litigation: Multiple shareholder class and derivative actions target the Firm, its board, and certain officers. Some relate to historical trading practices in precious metals and U.S. Treasuries, resolved with DOJ, CFTC, and SEC in September 2020, and separate OCC fiduciary matters in November 2020. A New York state derivative case (breach of fiduciary duty/unjust enrichment) was dismissed in December 2022. Another EDNY derivative case (breach of fiduciary duty/contribution; demand futility) remains pending. A consolidated EDNY shareholder class action alleges the Firm’s SEC filings were materially misleading for not disclosing historical trading practices; defendants moved to dismiss the amended complaint. A separate EDNY derivative action alleges inadequate board oversight of records preservation tied to SEC/CFTC resolutions; a motion to dismiss is pending.
- General legal posture and reserves: The Firm faces numerous additional legal proceedings, asserts meritorious defenses, and intends to defend vigorously. It accrues litigation reserves under U.S. GAAP when losses are probable and estimable, reassessing quarterly. Legal expenses were $266 million (2022), $426 million (2021), and $1.1 billion (2020), and reserves may be adjusted in the future.

nodes.title: Shareholder Litigation
nodes.heading: 8.37.10 Shareholder Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: Several shareholder putative class actions, as well as shareholder derivative actions purporting to act on behalf of the Firm, have been filed against the Firm, its Board of Directors and certain of its current and former officers.
nodes.summary:
- Ongoing benchmark-rate litigation: multiple individual and putative class actions tied to U.S. dollar LIBOR and other benchmarks. Some LIBOR cases dismissed, others progressing; SDNY certified an antitrust class for bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants; a consolidated LIBOR case for the ICE administration period was dismissed. An individual-plaintiff antitrust case over LIBOR was dismissed in Sept 2022; plaintiffs refiled and defendants moved to dismiss. Settlements for SIBOR/SOR and Australian BBSW received final approval in Nov 2022; a Swiss franc LIBOR settlement remains subject to court approval. Reference to a pending appeal before the European General Court.
- Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation: JPMorgan entities are defendants in an SDNY putative class action alleging a conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading for securities lending. Motion to dismiss was denied; plaintiffs seek class certification, which defendants oppose.
- Shareholder litigation: multiple shareholder class and derivative actions against the Firm, its Board, and certain officers.
  - Suits tied to historical precious metals and U.S. Treasuries trading practices resolved with DOJ/CFTC/SEC (Sept 2020) and OCC fiduciary matters (Nov 2020). A New York state derivative case was dismissed in Dec 2022. An E.D.N.Y. derivative case filed Dec 2022 alleges breach of fiduciary duty and contribution with demand futility. A consolidated E.D.N.Y. shareholder class action alleges SEC filings were misleading by omitting information about those practices; defendants moved to dismiss. A separate E.D.N.Y. derivative suit (filed Mar 2022) alleges oversight failures on records preservation tied to SEC/CFTC resolutions; motion to dismiss pending.
- Broad litigation posture: Numerous additional legal proceedings exist; the Firm asserts meritorious defenses and intends to defend vigorously; new matters may arise.
- Reserves and expenses: Litigation reserves established for several hundred matters; accruals follow U.S. GAAP (probable and reasonably estimable), reviewed quarterly. Legal expense was $266 million (2022), $426 million (2021), and $1.1 billion (2020); reserves may change.
- Risk assessment: Outcomes are uncertain and could exceed reserves or have reputational impacts. Based on current knowledge, counsel input, existing reserves, and estimated loss ranges, the Firm does not expect other pending matters to have a material adverse effect on consolidated financial condition, though particular-period results could be materially affected depending on loss size and earnings.

nodes.title: Note 32 – Business segments
nodes.heading: 8.39 Note 32 – Business segments
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
nodes.summary:
The partial document is Note 32 – Business segments from JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10‑K. It explains how the Firm is organized and reports performance, and summarizes each segment’s scope and offerings.

- Management and reporting: The Firm is managed on a line-of-business basis with four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment. Segments are defined by products/services or customer type, aligned with how the Operating Committee evaluates financial information. Results are presented on a managed basis.

- Consumer & Community Banking: Serves consumers and small businesses through branches, ATMs, digital and phone channels. Organized into:
  - Banking & Wealth Management: deposits, investments, lending, cash management, payments, and services.
  - Home Lending: mortgage origination and servicing; residential mortgage and home equity portfolios.
  - Card Services & Auto: credit cards and travel services; auto loans and leases.

- Corporate & Investment Bank: Comprises Banking and Markets & Securities Services, serving corporations, investors, financial institutions, merchants, and government/municipal entities globally.
  - Banking: investment banking across capital markets (advisory, capital raising, loan origination/syndication) and Payments (global payments and cross‑border financing).
  - Markets & Securities Services: Markets (global market‑making in cash and derivatives, risk management solutions, prime brokerage, research) and Securities Services (custody, fund accounting/administration, securities lending) for asset managers, insurers, and funds.

- Commercial Banking: Provides lending, payments, investment banking, and asset management across:
  - Middle Market Banking (small/midsize companies, local governments, nonprofits),
  - Corporate Client Banking (large corporations),
  - Commercial Real Estate Banking (investors, developers, and property owners across multifamily, office, retail, industrial, affordable housing).
  - “Other” captures amounts not aligned to a primary client segment.

- Asset & Wealth Management: A global leader with $4.0 trillion in client assets.
  - Asset Management: multi‑asset solutions across equities, fixed income, alternatives, and money markets for institutional and retail clients.
  - Global Private Bank: retirement, brokerage, custody, estate planning, lending, deposits, and investment management for high‑net‑worth clients.
  - Majority of client assets are actively managed.

- Corporate segment: Includes Treasury and Chief Investment Office (CIO) and Other Corporate.
  - Treasury and CIO: manages liquidity, funding, capital, and structural interest rate and foreign exchange risks.
  - Other Corporate: centrally managed staff functions and firm‑wide initiatives (e.g., Real Estate, Technology, Legal, Corporate Finance, HR, Internal Audit, Risk Management, Compliance, Control Management, Corporate Responsibility).

nodes.title: Segment results

- Capital allocation framework: Capital is allocated to business segments considering peer capital levels and regulatory requirements; performance measured by ROE with internal targets.   - Assets: deposits with banks; federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; trading assets – debt instruments; investment securities; loans; all other interest-earning assets.
  - Liabilities: interest-bearing deposits; federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; trading liabilities – debt, short-term and all other interest-bearing liabilities; beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs; long-term debt.
- Notable 2022 category rates: loans (U.S. 4.97%, non-U.S. 3.41%); investment securities (U.S. 1.76%, non-U.S. 1.96%); trading assets – debt instruments (~3.2%); interest-bearing deposits remained relatively low (U.S. 0.52%, non-U.S. 0.78%).

- Volume/rate attribution analysis:
  - Methodology: changes in NII are split into volume vs. rate effects using annual averages; when not isolatable, changes are allocated to volume; results reflect market rate moves and product mix; analysis is category-specific and judgmental.
  - 2022 vs. 2021: NII up $14.4B, primarily rate-driven (+$10.8B) with additional volume benefit (+$3.6B). Interest income up $34.9B (mostly rates), offset by higher interest expense up $20.5B (mostly rates).
  - 2021 vs. 2020: NII down $2.24B; rate effects (-$4.01B) more than offset volume gains (+$1.77B). Interest income decreased $6.65B (rate-driven) while interest expense fell $4.41B.
- Footnotes and clarifications: negative interest on securities borrowed reflects fees netting; trading liabilities include commercial paper; noninterest-bearing liabilities figure represents funding of interest-earning assets.

nodes.title: Changes in net interest income, volume and rate analysis
nodes.heading: Changes in net interest income, volume and rate analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The attribution between volume and rate is calculated using annual average balances for each category of assets and liabilities shown in the table and the corresponding annual rates (refer to pages 292-296 for more information on average balances and rates).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: A volume and rate attribution of net interest income, presented on a taxable‑equivalent basis, comparing 2022 vs. 2021 and 2021 vs. 2020.
- Methodology highlights:
  - Uses annual average balances and annual rates by asset/liability category.
  - When changes can’t be distinctly assigned to rate or volume, they are assigned to volume.
  - Rates reflect both market rate movements and product mix shifts.
  - Analysis is done by category independently (does not consider asset–liability funding relationships), so different groupings could yield different attributions; allocations are inherently judgmental.
  - Notes: negative interest for securities borrowed reflects netting with prime brokerage fees; trading liabilities include commercial paper.
- Scope of categories with U.S. and Non‑U.S. breakouts:
  - Interest‑earning assets: deposits with banks; federal funds sold and resale agreements; securities borrowed; trading assets (debt); investment securities; loans; other interest‑earning assets.
  - Interest‑bearing liabilities: interest‑bearing deposits; federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; trading liabilities and other interest‑bearing liabilities; beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs; long‑term debt.
- Key outcomes:
  - 2022 vs. 2021: Net interest income rose by about $14.4B, driven primarily by higher rates (rate +$10.8B; volume +$3.6B). Interest income increased substantially on higher rates; interest expense also rose notably due to higher rates.
  - 2021 vs. 2020: Net interest income declined by about $2.2B, largely from lower rates (rate −$4.0B) partially offset by volume (+$1.8B).
- Additional content: Excerpts from the 2022 Form 10‑K glossary defining numerous financial, regulatory, product, and accounting terms and acronyms (e.g., ABS, AFS, ALCO, amortized cost, AOCI, ARM, AUM, CECL, CET1 capital, CCP, CDS, client assets/deposits/investment assets, CLO, CLTV, collateral‑dependent, Commercial Card, credit derivatives and ISDA Determinations Committee, beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs, etc.).

nodes.title: Description of Depositary Shares
nodes.heading: 37.2.1 Description of Depositary Shares
nodes.start_phrase: The following summary of the terms of the depositary shares representing each series of the Listed Preferred Stock is not complete.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory implications under Federal Reserve Board rules if preferred stock gains voting rights due to dividend arrears: the series may be deemed a class of voting securities; holders of 25% (or 5% with controlling influence) may be regulated as bank holding companies under the Bank Holding Company Act; bank holding companies may need prior FRB approval to acquire/retain 5% or more; non-bank persons may need to notify the FRB before acquiring/retaining 10% or more.
- Depositary shares overview: each depositary share equals 1/400th of a share of the applicable Listed Preferred Stock and carries proportional powers, preferences, and rights; Computershare Inc. serves as depositary under deposit agreements filed on Form 8-K.
- Dividends and distributions: each depositary share receives 1/400th of dividends on the underlying preferred; depositary distributes cash and non-cash property (selling and distributing proceeds if necessary); record dates match the underlying; amounts may be reduced by required withholding.
- Redemption: redemption of underlying preferred stock triggers redemption of corresponding depositary shares at 1/400th of the preferred stock redemption price plus declared and unpaid dividends (no accumulation of undeclared dividends); partial redemptions allocated pro rata or by lot; 30–60 days’ notice; DTC procedures apply for book-entry holdings.
- Voting: depositary shares confer 1/400th of a vote per share when the underlying preferred has voting rights; depositary forwards meeting materials, solicits instructions, votes as instructed, and abstains absent instructions.
- Withdrawal of preferred shares: holders may surrender receipts and pay applicable fees/taxes to withdraw whole shares only; any non-whole remainder continues as depositary receipts; withdrawn shares cannot be re-deposited for depositary shares.
- Form and notices: preferred issued in registered form to the depositary; depositary shares issued in book-entry form through DTC; depositary forwards issuer reports, notices, and communications to holders.
- Amendment and termination of deposit agreements: amendments permitted; any materially adverse change requires approval by a majority of affected depositary shares; termination only if all depositary shares are redeemed or after final distribution of the underlying preferred upon liquidation/dissolution/winding up.
- Charges: issuer pays taxes/charges arising from the existence of the depositary arrangements, initial deposit, and redemptions; holders pay transfer taxes and other charges as specified in the deposit agreement.
- Depositary changes: depositary may resign and issuer may remove it; effectiveness occurs upon acceptance by a successor appointed within 60 days.
- Miscellaneous: depositary and issuer have limited liability, rely on counsel/accountants and competent sources, and require indemnity before prosecuting/defending related proceedings.
- Specific series details: 5.75% Non-Cumulative Preferred Stock, Series DD—169,625 shares issued on September 21, 2018, $1 par value, $10,000 liquidation preference per share; represented by depositary shares, each equal to 1/400th of a preferred share.
